Reverse transcription of the mature, spliced and polyadenylated mRNA into a cDNA, which subsequently integrated into the genome.
explanation: Every listed feature points to a processed pseudogene generated by retrotransposition. The absence of introns and exact colinearity with the mature mRNA show the template had already been spliced; the ~30-adenine tract corresponds to the mRNA's poly-A tail copied into DNA; the short flanking direct repeats are the target-site duplications created when the new DNA integrated; and the copy lies elsewhere in the genome and is non-transcribed (it lacks its own promoter). Producing a DNA copy from an RNA template requires reverse transcriptase, so the copy arose by reverse transcription of the mature mRNA into cDNA followed by insertion into the genome. DNA-level mechanisms (unequal crossing over, replication duplication) would copy the introns and place the duplicate adjacent to the original; reverse transcribing the pre-mRNA would retain the introns; and RNA cannot be inserted directly into DNA without a reverse-transcription step.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: introns are removed from RNA by the spliceosome, not excised from genomic DNA. There is no cellular mechanism that cleanly deletes introns from DNA, and this route would not generate a 3' poly-A tract or flanking direct repeats.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: RNA cannot be covalently ligated directly into chromosomal DNA. Generating a DNA copy from an RNA template necessarily requires reverse transcriptase, i.e. a DNA (cDNA) intermediate.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: unequal crossing over duplicates DNA and would therefore copy the introns as well, and it typically places the duplicate next to the original — not on a different chromosome, and with no poly-A tract or target-site repeats.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: if the pre-mRNA (before splicing) had been the template, the introns would still be present in the copy. The observed complete absence of introns shows the template was the already-spliced mature mRNA.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: the intronless, mRNA-colinear sequence with a 3' poly-A tract and flanking direct repeats is a processed pseudogene, made by reverse transcribing the fully processed mRNA into cDNA that then integrated into the genome.

subtopic: Signal amplification: multiplicative gain through a GPCR-cAMP-PKA enzyme cascade with a non-catalytic binding step
learningObjective: Quantify the amplification produced by a hormone-triggered enzyme cascade, correctly distinguishing catalytic (amplifying) steps from a stoichiometric binding step that does not amplify.
explanation: Follow the cascade one step at a time, amplifying only at catalytic steps. One receptor activates 50 Gs, each activating one adenylyl cyclase, giving 50 active adenylyl cyclase molecules. Each makes 200 cyclic AMP, so 50 x 200 = 10 000 cyclic AMP. The activation of PKA is a stoichiometric BINDING step, not a catalytic one: 4 cyclic AMP are consumed per PKA, so 10 000 / 4 = 2 500 active PKA. Each active PKA is again catalytic, phosphorylating 100 phosphorylase kinase molecules: 2 500 x 100 = 250 000. The key trap is treating the 4:1 cyclic-AMP-to-PKA binding ratio as though it amplifies.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 1 000 000 comes from treating the cyclic-AMP-to-PKA step as 1:1 (50 x 200 x 100), i.e. wrongly assuming every cyclic AMP activates its own PKA and ignoring that 4 are needed per PKA.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 10 000 is the number of cyclic AMP molecules; the candidate stopped at the second messenger and ignored the two downstream steps (PKA activation and phosphorylase kinase phosphorylation).
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 2 500 is the number of active PKA molecules; the candidate forgot the final catalytic step in which each PKA phosphorylates 100 phosphorylase kinase molecules.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 500 000 comes from dividing by 2 rather than 4 at the binding step (assuming 2 cyclic AMP per PKA), a common misremembering of the activation stoichiometry.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: 50 Gs -> 50 adenylyl cyclase -> 50 x 200 = 10 000 cyclic AMP -> 10 000/4 = 2 500 PKA -> 2 500 x 100 = 250 000 phosphorylase kinase.

subtopic: Gq-phospholipase C-IP3 pathway: calcium ions as a second messenger released from the endoplasmic reticulum
learningObjective: Interpret pharmacological and ionic-environment evidence to identify the Gq/phospholipase C/IP3 pathway and recognise that the resulting Ca2+ signal originates from intracellular stores.
choices: Diacylglycerol produced by phospholipase C diffuses to the endoplasmic reticulum and directly opens its Ca2+ release channels.
The receptor activates Gq and phospholipase C, generating IP3, which opens channels in the endoplasmic reticulum and releases Ca2+ from intracellular stores.
Membrane depolarisation opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, allowing Ca2+ to flow in from the extracellular fluid.
The hormone diffuses through the plasma membrane and binds an intracellular receptor that opens Ca2+ channels in the endoplasmic reticulum.
The receptor activates Gs and adenylyl cyclase, raising cyclic AMP, which opens Ca2+ channels in the plasma membrane.
explanation: The three clues pin down the pathway. Because the Ca2+ rise persists in Ca2+-free medium, the Ca2+ must come from an INTERNAL store (the endoplasmic reticulum), not from outside. Because it is blocked by a phospholipase C inhibitor but not an adenylyl cyclase inhibitor, the pathway runs through Gq -> phospholipase C, not Gs -> cyclic AMP. Phospholipase C cleaves PIP2 into IP3 and diacylglycerol; the water-soluble IP3 diffuses to the endoplasmic reticulum and opens IP3-gated Ca2+ channels, releasing stored Ca2+. Option B captures exactly this.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: it is IP3, not diacylglycerol, that opens the endoplasmic-reticulum Ca2+ channels (diacylglycerol activates protein kinase C at the membrane); this swaps the roles of the two phospholipase C products.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: Gq -> phospholipase C -> IP3 releases Ca2+ from the endoplasmic reticulum, consistent with persistence in Ca2+-free medium, block by phospholipase C inhibitor, and insensitivity to adenylyl cyclase inhibition.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: voltage-gated influx would require extracellular Ca2+ (contradicted by the Ca2+-free result) and would not be blocked by a phospholipase C inhibitor; reflects defaulting to the excitable-cell depolarisation model.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: this describes a steroid-type intracellular-receptor mechanism, which would not depend on a cell-surface GPCR or on phospholipase C activity; reflects confusing peptide/GPCR signalling with lipophilic-hormone action.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: a Gs/adenylyl cyclase/cyclic AMP mechanism would be blocked by the adenylyl cyclase inhibitor (it is not), and reliance on plasma-membrane influx contradicts the Ca2+-free-medium result; reflects conflating the cyclic AMP pathway with Ca2+ signalling.

subtopic: Steroid vs peptide hormone action: intracellular receptor and gene transcription versus membrane receptor and second messenger, distinguished by sensitivity to a transcription inhibitor
learningObjective: Use response latency and sensitivity to a transcription inhibitor to distinguish the intracellular-receptor/gene-regulation mechanism of steroid hormones from the membrane-receptor/second-messenger mechanism of peptide hormones.
stem: Two hormones act on the same target cell. Hormone P produces a measurable response within seconds, and this response is unaffected by a drug that blocks all new mRNA synthesis. Hormone Q produces a response only after several hours, and this response is completely prevented by the same drug. Which conclusion is best supported by these findings?
choices: P is a steroid hormone that crosses the plasma membrane, because its lipid solubility is what allows such a rapid response.
Q is a steroid hormone acting through an intracellular receptor that regulates gene transcription, whereas P acts through a membrane receptor and second messengers on proteins that already exist.
Both P and Q must enter the cytoplasm and bind intracellular receptors in order to exert their effects.
The drug blocks P's response because peptide hormones ultimately exert all of their effects by switching on new genes.
Q acts by binding a cell-surface receptor and generating a second messenger such as cyclic AMP.
explanation: The distinguishing feature is dependence on new mRNA synthesis. Hormone Q is slow and is abolished when transcription is blocked, which is the signature of a steroid hormone: it diffuses through the membrane, binds an intracellular receptor, and the hormone-receptor complex alters gene transcription, so the effect requires making new mRNA and protein and takes hours. Hormone P is fast and transcription-independent, the signature of a peptide hormone acting via a surface receptor and a second messenger that modifies pre-existing enzymes/proteins (e.g. by phosphorylation). Option D states both correctly.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: it labels the fast hormone as the steroid; steroids are in fact the SLOW hormones because their action requires gene transcription, not because lipid solubility gives speed. This is the classic 'lipid-soluble means fast' misconception.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: transcription-dependent slow response = steroid via intracellular receptor and gene regulation (Q); transcription-independent rapid response = peptide via membrane receptor and second messengers acting on existing proteins (P).
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: only the steroid (Q) enters the cell; the peptide (P) acts at the surface, as shown by its transcription-independent rapid response. Reflects the belief that all hormones use intracellular receptors.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: P's response is explicitly unaffected by the transcription blocker, so it cannot depend on new gene expression; reflects the misconception that peptide hormones act mainly by inducing transcription.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: Q is the transcription-dependent, slow-acting hormone (a steroid), so it does not work through a surface receptor and cyclic AMP; this mis-assigns the second-messenger mechanism to the steroid.

subtopic: Receptor tyrosine kinase: ligand-induced dimerisation and trans-autophosphorylation, and the dominant-negative effect of a kinase-dead mutant
learningObjective: Combine the trans-autophosphorylation mechanism of receptor tyrosine kinases with simple combinatorial probability to predict the dominant-negative effect of a kinase-dead receptor co-expressed with wild-type receptor.
stem:
A receptor tyrosine kinase is activated when a ligand causes two receptor molecules to form a dimer; the two kinase domains in a dimer then phosphorylate each other (trans-autophosphorylation), and a dimer can transmit a downstream signal only if BOTH of its partners have functional kinase activity.

A cell is engineered to express equal numbers of two forms of this receptor: the normal (wild-type) form and a 'kinase-dead' mutant that binds ligand and dimerises normally but has no catalytic activity. The two forms dimerise with each other at random. Compared with a control cell that expresses the same total number of receptors, all wild-type, the level of downstream signalling in the engineered cell is expected to be approximately:
choices: 100% (essentially unchanged)
explanation: Because the two forms are present in equal amounts and pair at random, each position in a dimer is wild-type (W) or dead (D) with probability 1/2. The four equally likely dimers are WW, WD, DW, DD, each 1/4. Only a dimer in which both partners are catalytically active can signal, i.e. only WW = 1/4 = 25%. Every dimer containing at least one dead subunit cannot complete trans-autophosphorylation, so the mutant 'poisons' the heterodimers. This is why a kinase-dead receptor is dominant-negative: it drops signalling to about a quarter of normal, far more than the 50% one might naively expect from losing half the receptors.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: assumes the mutant is simply a passive loss-of-function (recessive) so the remaining wild-type works normally; it ignores that mutant subunits inactivate the heterodimers they join.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 0% over-applies the dominant-negative idea; wild-type/wild-type homodimers (1/4 of all dimers) still form and signal, so activity is reduced but not abolished.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 50% treats the receptors individually ('half are mutant, so half the signal') and ignores that signalling requires pairs of active subunits, i.e. it neglects the dimerisation combinatorics.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 75% is the fraction of dimers containing at least one wild-type subunit (WW+WD+DW); it incorrectly assumes any dimer with one good partner can signal, whereas both partners must be active.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: only WW dimers (1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4) are fully active, giving about 25% of control signalling and demonstrating the dominant-negative effect.

subtopic: Apoptosis: the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway, cytochrome c/apoptosome/caspase activation and Bcl-2 regulation, contrasted with the extrinsic pathway and with necrosis
learningObjective: Interpret experimental evidence to order the events of the intrinsic apoptotic pathway, identify Bcl-2 as an upstream anti-apoptotic regulator, and distinguish apoptosis from the extrinsic pathway and from necrosis.
stem: In cells triggered to undergo apoptosis by severe, irreparable DNA damage, cytochrome c is detected in the cytosol before the executioner caspase (caspase-3) becomes active. Over-expression of the protein Bcl-2 prevents the appearance of cytosolic cytochrome c and blocks cell death. Which interpretation of these observations is correct?
choices: Bcl-2 is a pro-apoptotic protein that forms pores in the mitochondrial membrane to release cytochrome c into the cytosol.
The cells swell and burst, releasing cytochrome c to provoke inflammation, as is characteristic of apoptosis.
Activation of caspase-3 causes cytochrome c to be released from the mitochondria, which then inflicts the DNA damage that starts the process.
This is the extrinsic pathway, in which a death ligand binds a surface receptor and activates caspase-8 independently of the mitochondria.

Cytochrome c released from the mitochondria promotes assembly of a complex (the apoptosome) that activates an initiator caspase upstream of caspase-3; Bcl-2 acts earlier still, by preventing cytochrome c release.
explanation: DNA damage triggers the INTRINSIC (mitochondrial) apoptotic pathway. Pro-apoptotic proteins permeabilise the mitochondrial outer membrane, releasing cytochrome c into the cytosol; cytochrome c binds Apaf-1 to form the apoptosome, which activates the initiator caspase (caspase-9), which in turn activates the executioner caspase-3. The observed order (cytochrome c before caspase-3) fits this cascade. Bcl-2 is ANTI-apoptotic and acts upstream by preventing cytochrome c release, which is exactly why over-expressing it blocks both cytosolic cytochrome c and death. Option A states both the sequence and Bcl-2's role correctly.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: Bcl-2 is ANTI-apoptotic and preserves mitochondrial integrity; the pore-forming, cytochrome-c-releasing role belongs to pro-apoptotic proteins such as Bax/Bak. This confuses Bcl-2 with its antagonists.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: swelling, bursting and inflammation describe NECROSIS; apoptosis is a controlled process with cell shrinkage and no inflammatory release, and cytochrome c acts as an intracellular signal rather than an inflammatory mediator.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: this reverses cause and effect; cytochrome c release is upstream of caspase-3, not caused by it, and the DNA damage is the initiating stimulus, not a consequence of caspase activity.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: a DNA-damage trigger with cytochrome c release and Bcl-2 sensitivity defines the intrinsic pathway; the extrinsic (death-receptor/caspase-8) pathway is mitochondrion-independent, so the label is incorrect.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: cytochrome c -> apoptosome -> initiator caspase (caspase-9) -> executioner caspase-3 is the intrinsic pathway order, and Bcl-2 blocks apoptosis upstream by preventing cytochrome c release.

subtopic: Skeletal-muscle contraction: sliding-filament theory and sarcomere band changes
learningObjective: Apply the sliding-filament model quantitatively to predict which sarcomere bands change and by how much during contraction, recognising that filament lengths are invariant.
stem: A relaxed skeletal-muscle sarcomere is 2.6 μm long. Its thick filaments are 1.6 μm long (defining the A band) and each thin filament is 1.0 μm long, extending inward from its Z line. The muscle is stimulated and the sarcomere shortens to 2.0 μm. Assuming the filaments themselves do not change length, what are the lengths of the A band and the H zone in the contracted sarcomere?
choices: A band 1.6 μm; H zone 0.8 μm
A band 1.0 μm; H zone 0 μm
A band 1.6 μm; H zone 0 μm
A band 1.6 μm; H zone 0.3 μm
A band 1.6 μm; H zone 0.6 μm
explanation: In the sliding-filament model the filaments do not shorten; the thin filaments slide over the stationary thick filaments. The A band is simply the length of the thick filament, so it remains 1.6 μm at every sarcomere length. The H zone is the central part of the thick filament that no thin filament overlaps. Measuring from the sarcomere centre (M line), each thick filament reaches ±0.8 μm and each thin-filament tip lies at (L/2 − 1.0) μm from the centre, so the H zone width = 2 × (L/2 − 1.0) = L − 2.0. At the relaxed length L = 2.6 μm the H zone is 0.6 μm; at L = 2.0 μm the H zone = 2.0 − 2.0 = 0 μm — the two sets of thin-filament tips just meet at the M line. Hence A band 1.6 μm (unchanged) and H zone 0 μm.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: makes the H zone widen to 0.8 μm. During contraction the H zone narrows (and disappears), never widens. Misconception: reversing the direction of filament sliding, i.e. confusing contraction with stretch/relaxation.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: the A band equals the thick-filament length and cannot change, because myofilaments do not shorten during contraction. This option subtracts the whole 0.6 μm of sarcomere shortening from the A band. Misconception: believing the filaments (and therefore the A band) physically contract rather than slide.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: the A band stays at the thick-filament length of 1.6 μm, and the H zone width = L − 2.0 = 2.0 − 2.0 = 0 μm because the thin-filament tips meet at the M line.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 0.3 μm results from shrinking the H zone by only half of the sarcomere's shortening (0.6/2). The H zone actually shortens by the full 0.6 μm (0.3 μm of sliding at each end). Misconception: counting the sliding at only one Z line instead of both.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: keeps the H zone at its relaxed 0.6 μm value. The H zone must shrink as the thin filaments slide toward the centre. Misconception: treating the H zone as a fixed structure independent of sarcomere length.

subtopic: Visual phototransduction: the dark current and the cGMP-gated cation channel
learningObjective: Reason about the mechanism of rod phototransduction to predict how locking the cGMP-gated channel open uncouples the light-activated cascade from the membrane response.
stem: In vertebrate rod photoreceptors, cytoplasmic cGMP holds cation channels open in the dark, producing a steady inward 'dark current' that keeps the cell depolarised and releasing glutamate continuously. Absorption of light triggers a cascade (rhodopsin → transducin → phosphodiesterase) that lowers cGMP. A researcher applies a non-hydrolysable analogue of cGMP that keeps the cation channels open even when the light-activated phosphodiesterase is fully active. When a bright flash of light is delivered to a rod treated in this way, the rod membrane potential will most likely:
choices: hyperpolarise transiently and then depolarise, because guanylate cyclase resynthesises cGMP
depolarise further, because light increases the cation permeability of the membrane
lose its dark current entirely, because the analogue blocks the cation channel
remain depolarised, because the cation channels stay open despite the fall in cytoplasmic cGMP
hyperpolarise just as strongly as an untreated rod, because rhodopsin still bleaches normally
explanation: A rod's light response is a HYPERPOLARISATION caused by CLOSURE of the cGMP-gated cation channels: light lowers cGMP, cGMP unbinds, the channels shut, the inward dark current stops, the cell hyperpolarises, and glutamate release falls. The electrical response therefore depends entirely on the channels being able to close when cGMP drops. If a non-hydrolysable cGMP analogue holds the channels open regardless of the true cGMP level, then even a full light-driven fall in cGMP cannot shut them: the dark current persists, the rod stays depolarised, and no light signal is produced. The cascade upstream still runs, but it is now uncoupled from the membrane potential.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: guanylate cyclase does resynthesise cGMP during normal recovery, but here the channels never shut, so there is no initial hyperpolarisation to recover from. Misconception: importing the normal recovery phase into a situation where the response never occurs.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: light DECREASES cation entry (it closes channels); it does not increase permeability or depolarise the rod. Misconception: assuming a sensory stimulus must depolarise its receptor, as most receptors do.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: a non-hydrolysable cGMP analogue is an agonist that keeps the channel OPEN; it is not a channel blocker, so the dark current continues. Misconception: confusing a channel-opening analogue with an antagonist/blocker.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: the hyperpolarising response needs the channels to close when cGMP falls; with them locked open, the dark current and depolarisation are maintained and the rod cannot signal light.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: rhodopsin bleaching and the biochemical cascade are only intermediate steps; the actual electrical response requires channel closure, which the analogue prevents. Misconception: equating activation of the photopigment directly with the membrane response.

subtopic: Cochlear hair-cell mechanotransduction: K+ influx driven by the endocochlear potential
learningObjective: Combine chemical and electrical gradient information to deduce the direction of the transduction current in a cochlear hair cell and its effect on membrane potential.
stem: The endolymph bathing the apical stereocilia of cochlear hair cells is unusual: it has a high K+ concentration (~150 mmol/L, similar to the hair-cell cytoplasm) and is held at about +80 mV (the endocochlear potential) relative to the hair-cell interior, which sits near −45 mV. When the stereocilia are deflected toward the tallest, the mechanically-gated cation channels at their tips open. What is the immediate ionic event across the apical membrane and its effect on the hair cell?
choices: Cl− flows into the hair cell and hyperpolarises it
Na+ flows into the hair cell from the endolymph and depolarises it
Ca2+ flows out of the hair cell and repolarises it
K+ flows out of the hair cell and hyperpolarises it
K+ flows into the hair cell and depolarises it
explanation: The chemical K+ gradient across the apical membrane is almost flat (about 150 mmol/L on both sides), so it barely drives K+ either way. The decisive factor is the electrical gradient: the endolymph is roughly +80 mV while the cell interior is about −45 mV, a difference of ~125 mV with the outside strongly positive. A positive-outside field drives the positive K+ ion inward. So when the transduction channels open, K+ flows INTO the hair cell and depolarises it; this depolarisation then opens basolateral voltage-gated Ca2+ channels and triggers neurotransmitter release. This is the rare case where opening a K+-permeable channel depolarises rather than hyperpolarises a cell, precisely because of the endocochlear potential.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: the transduction channels are cation-selective, and Cl− entry would in any case tend to hyperpolarise, not signal sound. Misconception: assuming an inhibitory anion current underlies transduction.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: it assumes any depolarising inward current must be Na+, but the endolymph is K+-rich and Na+-poor, so the charge carrier here is K+. Misconception: automatically equating depolarisation with Na+ influx.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: Ca2+ entry (not efflux) occurs later at the basolateral membrane to drive transmitter release; it is not the apical transduction current. Misconception: conflating the downstream synaptic Ca2+ signal with the initial mechanotransduction event.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: this applies the usual rule that K+ leaves cells through leak channels and hyperpolarises them, ignoring that the +80 mV endolymph reverses the driving force at the apical membrane. Misconception: 'K+ always flows out / K+ movement always hyperpolarises.'
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: with a negligible chemical gradient but a large positive endocochlear potential, the net electrochemical driving force pushes K+ into the cell through the open channels, depolarising it.

subtopic: Coagulation cascade: localising a factor deficiency from PT and aPTT
learningObjective: Map the intrinsic, extrinsic and common coagulation pathways onto the PT and aPTT tests to localise a single-factor deficiency from a clinical pattern.
stem: The prothrombin time (PT) tests the extrinsic and common pathways of coagulation, whereas the activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) tests the intrinsic and common pathways. A young man with a lifelong history of bleeding into his joints is found to have a normal PT but a markedly prolonged aPTT. A deficiency of which of the following clotting factors best explains this pattern?
choices: Factor VIII
Factor VII
Factor X
Fibrinogen (factor I)
Factor XIII
explanation: A normal PT shows the extrinsic pathway (factor VII) and the common pathway (factors X, V, II/prothrombin, fibrinogen) are intact. A prolonged aPTT with a normal PT therefore localises the defect to a factor unique to the intrinsic pathway (factors XII, XI, IX or VIII). Recurrent bleeding into joints (haemarthrosis) in a young male is the classic presentation of haemophilia A, a deficiency of factor VIII. Of the options given, only factor VIII is an intrinsic-limb factor that would leave the PT normal while prolonging the aPTT.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: factor VIII is confined to the intrinsic pathway, so its deficiency prolongs the aPTT while leaving the PT normal, and joint bleeding in a young man fits haemophilia A.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: factor VII is the extrinsic-pathway factor, so its deficiency prolongs the PT and leaves the aPTT normal — the mirror image of the pattern described. Misconception: not tracking which pathway (and therefore which test) each factor belongs to.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: factor X is in the common pathway, so its deficiency prolongs BOTH the PT and the aPTT, not the aPTT alone. Misconception: forgetting that common-pathway factors affect both screening tests.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: fibrinogen is likewise a common-pathway factor, and its deficiency prolongs both PT and aPTT. Misconception: the same failure to recognise the shared common pathway.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: factor XIII cross-links fibrin AFTER the clot has already formed, so both PT and aPTT are normal even though the patient bleeds. Misconception: assuming every bleeding-factor deficiency must prolong a standard clotting time.

subtopic: Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation: arterial blood-gas interpretation
learningObjective: Integrate pH, PCO2 and bicarbonate to distinguish a primary metabolic disturbance with respiratory compensation from a primary respiratory disturbance, using pH direction to identify the primary process.
stem: Normal arterial values are: pH 7.35–7.45, PCO2 about 40 mmHg, and HCO3− about 24 mmol/L. A patient who has had several days of severe watery diarrhoea (losing large amounts of bicarbonate) has arterial blood showing pH 7.30, HCO3− 15 mmol/L and PCO2 30 mmHg. Which of the following best describes the acid–base status?
choices: Metabolic acidosis with partial respiratory compensation
Respiratory alkalosis with metabolic compensation
Metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation
Uncompensated respiratory acidosis
Respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation
explanation: First use the pH: 7.30 is below 7.35, so this is an acidaemia. Next find which measured variable has moved in the acidifying direction. A low HCO3− acidifies the blood (a metabolic cause), whereas a low PCO2 alkalinises it (it cannot be the cause of an acidosis). Therefore the primary disturbance is a metabolic acidosis — consistent with the loss of bicarbonate in the diarrhoea. The low PCO2 is not a primary problem but the respiratory compensation: the patient hyperventilates to blow off CO2 and pull the pH back toward normal. Because the pH is still below the normal range, the compensation is only partial. The key discriminator is that respiratory alkalosis would also show a low PCO2 but would RAISE the pH above 7.45; here the pH is low, proving the low PCO2 is compensatory, not primary.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: low pH with low HCO3− is a primary metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate loss from diarrhoea), and the low PCO2 is compensatory hyperventilation; the pH remaining below 7.35 shows the compensation is only partial.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: the low PCO2 is consistent with respiratory alkalosis, but a primary respiratory alkalosis would raise the pH above normal. The low pH shows the low PCO2 is compensation, not the primary event. Misconception: reading PCO2 first and mistaking the compensatory change for the primary disorder — the classic trap.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: an alkalosis requires pH above 7.45 and, if metabolic, a HIGH HCO3−; this patient has a low pH and low HCO3−. Misconception: ignoring the pH direction when naming the disorder.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: the PCO2 is low, not high, so there is no respiratory acidosis at all, and the disturbance is clearly compensated (PCO2 has shifted). Misconception: confusing which variable marks a respiratory disorder.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: respiratory acidosis requires a HIGH PCO2 (CO2 retention) with a compensatory HIGH HCO3−; here both are low. Misconception: labelling any acidosis 'respiratory' without checking that PCO2 is actually raised.

subtopic: Multiple alleles and codominance: predicting ABO x Rh offspring probability from parental phenotypes and an informative first child
learningObjective: Use an informative offspring phenotype to deduce parental genotypes at two independent loci (multiple-allele codominant ABO and simple-dominant Rh) and combine independent probabilities to predict a specific offspring phenotype.
stem: In humans, ABO blood group is controlled by three alleles at one locus (I^A and I^B are codominant to each other and both dominant to i) and Rhesus status by a separate, independently assorting gene in which the D allele (Rh-positive) is dominant to d (Rh-negative). A man of blood group A who is Rh-positive and a woman of blood group B who is Rh-positive have a first child who is blood group O and Rh-negative. If the couple have a second child, what is the probability that this child will be both blood group O and Rh-negative?
explanation: The first child fixes the parental genotypes. A group O (ii), Rh-negative (dd) child can only arise if each parent carries one i and one d allele. Therefore the group A father must be I^A i, Dd and the group B mother must be I^B i, Dd. For the next child, each locus behaves as an independent monohybrid cross: I^A i x I^B i gives P(ii) = 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4, and Dd x Dd gives P(dd) = 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4. Because the two genes assort independently, the joint probability is 1/4 x 1/4 = 1/16.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: takes P(Rh-negative) as 1/2, as if only one parent needed to pass on d, rather than 1/4 for a dd child from two Dd parents; this gives 1/4 x 1/2.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: uses 3/4 for the Rh term, which is the probability of being Rh-positive (D_), instead of 1/4 for Rh-negative; this gives 1/4 x 3/4.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: the O, Rh-negative first child shows both parents are heterozygous at both loci (I^A i Dd and I^B i Dd); P(ii) = 1/4 and P(dd) = 1/4, and since the loci are independent the answer is 1/4 x 1/4 = 1/16.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: treats both required outcomes as dominant phenotypes (3/4 each) and multiplies them, ignoring that group O and Rh-negative are both recessive/homozygous states each with probability 1/4.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: computes only the ABO term P(group O) = 1/4 and ignores the Rh locus entirely, failing to multiply by the independent probability of being Rh-negative.

subtopic: Incomplete dominance combined with simple dominance: F2 phenotype fraction in a dihybrid self-cross
learningObjective: Predict an F2 phenotype fraction in a dihybrid cross where one locus shows incomplete dominance (heterozygote is a distinct intermediate phenotype at frequency 1/2) and the other shows complete dominance, and combine the two using independent assortment.
stem: In a species of ornamental plant, flower colour is controlled by a gene showing incomplete dominance: C^R C^R plants are red, C^W C^W plants are white, and C^R C^W heterozygotes are pink. An independently assorting gene controls stem colour, where the allele A (purple stem) is completely dominant to a (green stem). A true-breeding red, purple-stemmed plant is crossed with a true-breeding white, green-stemmed plant, and the F1 are all pink with purple stems. If the F1 are allowed to self-fertilise, what fraction of the F2 generation is expected to be pink-flowered with purple stems?
explanation: The F1 are C^R C^W (pink), Aa (purple). Selfing gives two independent monohybrid crosses. For flower colour, C^R C^W x C^R C^W yields genotypic and phenotypic ratio 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white because the heterozygote has its own distinct phenotype; therefore P(pink) = 1/2. For stem colour, Aa x Aa yields 3 purple (A_) : 1 green, so P(purple) = 3/4. Because the genes assort independently, P(pink and purple) = 1/2 x 3/4 = 3/8.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: treats the heterozygous pink class as if it had frequency 1/4 (like an ordinary recessive class) rather than 1/2, giving 1/4 x 3/4.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: computes only the flower-colour locus (pink = 1/2) and omits the independent stem-colour probability.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: computes only the stem-colour locus (purple = 3/4) and omits the flower-colour term.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: ignores incomplete dominance, treating red as dominant to white, and calculates the double-dominant class 3/4 x 3/4 = 9/16.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: under incomplete dominance the pink heterozygote has frequency 1/2, and purple (A_) has frequency 3/4; independent assortment gives 1/2 x 3/4 = 3/8.

subtopic: Recessive epistasis (9:3:4): conditional genotype probability within an epistatic phenotype class
learningObjective: Recognise recessive epistasis from a 9:3:4 dihybrid ratio, identify the parental genotypes, and calculate a conditional genotype probability restricted to one epistatic phenotype class.
stem: Coat colour in a breed of dog depends on two independently assorting genes. Gene B determines pigment type: B (black) is dominant to b (chocolate). Gene E controls pigment deposition: at least one E allele allows the coat pigment to be deposited, whereas the genotype ee prevents deposition, giving a yellow coat irrespective of the B genotype. When two black dogs are mated, their offspring over many litters appear in the approximate ratio 9 black : 3 chocolate : 4 yellow. If a single black puppy is chosen at random from this cross, what is the probability that it is homozygous at both loci (genotype BBEE)?
explanation: The 9:3:4 ratio identifies recessive epistasis (ee masks the B locus), and it arises from BbEe x BbEe. Black puppies are those with genotype B_E_, which make up 9/16 of all offspring. Among all offspring, only 1/16 are BBEE. The conditional probability that a black puppy is BBEE is therefore (1/16) / (9/16) = 1/9. Equivalently, given a black (B_E_) dog, P(BB | B_) = 1/3 and P(EE | E_) = 1/3, so 1/3 x 1/3 = 1/9.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: gives the unconditional probability of BBEE among all offspring and fails to condition on the puppy already being black.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: conditions only one locus (1/3) and forgets that both loci must be homozygous dominant, omitting the second independent 1/3 factor.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: uses P(BB | B_) = 1/2 and P(EE | E_) = 1/2 instead of the correct 1/3 for a homozygous-dominant genotype given a dominant phenotype from a monohybrid cross, giving 1/2 x 1/2.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: black = B_E_ = 9/16 of offspring and BBEE = 1/16, so P(BBEE | black) = (1/16)/(9/16) = 1/9 (equivalently 1/3 x 1/3).
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: reports the overall frequency of the black phenotype (9/16) rather than the requested conditional probability.

subtopic: Recessive lethal allele: modified survivor ratio combined with an independent locus
learningObjective: Adjust a monohybrid phenotype ratio for a recessive lethal genotype (2:1 among survivors) and combine it with an independent, fully dominant locus to predict the fraction of live-born offspring of a specified compound phenotype.
stem: In mice, the coat-colour allele A^Y (yellow) is dominant to a (black) for coat colour but is a recessive lethal: A^Y A^Y embryos die before birth. An independently assorting gene controls hair length, where L (short hair) is completely dominant to l (long hair). Two yellow, short-haired mice, each heterozygous at both loci (genotype A^Y a L l), are crossed. Considering only the live-born offspring, what fraction are expected to be black with long hair?
explanation: For coat colour, A^Y a x A^Y a gives 1 A^YA^Y : 2 A^Ya : 1 aa, but the A^YA^Y class dies, so among survivors the ratio is 2 yellow : 1 black, making P(black) = 1/3. For hair length, Ll x Ll gives 3 short : 1 long, so P(long hair, ll) = 1/4. The hair-length locus is not affected by the lethality and assorts independently, so P(black and long-haired among survivors) = 1/3 x 1/4 = 1/12.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: uses the correct survivor black fraction (1/3) but takes long hair as 1/2, forgetting that the 3:1 ratio makes ll = 1/4.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: gives only the coat-colour probability among survivors (1/3) and ignores the hair-length locus.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: gives only the long-hair probability (ll = 1/4) and ignores the coat-colour requirement.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: the lethal A^YA^Y class is removed, so survivors are 2/3 yellow : 1/3 black (black = 1/3); long hair (ll) = 1/4; independent loci give 1/3 x 1/4 = 1/12.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: ignores the lethal allele and treats coat colour as an ordinary 3:1 cross, taking black = 1/4, then multiplying by 1/4.

subtopic: Bombay phenotype: recessive epistasis of the H locus on ABO expression and apparent group-O probability
learningObjective: Integrate recessive epistasis (the H locus masking ABO expression, Bombay phenotype) with multiple-allele ABO inheritance and apply the addition rule with inclusion-exclusion to compute the probability of an apparent group-O child.
stem: Expression of the ABO blood group antigens requires the H antigen, made by a separate, independently assorting gene: individuals homozygous hh (the Bombay phenotype) cannot synthesise the H antigen, so their red cells display neither A nor B antigen and they type as blood group O regardless of their ABO genotype. A woman of blood group A has the genotype I^A i, H h, and her husband of blood group B has the genotype I^B i, H h. What is the probability that a child of this couple will type as blood group O?
explanation: A child types as group O whenever no A or B antigen is displayed, which happens in either of two ways: (1) the child is Bombay (hh), which suppresses any ABO genotype, or (2) the child expresses H (H_) but has ABO genotype ii. From H h x H h, P(hh) = 1/4; from I^A i x I^B i, P(ii) = 1/4. The apparent-O set is (hh) union (ii), because ii combined with hh is already included in hh. By inclusion-exclusion, P = P(hh) + P(ii) - P(hh and ii) = 1/4 + 1/4 - (1/4 x 1/4) = 4/16 + 4/16 - 1/16 = 7/16.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: assumes apparent group O requires ABO genotype ii together with a functional H antigen (H_ and ii = 3/4 x 1/4), overlooking that hh Bombay individuals also type as O whatever their ABO genotype.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: ignores the H locus entirely and treats group O as simply the ABO genotype ii = 1/4, missing the Bombay contribution.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: apparent O = (hh, any ABO) union (ii, with H); using inclusion-exclusion, P(hh) + P(ii) - P(hh and ii) = 1/4 + 1/4 - 1/16 = 7/16.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: adds P(hh) and P(ii) as 1/4 + 1/4 without subtracting the double-counted overlap of children who are both hh and ii (1/16).
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: applies inclusion-exclusion but subtracts the overlap twice, giving 1/4 + 1/4 - 2 x 1/16 = 6/16 = 3/8.

topic: Cell biology — endomembrane system and protein trafficking
subtopic: Protein targeting: N-terminal ER signal sequence, SRP-dependent co-translational import, and the consequence of its deletion
learningObjective: Predict the subcellular fate of a secretory protein when its N-terminal ER signal sequence is deleted, using the SRP-dependent co-translational targeting mechanism.
stem: A researcher studies a soluble enzyme, protein X, that is normally synthesised and then secreted from a mammalian cell. Protein X carries a single cleavable N-terminal signal sequence and no other targeting information. Using recombinant DNA, the researcher deletes only the codons encoding this N-terminal signal sequence, leaving the rest of the coding sequence and all gene-regulatory elements intact, and expresses the altered gene in the same cell type. Where is the newly synthesised, altered protein X most likely to accumulate, and why?
choices: In the mitochondrial matrix, because removing the ER signal exposes a default mitochondrial import signal at the new N-terminus.
Anchored in the plasma membrane, because the sequence that remains after the deletion now acts as a stop-transfer membrane anchor.
Secreted normally, because the information needed for secretion is distributed throughout the mature portion of the protein.
In the cytosol, because without the signal sequence the signal-recognition particle (SRP) cannot target the translating ribosome to the ER membrane.
In the lumen of the rough endoplasmic reticulum, because ribosomes are permanently bound to the ER membrane and deliver all newly made proteins into it.
explanation: Entry into the secretory pathway is co-translational. As the N-terminal signal sequence emerges from a free ribosome, the signal-recognition particle (SRP) binds it, pauses translation, and docks the complex onto the SRP receptor of the rough ER, so translation resumes with the growing chain threaded into the ER lumen. All downstream sorting (Golgi, vesicles, secretion) depends on the protein first getting into the ER via this signal. Delete the signal sequence and SRP has nothing to recognise: the ribosome is never targeted to the ER, translation completes in the cytosol, and the finished (signal-less) protein is released into the cytosol. Because protein X has no other targeting information, that is where it stays.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: there is no 'default' mitochondrial import. Matrix targeting requires its own specific N-terminal presequence; removing the ER signal does not create one.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: confuses a cleavable N-terminal signal sequence with an internal stop-transfer/transmembrane anchor. A soluble secreted protein has no such anchor, so nothing tethers it in the membrane after the signal is removed.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: assumes secretion information is spread through the mature chain. Access to the entire secretory pathway is gated by the single N-terminal signal sequence, so removing it prevents secretion.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: SRP recognises the emerging signal sequence and delivers the ribosome to the ER; with the signal deleted there is no recognition event, translation finishes on free cytosolic ribosomes, and the protein accumulates in the cytosol.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: assumes ribosomes are permanently ER-bound. Ribosomes are recruited to the ER only when they happen to be translating a signal-bearing protein; without the signal the ribosome stays free in the cytosol.

topic: Cell biology — endomembrane system and protein trafficking
subtopic: Lysosomal enzyme sorting: mannose-6-phosphate tagging failure (I-cell disease) causing secretion of acid hydrolases
learningObjective: Explain how failure of mannose-6-phosphate tagging mis-sorts multiple lysosomal hydrolases to secretion, and relate this to the cellular phenotype of I-cell disease.
stem: Cultured fibroblasts from a patient with a rare inherited disorder contain lysosomes engorged with undigested material (dense 'inclusion bodies'). Paradoxically, the culture medium bathing these cells shows unusually high activities of many different soluble lysosomal acid hydrolases. When those secreted hydrolases are purified and assayed in vitro, each one is catalytically normal. Which single underlying defect best accounts for all of these observations together?
choices: A loss-of-function mutation in one lysosomal hydrolase gene, so that a single substrate accumulates inside the lysosome.
Failure of endosomes to acidify enough to release hydrolases from their receptor, so the enzymes are continuously recycled back to the Golgi.
Over-expression of the hydrolase genes, which saturates the normal lysosomal targeting pathway.
A defect in the lysosomal vacuolar H+-ATPase, so that the lysosome cannot be acidified for digestion.
Failure to add the mannose-6-phosphate tag to newly made lysosomal hydrolases, so that they are secreted by default instead of being delivered to lysosomes.
explanation: Soluble lysosomal hydrolases are recognised in the cis-Golgi by a phosphotransferase that adds mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tags to their N-linked glycans. In the trans-Golgi network, M6P receptors bind these tagged enzymes and package them into vesicles bound for the endosomal/lysosomal system; without the tag the enzymes follow the default bulk-flow route and are secreted. If the tagging enzyme (GlcNAc-phosphotransferase) is defective, essentially all soluble hydrolases lose their address label at once: they are secreted into the medium (explaining the high extracellular activity of many enzymes), while lysosomes are starved of hydrolases and fill with undigested substrate (explaining the inclusion bodies). The enzymes themselves are structurally fine, so they assay normally in vitro. This is I-cell disease (mucolipidosis II).

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: a single hydrolase defect would let one substrate build up but could not raise the activities of many different hydrolases in the medium or send them out of the cell; the phenotype is broad, not enzyme-specific.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: failure to release enzymes in an acidified endosome would trap them in the endosomal system, not secrete them into the medium; it also misidentifies the step, which is tagging in the Golgi, not receptor release.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 'saturation by over-expression' is a misconception; the enzymes are not over-produced, and simple saturation would not simultaneously empty the lysosomes and secrete many enzymes at the scale observed.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: a dead vacuolar H+-ATPase would impair digestion (some inclusions) but the hydrolases would still be delivered to lysosomes, so it cannot explain their abundant secretion into the medium.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: loss of the M6P tag mis-sorts all soluble hydrolases to secretion (high extracellular enzyme activity) while depriving lysosomes of them (inclusion bodies); the enzymes remain catalytically intact, matching the normal in-vitro assays.

topic: Cell biology — endomembrane system and protein trafficking
subtopic: ER protein retrieval: the KDEL signal and KDEL-receptor-mediated COPI retrograde transport from the Golgi
learningObjective: Describe how soluble ER-resident proteins are retained by KDEL/KDEL-receptor-mediated retrieval in COPI vesicles, and predict the effect of removing the KDEL signal.
stem: Protein disulfide isomerase (PDI) is a soluble enzyme that normally resides in the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum, where it assists the folding of secretory proteins. PDI carries a C-terminal Lys-Asp-Glu-Leu (KDEL) sequence. In a mutant cell line the four C-terminal residues of PDI are deleted, but the enzyme is otherwise fully folded and active. Compared with normal cells, where does most of the mutant PDI end up over time, and how is the normal localisation of PDI maintained?
choices: It stays retained in the ER lumen, because KDEL is a membrane anchor that physically holds PDI in the ER regardless of the deletion.
It is secreted from the cell, because normal PDI that escapes to the Golgi is captured by the KDEL receptor and returned to the ER in COPI-coated vesicles.
It accumulates in the cis-Golgi, because the KDEL sequence normally blocks a protein from moving forward out of the Golgi.
It is secreted from the cell, because COPII vesicles are normally unable to package any soluble luminal protein such as PDI.
It is delivered to lysosomes, because loss of KDEL exposes a mannose-6-phosphate signal that reroutes PDI.
explanation: ER-resident soluble proteins are not held perfectly in place; they continually leak forward into COPII vesicles and reach the cis/medial-Golgi. There, the slightly acidic environment lets the KDEL receptor bind their C-terminal KDEL signal and package them into COPI-coated retrograde vesicles that carry them back to the ER, where the higher pH releases them. Localisation is therefore maintained by continuous retrieval, not by static retention. Delete the KDEL tag and the receptor can no longer recapture PDI once it reaches the Golgi; the enzyme then rides the default anterograde (bulk-flow) route and is secreted. Note that the outcome (secretion) is correctly stated in option E as well, but E gives a false mechanism.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: treats KDEL as a membrane anchor. KDEL is a soluble retrieval signal read by a receptor in the Golgi; removing it does not leave PDI anchored, and PDI is a soluble luminal protein with no membrane attachment.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: normal localisation is dynamic retrieval by the KDEL receptor, which returns escaped PDI to the ER in COPI (retrograde) vesicles; without KDEL, PDI cannot be retrieved and is secreted along the default anterograde path.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: KDEL does not block forward transport. Normal PDI does move forward to the Golgi transiently, but it is retrieved; the mutant is not blocked in the Golgi, it is secreted.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: the outcome (secretion) is right but the mechanism is false—COPII vesicles do package soluble luminal cargo; ER residence is maintained by KDEL-based retrieval, not by exclusion from COPII.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: conflates the two independent sorting systems. PDI has no mannose-6-phosphate route; losing KDEL does not create a lysosomal address.

topic: Cell biology — cell junctions and tissue organisation
subtopic: Cell junctions of the intercalated disc: gap junctions for electrical coupling versus desmosomes for mechanical coupling
learningObjective: Distinguish the functions of gap junctions, desmosomes and tight junctions, and identify which junction mediates electrical coupling in cardiac muscle.
stem: Cardiac muscle behaves as a functional syncytium: neighbouring cells are mechanically coupled so that contractile force is transmitted from cell to cell, and they are electrically coupled so that a wave of depolarisation passes directly from the cytoplasm of one cell into the next, without any chemical synapse. An experimental toxin selectively destroys only the junctions responsible for the direct cell-to-cell spread of depolarisation, while leaving every other junction intact. Which junction is destroyed, and what is the immediate functional consequence?
choices: Desmosomes are destroyed, so the cells lose their electrical coupling and depolarisation can no longer spread between them.
Gap junctions are destroyed, and because gap junctions provide the main mechanical attachment the cells also immediately fall apart.
Gap junctions are destroyed, so the cells stay mechanically joined but action potentials can no longer pass directly from one cytoplasm to the next.
Tight junctions are destroyed, so ions leak into the spaces between cells and short-circuit the spreading action potential.
Plasmodesmata are destroyed, so the cytoplasmic bridges that normally couple these animal cells are lost.
explanation: The three junction types have distinct jobs. Gap junctions are clusters of connexon channels that link the cytoplasms of adjacent cells, allowing ions (and therefore depolarising current) and small molecules to pass directly between them—this is what makes cardiac (and smooth) muscle electrically continuous. Desmosomes anchor cells mechanically by linking to intermediate filaments and resist shear/tension. Tight junctions seal the space between epithelial cells to block paracellular leakage and to keep membrane domains separate. The direct cytoplasm-to-cytoplasm spread of depolarisation is a gap-junction function, so destroying gap junctions abolishes electrical coupling while the desmosomes (untouched) keep the cells mechanically bound.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: attributes electrical coupling to desmosomes. Desmosomes provide mechanical anchorage via intermediate filaments; they do not conduct depolarisation between cells.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: identifies the correct junction but adds a false consequence—mechanical attachment is provided by desmosomes/adherens junctions (left intact), so the cells do not fall apart.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: gap junctions carry the intercellular current, so destroying them abolishes direct electrical coupling while the intact desmosomes keep the cells mechanically joined.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: cardiac cells are coupled by gap junctions, not tight junctions. Tight junctions seal paracellular spaces in epithelia and play no role in cardiac cell-to-cell current flow.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: plasmodesmata are cytoplasmic channels of plant cells. Animal cells use gap junctions for direct cytoplasmic communication.

topic: Cell biology — secretory pathway and the extracellular matrix
subtopic: Collagen biosynthesis and scurvy: ER prolyl hydroxylation (vitamin C), triple-helix stability and intracellular quality control
learningObjective: Integrate ER prolyl hydroxylation, triple-helix stability and intracellular quality control to explain the connective-tissue phenotype of vitamin C deficiency (scurvy).
stem: Collagen is synthesised as procollagen inside cells and later processed into mature collagen fibrils of the extracellular matrix. Within the lumen of the rough endoplasmic reticulum, specific proline residues of the procollagen chains are enzymatically hydroxylated; the resulting hydroxyproline residues form hydrogen bonds that stabilise the collagen triple helix. This hydroxylation reaction absolutely requires ascorbic acid (vitamin C). A patient with severe, long-standing vitamin C deficiency has weak connective tissue, bleeding gums and poor wound healing. In fibroblasts cultured from this patient in the continued absence of vitamin C, which single set of observations is expected?
choices: Procollagen polypeptides are made at a normal rate but are under-hydroxylated, so they form an unstable triple helix; much of this abnormal procollagen is degraded inside the cell instead of being secreted as functional collagen.
Proline hydroxylation instead takes place normally in the Golgi apparatus, so the only defect is a failure to package collagen into secretory vesicles.
Fully hydroxylated, stable triple helices are still formed and secreted normally, and the only defect is that they cannot be cross-linked once they are in the extracellular matrix.
The signal sequence of procollagen fails to be cleaved, so procollagen remains permanently anchored in the ER membrane.
No procollagen polypeptide can be made at all, because proline hydroxylation must be completed before the ribosome can finish translating the chain.
explanation: Prolyl hydroxylation is a co-/post-translational modification carried out in the ER lumen; it does not gate the synthesis of the polypeptide, so chains are still translated at a normal rate. Without vitamin C the enzyme cannot hydroxylate proline, so the chains lack the hydroxyproline hydrogen bonds needed to stabilise the triple helix. The under-hydroxylated procollagen is unstable at body temperature, fails ER quality control, and is largely retained and degraded intracellularly rather than being secreted and assembled into strong fibrils. Too little functional collagen reaches the matrix, giving the classic scurvy phenotype (fragile vessels/bleeding gums, poor wound healing). The ascorbate-dependent step is hydroxylation in the ER—distinct from the later, copper-dependent lysyl-oxidase cross-linking that occurs extracellularly.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: hydroxylation is a modification of an already-translated chain, so synthesis proceeds; loss of hydroxyproline destabilises the triple helix, and the misfolded procollagen is degraded intracellularly rather than secreted, producing the connective-tissue defect.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: prolyl hydroxylation occurs in the ER lumen, not the Golgi, and the primary lesion is failed hydroxylation/helix instability, not a vesicle-packaging defect.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: confuses the vitamin-C-dependent prolyl hydroxylation step with the separate copper-dependent lysyl-oxidase cross-linking step. In vitamin C deficiency the helix is not stable and hydroxylation—not cross-linking—is the impaired reaction.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: vitamin C has nothing to do with signal-peptide cleavage; procollagen is a soluble luminal protein whose signal sequence is removed normally.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: treats hydroxylation as a prerequisite for translation. Hydroxylation is a co-/post-translational modification; the polypeptide is still fully synthesised even when it is not hydroxylated.

subtopic: Cardiac conduction system: third-degree (complete) AV block and AV dissociation read from a described ECG
learningObjective: Interpret a described ECG showing independent atrial and ventricular rates to diagnose complete AV block and correctly locate the atrial and ventricular pacemakers.
stem: An ECG shows regular P waves at a rate of 88 per minute and regular, abnormally broad QRS complexes at a rate of 38 per minute. There is no consistent relationship between the P waves and the QRS complexes: the interval from each P wave to the next QRS complex varies randomly. Which statement best accounts for these findings?
choices: Impulses are conducted through the atrioventricular node with a progressively lengthening PR interval until one impulse is dropped.
The sinoatrial node is discharging at 38 per minute and only every second impulse succeeds in reaching the ventricles.
A re-entrant circuit in the ventricles is driving the ventricles faster than the atria are being driven by the sinoatrial node.
The atrioventricular node is acting as a single pacemaker that depolarises both the atria and the ventricles at 88 per minute.
Conduction is completely interrupted at or below the atrioventricular node, so the atria are driven by the sinoatrial node while the ventricles are driven by an independent, slower distal pacemaker.
explanation: Two features must be reconciled: the atrial rate (P waves, 88/min) and the ventricular rate (QRS, 38/min) are each regular but bear no fixed relationship to one another — atrioventricular (AV) dissociation. This is third-degree (complete) heart block: no atrial impulse crosses the block, so the SA node continues to pace the atria at 88/min while a subsidiary pacemaker below the block escapes to pace the ventricles independently. The abnormally broad QRS and the very slow rate (~38/min) identify the escape focus as ventricular (distal His–Purkinje) tissue rather than the AV junction. The absence of any fixed P:QRS ratio or progressive PR change rules out the second-degree blocks.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: progressive PR lengthening ending in a dropped beat is Mobitz I (Wenckebach) second-degree block, in which P waves and QRS complexes remain conducted and related. The stem states there is no relationship between them, which is complete dissociation. Misconception: mistaking third-degree (complete) block for a second-degree block.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: this describes a fixed 2:1 second-degree block, and it also misplaces the pacemaker. The atria are paced by the SA node at 88/min, not by a 38/min focus, and a 2:1 block would give a ventricular rate near 44 with a fixed relationship to the P waves — here the P:QRS relationship is random. Misconception: reading any slow ventricular rate as a fixed conduction ratio.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: the ventricular rate (38/min) is slower than the atrial rate (88/min), so the ventricles are not being driven faster than the atria; escape rhythms are slow, whereas re-entrant ventricular tachycardia is fast. Misconception: equating any AV dissociation with ventricular tachycardia.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: the atrial rate of 88/min is set by the SA node, not the AV node, and in this trace the AV node is the site of block, not a fast pacemaker for the whole heart. A single pacemaker could not produce two different regular rates. Misconception: assuming the AV node normally paces the whole heart.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: complete block at or below the AV node dissociates the atria from the ventricles. The SA node still paces the atria at 88/min while an independent, slower ventricular (His–Purkinje) pacemaker escapes at ~38/min; the broad QRS confirms a distal ventricular origin, exactly matching regular but unrelated atrial and ventricular rhythms.

subtopic: Baroreceptor reflex: integrated afferent and efferent autonomic response to acute haemorrhage
learningObjective: Trace the arterial baroreceptor reflex from a fall in mean arterial pressure through changes in afferent firing to the coordinated efferent (sympathetic and parasympathetic) response.
stem: A healthy adult suffers acute blood loss and mean arterial pressure falls from 95 mmHg to 70 mmHg within one minute, before any correction of blood volume has occurred. Considering the immediate arterial (carotid sinus) baroreceptor reflex, which combination correctly describes the change in carotid sinus afferent firing, sympathetic outflow, heart rate and the state of the systemic arterioles?
choices: Afferent firing increases; sympathetic outflow decreases; heart rate decreases; arterioles dilate.
Afferent firing increases; sympathetic outflow increases; heart rate increases; arterioles constrict.
Afferent firing decreases; sympathetic outflow decreases; heart rate decreases; arterioles dilate.
Afferent firing decreases; sympathetic outflow increases; heart rate decreases; arterioles constrict.
Afferent firing decreases; sympathetic outflow increases; heart rate increases; arterioles constrict.
explanation: Carotid sinus baroreceptors are stretch receptors: their firing rate rises and falls with arterial wall stretch, i.e. with blood pressure. A fall in mean arterial pressure reduces stretch, so afferent firing DECREASES. This afferent traffic normally inhibits the medullary cardiovascular (vasomotor) centre; less inhibition means sympathetic outflow rises and vagal (parasympathetic) tone to the heart falls. The efferent result is an increased heart rate and contractility together with arteriolar and venous constriction, all acting to raise pressure back toward normal. The correct pattern is therefore: firing down, sympathetic up, heart rate up, arterioles constricted.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: this is the reflex response to a RISE in arterial pressure, not a fall. Increased stretch would raise afferent firing and reflexly lower sympathetic drive and heart rate; here pressure has fallen. Misconception: thinking hypotension increases baroreceptor firing.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: the efferent limb (raised sympathetic tone, faster heart, constricted arterioles) is appropriate for hypotension, but the afferent limb is inverted — a fall in pressure must reduce, not increase, baroreceptor firing. Misconception: believing the receptors fire more to 'demand' a higher pressure.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: it correctly has afferent firing falling, but then makes sympathetic outflow fall as well. Reduced afferent firing disinhibits the vasomotor centre, so sympathetic drive rises. Misconception: assuming afferent firing and efferent sympathetic output always move in the same direction.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: with sympathetic outflow raised and vagal tone withdrawn, the heart rate must increase; a slowing heart would deepen the hypotension. Every other element is correct, which is what makes the heart-rate error tempting. Misconception: forgetting that reduced vagal tone accelerates the heart.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: the lower mean arterial pressure reduces carotid sinus stretch and hence afferent firing; this disinhibits the medullary vasomotor centre, raising sympathetic outflow and reducing vagal tone. Heart rate and contractility rise and the arterioles (and veins) constrict, all tending to restore arterial pressure.

subtopic: Capillary fluid exchange: net filtration pressure from the four Starling pressures at the arteriolar end
learningObjective: Combine capillary and interstitial hydrostatic and colloid osmotic pressures to compute the net filtration pressure and determine the direction of fluid movement across a capillary wall.
stem: At the arteriolar end of a systemic capillary the following pressures are measured: capillary hydrostatic pressure = 35 mmHg; interstitial fluid hydrostatic pressure = 2 mmHg; plasma colloid osmotic (oncotic) pressure = 26 mmHg; interstitial fluid colloid osmotic pressure = 5 mmHg. Taking the reflection coefficient as 1, what is the net filtration pressure and in which direction does fluid move?
choices: 9 mmHg, giving net filtration (fluid leaving the capillary).
7 mmHg, giving net filtration (fluid leaving the capillary).
14 mmHg, giving net filtration (fluid leaving the capillary).
12 mmHg, giving net reabsorption (fluid entering the capillary).
12 mmHg, giving net filtration (fluid leaving the capillary).
explanation: The net filtration pressure (NFP) is the net outward hydrostatic pressure minus the net inward oncotic pressure: NFP = (Pc − Pi) − (πc − πi), where Pc and Pi are capillary and interstitial hydrostatic pressures and πc and πi are plasma and interstitial oncotic pressures. Substituting: (35 − 2) − (26 − 5) = 33 − 21 = +12 mmHg. A positive value means the outward (filtration) forces exceed the inward (reabsorption) forces, so fluid is filtered out of the capillary at the arteriolar end. All four pressures must be included; dropping any term gives a wrong value.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 9 mmHg is (Pc − πc) = 35 − 26, which ignores both interstitial pressures. The interstitial hydrostatic term (2 mmHg) and interstitial oncotic term (5 mmHg) both belong in the balance. Misconception: reducing Starling's equation to capillary pressure minus plasma oncotic pressure only.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 7 mmHg comes from (Pc − Pi) − πc = (35 − 2) − 26, omitting the interstitial oncotic pressure (5 mmHg), which pulls fluid outward and must be subtracted from the plasma oncotic term. Misconception: forgetting that interstitial protein exerts an outward oncotic pull.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 14 mmHg comes from Pc − (πc − πi) = 35 − (26 − 5), omitting the interstitial hydrostatic pressure (2 mmHg), which opposes filtration and must be subtracted from the capillary hydrostatic pressure. Misconception: neglecting the small back-pressure of interstitial fluid.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: the magnitude (12 mmHg) is right but the direction is reversed. A positive net filtration pressure means outward filtration, not reabsorption; reabsorption would require the oncotic forces to exceed the hydrostatic forces (a negative NFP). Misconception: assuming oncotic pressure always wins at the arteriolar end.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: NFP = (Pc − Pi) − (πc − πi) = (35 − 2) − (26 − 5) = 33 − 21 = +12 mmHg. The positive result means outward forces dominate, so there is net filtration out of the capillary at the arteriolar end.

subtopic: Angiotensin II efferent arteriolar constriction and the fall in GFR when an ACE inhibitor is given in renal artery stenosis
learningObjective: Integrate the intrarenal action of angiotensin II on the efferent arteriole with glomerular capillary pressure to predict the effect of ACE inhibition on GFR when renal perfusion is already low.
stem: Within the kidney, angiotensin II constricts the efferent (post-glomerular) arteriole more strongly than the afferent arteriole, which helps to preserve glomerular filtration when renal perfusion pressure is low. A patient has bilateral narrowing of the renal arteries, so renal perfusion pressure is chronically reduced, and is then started on an ACE inhibitor. What is the most likely immediate effect on glomerular filtration rate (GFR), and why?
choices: GFR rises, because the fall in aldosterone reduces blood volume and so relieves the load on the glomerulus.
GFR rises, because blocking angiotensin II dilates the afferent arteriole and increases blood flow into the glomerulus.
GFR falls, because angiotensin II is normally required to dilate the efferent arteriole and maintain outflow from the glomerulus.
GFR falls, because loss of angiotensin II–mediated efferent arteriolar constriction lowers glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure.
GFR is essentially unchanged, because angiotensin II acts only on systemic blood vessels and not within the glomerulus.
explanation: Glomerular filtration is driven by the hydrostatic pressure in the glomerular capillaries. When renal perfusion pressure is low (as in renal artery stenosis), angiotensin II preferentially constricts the efferent arteriole; this raises the resistance downstream of the glomerulus and props up glomerular capillary pressure, keeping GFR near normal despite poor inflow. An ACE inhibitor blocks angiotensin II formation, so this efferent constriction is lost, the efferent arteriole dilates, glomerular capillary pressure falls and GFR drops. This is why ACE inhibitors can precipitate acute kidney injury in bilateral renal artery stenosis.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: any reduction in blood volume from lower aldosterone would tend to lower GFR, not raise it, and it develops far too slowly to explain the immediate change, which is haemodynamic. Misconception: confusing the slow volume-mediated effect of aldosterone with acute glomerular haemodynamics.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: angiotensin II acts predominantly on the efferent arteriole, not by constricting the afferent arteriole, so removing it does not produce a dominant afferent dilation that raises glomerular flow and pressure. The net effect on glomerular pressure is a fall. Misconception: attributing angiotensin II's key renal action to the afferent arteriole.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: the predicted direction of GFR change is right, but the mechanism is inverted — angiotensin II CONSTRICTS the efferent arteriole; it does not dilate it. Losing constriction (not losing dilation) is what lowers glomerular pressure. Misconception: reversing the vasomotor action of angiotensin II on the efferent arteriole.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: angiotensin II normally constricts the efferent arteriole to sustain glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure when perfusion is low. An ACE inhibitor removes this constriction, so glomerular capillary pressure and therefore GFR fall — the basis of acute kidney injury when ACE inhibitors are used in bilateral renal artery stenosis.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: angiotensin II has a specific intrarenal action on the efferent arteriole (and mesangium), not merely systemic vasoconstriction, so an ACE inhibitor does change glomerular haemodynamics. Misconception: treating angiotensin II as purely a systemic pressor with no glomerular role.

subtopic: Lymphoedema from lymphatic obstruction: interstitial protein accumulation raising interstitial oncotic pressure
learningObjective: Explain how failure of lymphatic drainage causes oedema by allowing filtered protein to accumulate in the interstitium, raising interstitial oncotic pressure and increasing net filtration even when the other Starling parameters are normal.
stem: Under normal conditions capillary filtration slightly exceeds reabsorption, and the small volume of protein-containing fluid left in the interstitium is returned to the bloodstream by the lymphatic system. Consider a limb in which the major lymphatic vessels have become obstructed, while cardiac function, plasma protein concentration and capillary hydrostatic pressure all remain normal. Which mechanism best explains the oedema that develops?
choices: Capillary hydrostatic pressure rises because the obstructed lymph backs up directly into the capillaries and increases their internal pressure.
Reduced lymph flow lowers interstitial hydrostatic pressure, which draws water out of the cells and into the interstitial space.
The obstruction stimulates aldosterone release, causing salt and water to be retained specifically within the affected limb.

Plasma proteins that would normally be carried away in the lymph accumulate in the interstitium, raising interstitial oncotic pressure and increasing net filtration, while the surplus fluid can no longer be drained.
Plasma oncotic pressure falls because plasma proteins are continuously lost into the obstructed lymphatic vessels.
explanation: Capillaries inevitably leak a small amount of protein into the interstitium; a key job of the lymphatic system is to return this protein (and the accompanying fluid) to the circulation. If lymph drainage fails, that protein is no longer removed, so interstitial protein concentration and hence interstitial colloid osmotic (oncotic) pressure rise. This weakens the oncotic gradient that normally opposes filtration, so net filtration out of the capillaries increases; at the same time the filtered fluid can no longer be carried away. Both effects promote accumulation of protein-rich interstitial fluid — lymphoedema — even though plasma proteins, capillary pressure and cardiac function are all normal.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: lymph ultimately drains into the great veins, not back into the capillary bed, so an obstruction does not raise capillary hydrostatic pressure, which the stem states remains normal. Misconception: imagining that blocked lymph flows backwards into the capillaries.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: blocked lymphatics cause interstitial fluid to accumulate, raising interstitial volume and pressure rather than lowering it, and Starling exchange occurs across capillary walls, not cell membranes, so intracellular water is not the source. Misconception: conflating interstitial fluid with intracellular water.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: a local lymphatic blockage does not release aldosterone, and aldosterone acts on the kidney to cause systemic (whole-body) salt and water retention, not retention confined to one limb. Misconception: invoking a systemic salt-retaining hormone to explain a purely local drainage failure.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: the lymphatics normally return filtered protein and fluid to the blood. When they are blocked, interstitial protein accumulates, raising interstitial oncotic pressure; this reduces the net oncotic force opposing filtration, so filtration exceeds the (now absent) drainage, giving progressive protein-rich lymphoedema.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: plasma protein concentration is stated to remain normal, so plasma oncotic pressure is not the changed variable; the protein problem is a gain in the interstitium, not a loss from plasma. Misconception: confusing local interstitial protein accumulation with a fall in plasma oncotic pressure.

subtopic: Immunoglobulin structure: papain vs pepsin fragmentation and the valency requirement for agglutination versus complement activation
learningObjective: Relate antibody domain structure (Fab/F(ab')2/Fc) to effector functions, deducing how proteolytic fragmentation separates antigen-binding valency from complement activation.
stem: A monoclonal IgG antibody is raised against a repeating polysaccharide epitope displayed on the surface of a bacterium. Portions of the purified antibody are digested either with papain (which cleaves on the N-terminal side of the hinge disulfide bonds, releasing two separate Fab fragments and one Fc fragment) or with pepsin (which cleaves on the C-terminal side of the hinge disulfides, releasing a single F(ab')2 fragment while the Fc region is broken down into small peptides). Each digest is then tested both for its ability to agglutinate the bacteria and for its ability to trigger complement-mediated lysis. Which result is expected?
choices: The pepsin F(ab')2 fragment agglutinates the bacteria but does not trigger complement-mediated lysis.
Neither digest is able to bind the bacterial surface at all.
The papain digest agglutinates the bacteria but does not trigger complement-mediated lysis.
The pepsin F(ab')2 fragment triggers complement-mediated lysis but fails to agglutinate the bacteria.
Both digests retain full agglutinating and complement-activating activity.
explanation: Agglutination requires an antibody (or fragment) to bridge adjacent particles, which needs at least two linked antigen-binding sites (bivalency). Complement activation via the classical pathway requires an intact Fc region to recruit C1q. Papain yields two independent, monovalent Fab fragments (one binding site each) plus a separate Fc: the Fab fragments bind antigen but cannot cross-link, so no agglutination. Pepsin yields one bivalent F(ab')2 fragment (two binding sites held together by the hinge disulfides) but destroys the Fc: F(ab')2 can therefore still agglutinate but cannot activate complement. Only option C matches both outcomes.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: F(ab')2 retains two hinge-linked antigen-binding sites, so it remains bivalent and can bridge adjacent bacteria to agglutinate them; because pepsin destroys the Fc region, it can no longer engage C1q or Fc receptors, so complement-mediated lysis is lost.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: both Fab and F(ab')2 fragments still contain the variable regions, so they retain antigen-binding activity; only the Fc-dependent functions are abolished. Misconception: assuming proteolysis destroys the antigen-binding site itself.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: papain produces monovalent Fab fragments, each with a single antigen-binding site; a monovalent fragment cannot bridge two bacteria, so no agglutination occurs. Misconception: treating each separated Fab as though it were still bivalent like the intact antibody.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: this reverses the two properties.
