optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: assumes plasma bicarbonate can be turned back into CO2 in the plasma. The catalyst carbonic anhydrase is intracellular, so bicarbonate must re-enter the red cell to be reconverted — plasma-only conversion is far too slow to matter.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: this describes the tissue (systemic-capillary) chloride shift, not the lung. Misconception that the same ion directions apply everywhere — the process must reverse in the lung so that CO2 can be regenerated and exhaled.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: in the lung the chloride shift reverses — HCO3- enters the red cell (Cl- leaves), then combines with H+ to reform CO2 via carbonic anhydrase, and the CO2 diffuses into the alveolus to be exhaled.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: has both anions leaving the cell. Like option B it ignores the antiport nature of the exchange, and it would leave no bicarbonate inside the cell to regenerate the CO2 that must be exhaled.

subtopic: Foetal versus adult haemoglobin: differential 2,3-BPG binding as the basis of the oxygen-affinity difference
learningObjective: Interpret an experiment in which 2,3-BPG is removed from purified adult and foetal haemoglobin to deduce that the physiological affinity difference arises from differential allosteric binding of 2,3-BPG rather than from any intrinsic difference at the oxygen-binding site.
stem: Foetal haemoglobin (HbF, alpha2-gamma2) has a higher oxygen affinity than adult haemoglobin (HbA, alpha2-beta2) in whole blood, which favours transfer of oxygen from mother to foetus across the placenta. In an experiment, purified HbA and purified HbF are each studied first with 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) present at physiological concentration, and then again after the 2,3-BPG has been completely removed. With 2,3-BPG present, the HbF oxygen-dissociation curve lies well to the left of the HbA curve; but after 2,3-BPG is removed, the two curves almost coincide, both lying far to the left. Which conclusion is best supported by these results?
choices: The gamma chains of HbF carry extra haem groups that bind oxygen more tightly than the haems of HbA.
The higher affinity of HbF in blood arises mainly because 2,3-BPG lowers the affinity of HbA more than it lowers that of HbF.
HbF binds 2,3-BPG more strongly than HbA does, and this stronger binding is what raises its oxygen affinity.
The intrinsic oxygen affinity of the isolated haem groups is far greater in HbF than in HbA, independently of 2,3-BPG.
Oxygen binds to a chemically different type of site on HbF than it does on HbA.
explanation: 2,3-BPG is an allosteric regulator that binds in the central cavity of haemoglobin between the two beta chains, stabilising the low-affinity T (deoxy) state and thereby lowering oxygen affinity. HbF has gamma chains in place of beta chains; the gamma chains lack some of the positively charged residues that grip 2,3-BPG, so 2,3-BPG binds HbF much more weakly and lowers its affinity much less. Hence in blood (where 2,3-BPG is present) HbF stays higher-affinity than HbA. The experiment is diagnostic: once 2,3-BPG is stripped from both proteins, the curves coincide and both are high-affinity — showing that the intrinsic oxygen chemistry of the two haemoglobins is essentially the same, and that the physiological difference is produced by the differential effect of 2,3-BPG.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: both HbA and HbF contain four haem groups (one per globin chain); the gamma chains do not add extra haems. Misconception that foetal blood carries more oxygen per molecule via additional binding sites.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: the curves coincide once 2,3-BPG is removed, so the intrinsic affinities are essentially equal; the in-blood difference must therefore come from 2,3-BPG depressing HbA's affinity more than HbF's.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: it reverses the binding relationship. The effect on affinity is stated correctly, but HbF actually binds 2,3-BPG more WEAKLY (its gamma chains lack key cationic residues) — which is exactly why 2,3-BPG lowers its affinity less.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: directly contradicted by the data. After 2,3-BPG removal the two curves coincide, showing the intrinsic (BPG-free) affinities are nearly identical, not far greater for HbF.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: oxygen binds the ferrous ion of a haem group in both haemoglobins — the same chemistry. Misinterpreting 'higher affinity' as implying a different kind of binding site.

subtopic: Chemical control of breathing: carbon dioxide as the primary ventilatory drive and hypoxic blackout after pre-dive hyperventilation
learningObjective: Reason that the urge to breathe during breath-holding is set primarily by rising arterial CO2, and use this to explain why pre-dive hyperventilation delays the breakpoint while allowing dangerous hypoxia to develop.
stem: Before attempting a long underwater breath-hold, a swimmer deliberately takes several very deep, rapid breaths (voluntary hyperventilation). While breathing normal air the swimmer's haemoglobin is already about 97% saturated with oxygen, so this manoeuvre adds very little extra oxygen to the blood; nevertheless it noticeably lengthens the time the swimmer can stay submerged before feeling an overwhelming urge to breathe, and it makes fainting underwater ('blackout') more likely. Which explanation best accounts for BOTH the delayed urge to breathe and the increased risk of blackout?
choices: Hyperventilation raises arterial CO2, which directly suppresses the respiratory centre; the swimmer faints because the accumulated CO2 is toxic to the brain.
Hyperventilation drives haemoglobin saturation far above 97%, and since the urge to breathe is triggered by falling oxygen, the enlarged oxygen store simply delays that urge.
Hyperventilation greatly increases the oxygen physically dissolved in the plasma, giving a much larger oxygen store; blackout occurs only because that extra oxygen is eventually consumed.

Hyperventilation lowers arterial CO2; because the urge to breathe is driven mainly by rising CO2, the breakpoint is postponed while oxygen keeps falling, so the swimmer may become severely hypoxic and faint before the urge to breathe forces a breath.
Hyperventilation lowers arterial oxygen while raising CO2, and the low oxygen directly relaxes the respiratory muscles, which is what delays the next breath.
explanation: At rest and during breath-holding the dominant stimulus to breathe is a rise in arterial PCO2, sensed as a fall in CSF pH by the central chemoreceptors; the compelling urge to breathe (the 'breakpoint') is normally reached because CO2 accumulates, well before oxygen becomes critically low. Voluntary hyperventilation blows off CO2, driving arterial PCO2 far below normal, but it adds almost no oxygen because haemoglobin is already near-fully saturated. During the subsequent breath-hold, metabolism steadily consumes O2 and produces CO2; because PCO2 started abnormally low, it takes much longer to climb back to the breakpoint, so the urge to breathe is delayed. Meanwhile PO2 falls unchecked and can reach levels that cause loss of consciousness before CO2 has risen enough to force a breath — hypoxic ('shallow-water') blackout. The single mechanism therefore explains both effects.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: hyperventilation LOWERS arterial CO2, it does not raise it. The option reverses the direction of the CO2 change and misattributes the blackout to CO2 toxicity rather than to hypoxia.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: haemoglobin is already about 97% saturated, so it cannot be pushed 'far above' that. It also assumes falling O2, not rising CO2, is the primary drive — the very misconception the scenario is designed to expose.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: at normal atmospheric pressure the oxygen dissolved in plasma is negligible, and the stem explicitly states little extra oxygen is added. Misconception that hyperventilation meaningfully enlarges the oxygen store.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: hyperventilation lowers PCO2 so the CO2-driven breakpoint is delayed, but oxygen consumption continues, allowing hypoxia to develop to the point of blackout before the urge to breathe returns.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: hyperventilation does not lower arterial oxygen (it is maintained or slightly raised), and low oxygen does not 'relax' the respiratory muscles to delay breathing; the mechanism described is physiologically incoherent.

subtopic: Oxygen transport: carbon-monoxide poisoning versus anaemia — loss of carrying capacity combined with a leftward shift of the dissociation curve
learningObjective: Integrate oxygen-carrying capacity, cooperative binding (leftward shift) and the distinction between oxygen content and arterial PO2 to explain why carbon-monoxide poisoning impairs tissue oxygen delivery more than an equal loss of haemoglobin from anaemia.
stem: Two patients each have their effective oxygen-carrying capacity reduced by half. In patient X this is because carbon monoxide (CO) has bound to half of the haemoglobin, forming carboxyhaemoglobin. In patient Y it is because a haemorrhage has halved the concentration of otherwise-normal haemoglobin. In both patients the arterial partial pressure of oxygen (PO2) is normal. Which statement correctly compares how well the blood can deliver oxygen to the tissues in the two patients?
choices: Patient X (CO) releases oxygen to the tissues more readily, because carbon monoxide lowers the oxygen affinity of the haemoglobin that is still available.

Patient X (CO) delivers oxygen to the tissues less effectively than patient Y, because carbon monoxide not only removes half the carrying capacity but also raises the oxygen affinity of the remaining haemoglobin, hindering its release at the tissues.
Patient Y (anaemia) delivers less oxygen to the tissues than patient X, because losing whole haemoglobin molecules is always worse than blocking existing ones.
The two patients are equivalent, because in both the oxygen-carrying capacity is halved while the arterial PO2 remains normal.
Both patients breathe much faster, driven by their peripheral chemoreceptors, because the reduced oxygen content is sensed directly as a low arterial PO2.
explanation: Both conditions halve the amount of haemoglobin available to carry oxygen, so both halve oxygen-carrying capacity. But carbon monoxide does a second, subtler thing: because haemoglobin binds oxygen cooperatively, CO occupying some subunits shifts the remaining functional subunits toward the high-affinity (R) state, moving their oxygen-dissociation curve to the LEFT. The half of the haemoglobin that can still carry oxygen therefore holds onto it more tightly and unloads less of it at the low tissue PO2. Anaemia has no such effect: the remaining haemoglobin is entirely normal and unloads normally. Hence, for the same halving of capacity, CO poisoning is worse because it combines reduced capacity with impaired unloading. A further insidious feature (option D) is that arterial PO2 — the physically dissolved oxygen — is normal in both, so the peripheral chemoreceptors, which respond to PO2 rather than to oxygen content, are not strongly stimulated in CO poisoning.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: it reverses the affinity effect. CO INCREASES the oxygen affinity of the remaining subunits (leftward shift), so oxygen is released less, not more, readily.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: CO delivers a double hit — it removes half the carrying capacity AND, through cooperativity, raises the affinity of the remaining haemoglobin so it unloads less at the tissues; anaemia produces only the capacity loss, so tissue delivery is better preserved in patient Y.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: asserts the reverse of the truth, and offers only a bare 'always worse' assertion with no mechanism. Removing whole molecules (anaemia) preserves normal unloading of the remainder, whereas CO impairs it.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: treats the two as equivalent by counting only capacity and PO2. It omits the extra leftward shift (increased affinity) that CO produces in the still-functional haemoglobin, which anaemia does not cause.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: arterial PO2 (dissolved oxygen) is normal in both patients, and peripheral chemoreceptors sense PO2, not oxygen content; they are therefore not strongly stimulated — the classic reason CO poisoning can be deceptively asymptomatic in its ventilatory response.

topic: Human physiology — renal system and osmoregulation
subtopic: Glomerular ultrafiltration: net filtration pressure and GFR from Starling forces and the ultrafiltration coefficient (Kf)
learningObjective: Calculate the net glomerular filtration pressure from the balance of hydrostatic and colloid osmotic pressures and combine it with the ultrafiltration coefficient to obtain the glomerular filtration rate.
stem: Filtration across a glomerular capillary is set by the balance of hydrostatic and colloid osmotic (oncotic) pressures. In a healthy adult the following mean values are recorded: glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure = 48 mmHg; hydrostatic pressure in Bowman's (glomerular) capsule = 8 mmHg; plasma colloid osmotic (oncotic) pressure in the glomerular capillary = 30 mmHg; colloid osmotic pressure of the fluid in Bowman's capsule = 0 mmHg. The glomerular ultrafiltration coefficient (Kf) is 12.5 mL min⁻¹ mmHg⁻¹. Assuming these values are constant, what is the glomerular filtration rate (GFR)?
choices: 125 mL/min
600 mL/min
875 mL/min
500 mL/min
225 mL/min
explanation: Filtration is favoured by the glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure and opposed by the hydrostatic pressure inside Bowman's capsule and by the plasma oncotic pressure (the capsular fluid oncotic pressure is ~0 because essentially no protein is filtered). Net filtration pressure = 48 − 8 − 30 = 10 mmHg. GFR = Kf × net filtration pressure = 12.5 mL min⁻¹ mmHg⁻¹ × 10 mmHg = 125 mL/min, the normal value.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: net filtration pressure = Pgc − Pbc − πgc = 48 − 8 − 30 = 10 mmHg, so GFR = Kf × 10 = 12.5 × 10 = 125 mL/min.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: the glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure (48 mmHg) has been used alone as the net pressure, ignoring both opposing pressures. Misconception: capillary blood pressure equals the net filtration pressure.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: net pressure has been computed as 48 − 8 + 30 = 70 mmHg, adding the oncotic pressure as though it favoured filtration. Misconception: plasma oncotic pressure drives filtration rather than opposing it.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: net pressure has been taken as 48 − 8 = 40 mmHg, ignoring the plasma colloid osmotic (oncotic) pressure that opposes filtration. Misconception: glomerular filtration is governed by hydrostatic pressures alone.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: net pressure has been taken as 48 − 30 = 18 mmHg, omitting the hydrostatic pressure in Bowman's capsule, which also opposes filtration. Misconception: only the capillary hydrostatic and oncotic pressures need be considered.

topic: Human physiology — renal system and osmoregulation
subtopic: Proximal tubule selective reabsorption: glucose transport maximum (Tm), renal threshold and urinary excretion rate
learningObjective: Compute the filtered load of a solute and apply a saturable transport maximum to determine the rate of urinary excretion when the filtered load exceeds the tubular maximum.
stem: A patient with poorly controlled diabetes has a plasma glucose concentration of 25 mmol/L and a glomerular filtration rate of 120 mL/min. Glucose is freely filtered at the glomerulus. The combined tubular maximum (Tm) for glucose reabsorption in the two kidneys is 2.0 mmol/min; once the filtered load exceeds this rate, reabsorption proceeds at the Tm and the remaining glucose is excreted. Assuming glucose is not secreted, at what rate is glucose excreted in the urine?
choices: 2.0 mmol/min
1.5 mmol/min
0 mmol/min
3.0 mmol/min
1.0 mmol/min
explanation: Filtered load = GFR × plasma concentration = 0.120 L/min × 25 mmol/L = 3.0 mmol/min. Because this exceeds the transport maximum, reabsorption saturates at Tm = 2.0 mmol/min. The excess is excreted: 3.0 − 2.0 = 1.0 mmol/min. This is why glucose appears in the urine (glycosuria) only once the plasma level pushes the filtered load above the renal threshold.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 2.0 mmol/min is the reabsorbed rate (the Tm), not the excreted rate. Misconception: confuses the amount reabsorbed with the amount excreted.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 3.0 × 0.5 assumes a constant fractional (50%) reabsorption, as for bulk proximal fluid, instead of a saturable carrier. Misconception: glucose is reabsorbed as a fixed proportion rather than up to a fixed maximum.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: assumes the tubule reabsorbs the entire filtered load, ignoring that the filtered load (3.0 mmol/min) exceeds the transport maximum (2.0 mmol/min). Misconception: glucose reabsorption has no upper limit.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: assumes that once the threshold is exceeded no glucose is reabsorbed, so the whole filtered load is excreted; in fact reabsorption continues at the Tm. Misconception: exceeding the threshold abolishes reabsorption entirely.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: filtered load = 0.120 L/min × 25 mmol/L = 3.0 mmol/min; reabsorption saturates at Tm = 2.0 mmol/min; excreted = 3.0 − 2.0 = 1.0 mmol/min.

topic: Human physiology — renal system and osmoregulation
subtopic: Loop of Henle countercurrent multiplier: thick ascending limb Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ transport, the medullary osmotic gradient and loop-diuretic action
learningObjective: Predict how blocking active NaCl reabsorption in the thick ascending limb disrupts the medullary osmotic gradient and, through it, the ability of the collecting duct to reabsorb water.
stem: The loop diuretic furosemide inhibits the Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ cotransporter in the apical membrane of the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. In a person given furosemide, which statement best describes the immediate effect on the nephron and the urine produced?
choices: The thick ascending limb becomes permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed there and the urine volume falls.
The fluid leaving the loop becomes strongly hypo-osmotic, and this drives the formation of a small volume of highly concentrated urine.
ADH secretion is directly suppressed, aquaporins are withdrawn from the collecting duct, and a water diuresis follows.
The medullary interstitial osmotic gradient is reduced, so the collecting duct reabsorbs less water even when ADH is present, and a large volume of dilute urine is produced.
The countercurrent multiplier is unaffected, because the active NaCl pumping that builds the gradient occurs in the descending limb.
explanation: The thick ascending limb actively reabsorbs NaCl (via the Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ cotransporter) while remaining impermeable to water; this is the 'single effect' that the countercurrent arrangement multiplies into a steep corticomedullary osmotic gradient. Blocking the cotransporter removes solute from the interstitium, so the medullary gradient collapses. Because the collecting duct concentrates urine only by drawing water osmotically into this hypertonic interstitium, a weakened gradient means little water is reabsorbed there even if ADH is present and aquaporins are inserted. The result is a large volume of dilute urine — the basis of the diuretic effect.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: the thick ascending limb is impermeable to water regardless of transporter activity and never reabsorbs water there. Misconception: solute transport in the ascending limb drives local water reabsorption.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: blocking solute reabsorption makes the fluid leaving the loop LESS hypo-osmotic (nearer iso-osmotic), and the urine is dilute, not concentrated. Misconception: reverses the role of the ascending limb as the diluting segment.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: furosemide acts on the tubular cotransporter, not on ADH secretion or its receptor. Misconception: all diuretics work by suppressing ADH.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: inhibiting NaCl entry into the medullary interstitium dissipates the corticomedullary osmotic gradient, so the collecting duct cannot reabsorb water even when ADH opens aquaporins, giving a large volume of dilute urine.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: the active NaCl pump is in the thick ascending limb; the descending limb has no active NaCl transport and is permeable to water. Misconception: the descending limb performs the active pumping.

topic: Human physiology — renal system and osmoregulation
subtopic: ADH (vasopressin) control of collecting-duct water reabsorption: distinguishing central from nephrogenic diabetes insipidus by the desmopressin response
learningObjective: Interpret a water-deprivation and desmopressin challenge to localise a urinary concentrating defect to ADH deficiency (central) versus collecting-duct unresponsiveness (nephrogenic).
stem: Two patients, X and Y, both pass large volumes of dilute urine (osmolality ≈ 90 mOsm/kg) and both fail to concentrate their urine after overnight water deprivation. Each is then given desmopressin, a synthetic ADH analogue resistant to breakdown. Afterwards, patient X's urine osmolality rises to 600 mOsm/kg, whereas patient Y's remains ≈ 95 mOsm/kg. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Patient X has central (ADH-deficient) diabetes insipidus, while patient Y has nephrogenic diabetes insipidus in which the collecting duct cannot respond to ADH.
Patient Y's collecting duct responds normally to ADH but lacks a medullary osmotic gradient, whereas patient X over-secretes ADH.
Both patients have central diabetes insipidus and differ only in the severity of ADH deficiency.
Patient X has primary polydipsia from excess water intake, while patient Y has central diabetes insipidus.
Patient X has nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and patient Y has central (ADH-deficient) diabetes insipidus.
explanation: ADH acts on V2 receptors of the collecting-duct cells to insert aquaporin-2 into the apical membrane, allowing water to be reabsorbed into the hypertonic medulla and the urine to be concentrated. If exogenous desmopressin restores concentrating ability (patient X), the collecting duct is competent and the defect must be a lack of endogenous ADH — central (cranial) diabetes insipidus. If the urine stays dilute despite desmopressin (patient Y), the collecting duct cannot respond to ADH (for example a V2-receptor or aquaporin-2 defect) — nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: X's urine concentrates with exogenous ADH, so X lacks endogenous ADH (central DI); Y cannot concentrate despite ADH, indicating collecting-duct unresponsiveness (nephrogenic DI).
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: a fully ADH-responsive collecting duct would concentrate the urine after desmopressin, which Y does not; and X is ADH-deficient, not an over-secretor. Misconception: attributes the failure to a missing medullary gradient rather than receptor unresponsiveness.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: patient Y does not respond to desmopressin, which is incompatible with simple ADH deficiency in both. Misconception: ignores the diagnostic non-response of Y.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: in primary polydipsia the kidney can concentrate urine after water deprivation, yet both patients failed to, so neither fits. Misconception: any dilute urine indicates excessive drinking.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: this reverses the interpretation; the patient whose urine concentrates after desmopressin (X) has central, not nephrogenic, DI. Misconception: confuses which defect responds to exogenous ADH.

topic: Human physiology — renal system and osmoregulation
subtopic: Interpreting filtrate composition along the nephron: TF/P inulin as a water-reabsorption marker to obtain fractional solute reabsorption
learningObjective: Use the tubular-fluid-to-plasma inulin ratio as a marker of water reabsorption and combine it with a solute's TF/P ratio to calculate the fraction of the filtered solute load reabsorbed at a point along the nephron.
stem: In a micropuncture experiment, tubular fluid is sampled at the end of the proximal convoluted tubule while inulin (freely filtered, neither reabsorbed nor secreted) is infused to a steady plasma level. At the sampling point the tubular-fluid-to-plasma concentration ratio (TF/P) for inulin is 3.0, and the TF/P for a freely filtered solute X is 1.2. What fraction of the filtered load of X has been reabsorbed up to this point?
explanation: Because inulin is neither reabsorbed nor secreted, its amount in the tubule is unchanged; its concentration rises only as water is reabsorbed. So the fraction of filtered water still remaining in the tubule = 1 ÷ (TF/P inulin) = 1/3. The amount of X remaining, relative to the filtered load, equals its concentration ratio times the remaining water fraction: fraction of X remaining = TF/P(X) ÷ TF/P(inulin) = 1.2 / 3.0 = 0.4. Therefore the fraction reabsorbed = 1 − 0.4 = 0.6, i.e. 60%. Note that X's concentration rose (TF/P = 1.2 > 1) yet far less than inulin's, showing that X was reabsorbed, but proportionally less than water.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 1/(TF/P inulin) = 1/3 ≈ 33% is the fraction of filtered water still in the tubule, not the fraction of X reabsorbed. Misconception: conflates the water-volume marker with solute handling.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 1 − 1/3 = 67% is the fraction of WATER reabsorbed; it assumes X is reabsorbed in exactly the same proportion as water. Since TF/P(X) rose (to 1.2), X was reabsorbed less completely than water. Misconception: solute is reabsorbed isosmotically with water.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: this reads TF/P(X) = 1.2 as a '20% rise' and equates it with 20% reabsorption, ignoring that the concentration also rises simply because water was removed. Misconception: a concentration ratio can be read directly as a reabsorbed fraction.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: fraction of X remaining = TF/P(X) / TF/P(inulin) = 1.2/3.0 = 0.4, so the fraction reabsorbed = 1 − 0.4 = 0.60 = 60%.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 1.2/3.0 = 0.4 is the fraction of X still remaining in the tubule, not the fraction reabsorbed. Misconception: forgets to subtract the remaining fraction from 1.

subtopic: Thyroid hormone feedback: exogenous T3 suppresses TSH, lowering endogenous T4 output and causing thyroid atrophy
learningObjective: Predict how supplying an exogenous end-product hormone perturbs a negative-feedback axis, reasoning through the fall in the trophic hormone and its consequences for the gland's own secretion and mass.
stem: A healthy adult with a normally functioning thyroid gland and an intact hypothalamic–pituitary axis begins taking daily tablets of tri-iodothyronine (T3, the biologically active thyroid hormone). The dose is chosen so that total thyroid-hormone activity in the blood is kept slightly above the normal level. After several weeks, which single set of changes best describes the pituitary secretion of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), the gland's own (endogenous) secretion of thyroxine (T4), and the size of the thyroid gland?
choices: TSH decreased; endogenous T4 secretion decreased; thyroid gland shrunken
TSH increased; endogenous T4 secretion decreased; thyroid gland enlarged
TSH unchanged; endogenous T4 secretion decreased; thyroid gland unchanged
TSH increased; endogenous T4 secretion increased; thyroid gland enlarged
TSH decreased; endogenous T4 secretion increased; thyroid gland enlarged
explanation: The active hormone supplied by tablet acts on the hypothalamus and pituitary exactly as the body's own thyroid hormone would. Because total hormone activity is held slightly above normal, negative feedback suppresses TSH secretion. TSH is the trophic hormone that both drives thyroxine synthesis by the follicular cells and maintains their mass, so a sustained fall in TSH reduces the gland's own T4 output and causes the gland to atrophy (shrink). This is why thyroid-hormone therapy suppresses an overactive or enlarged gland: all three variables move in the 'reduced' direction together.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: excess circulating T3 suppresses TSH by negative feedback; the resulting loss of trophic drive lowers endogenous T4 secretion and causes the gland to atrophy.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: correctly sees endogenous T4 fall but pairs it with rising TSH and a goitre; this mixes up the feedback direction (extra hormone lowers, not raises, TSH) and assumes the gland must enlarge.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: assumes hormone taken as a tablet is not 'sensed' by the pituitary, so TSH stays constant; in fact exogenous hormone is indistinguishable to the feedback receptors and does suppress TSH.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: assumes the body responds to extra thyroid hormone by raising TSH and boosting the gland — a reversal of negative feedback in which the controlled hormone and its trophic driver are wrongly expected to rise together.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: recognises that TSH falls but then claims endogenous T4 rises and the gland enlarges — the common 'goitre always forms' error that ignores that low TSH means less stimulation of the gland, not more.

subtopic: HPA axis: iatrogenic adrenal-cortex atrophy and secondary adrenal insufficiency after abrupt withdrawal of long-term glucocorticoid therapy
learningObjective: Explain how prolonged feedback suppression of a trophic hormone leads to atrophy of its target gland, and why abrupt removal of the exogenous hormone precipitates a deficiency state.
stem: A patient with a chronic inflammatory disease is treated for many months with high daily doses of a synthetic glucocorticoid (a cortisol-like drug). The medication is then stopped abruptly. Within a day or two the patient becomes severely ill, with very low blood pressure, profound weakness and a dangerously low blood glucose concentration. Which explanation best accounts for this crisis?
choices: The adrenal medulla ceased producing adrenaline once the daily drug was withdrawn, causing the collapse.
Prolonged feedback suppression of ACTH had caused the adrenal cortex to atrophy, so it could not resume cortisol secretion when the drug was suddenly withdrawn.
The drug had permanently increased the pituitary's sensitivity, so normal cortisol levels now over-suppress ACTH for life.
The synthetic drug directly poisoned and destroyed the adrenal cortex, which is now permanently unable to make cortisol.
Stopping the drug triggered a sudden surge of ACTH that over-stimulated and exhausted the adrenal glands.
explanation: Sustained high levels of the glucocorticoid act on the hypothalamus and pituitary and, by negative feedback, chronically suppress CRH and ACTH secretion. Without ACTH stimulation the cortisol-producing zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex atrophies. While the drug is present this does not matter, because the drug replaces cortisol. But when the drug is stopped abruptly, the atrophied cortex cannot immediately make cortisol, and the suppressed pituitary cannot quickly restore ACTH, so the patient is acutely cortisol-deficient — hence the hypotension, weakness and hypoglycaemia. Recovery of the axis takes weeks to months, which is why such therapy must be tapered, not stopped suddenly.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: the adrenal medulla and its adrenaline output are controlled by sympathetic nerves, not by this cortisol/ACTH feedback loop — it confuses the medulla with the cortex.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: chronic feedback suppression of ACTH atrophies the adrenal cortex, so on abrupt withdrawal neither gland can restore cortisol quickly, producing acute adrenal insufficiency.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: there is no permanent resetting of pituitary sensitivity; the axis is transiently suppressed and recovers over time, so a lifelong hypersensitivity is not the cause.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: the drug does not chemically destroy the cortex; the gland is atrophied through disuse and can recover if ACTH is restored gradually — a misconception that exogenous steroid is cytotoxic to the adrenal.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: after withdrawal ACTH is suppressed and slow to recover, not surging; this invents a rebound over-stimulation that the feedback logic does not support.

subtopic: Calcium homeostasis: hypercalcaemia with appropriately suppressed PTH indicates a PTH-independent (non-parathyroid) source
learningObjective: Use the direction of a hormone level relative to its controlled variable to decide whether a gland is the cause of a disturbance or is responding appropriately to it.
stem: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) raises the blood calcium concentration, and its secretion is normally switched off when blood calcium rises (negative feedback). A patient is found to have a persistently high blood calcium concentration, yet the plasma PTH concentration is very low. Assuming that the parathyroid glands themselves are responding normally to calcium, which conclusion is best supported by these findings?
choices: The high blood calcium is being produced by a source other than the parathyroid glands, and the low PTH is the normal feedback response to that high calcium.
The parathyroid glands have failed, and this failure is what has raised the blood calcium.
Calcium is high because the low PTH has signalled the kidneys to retain more calcium.
A tumour of the parathyroid glands is autonomously over-secreting PTH and driving the calcium up.
The low PTH result must be a laboratory error, because a low PTH cannot occur together with a high calcium.
explanation: If the parathyroid glands are working normally, a high blood calcium should switch PTH secretion off — and that is exactly what is observed (PTH is low). So the parathyroids are behaving appropriately and are not the cause: the calcium must be raised by a PTH-independent mechanism (for example a tumour secreting a PTH-related substance, excess vitamin D, or accelerated bone breakdown). A parathyroid cause would instead show an inappropriately high or 'normal' PTH in the face of high calcium. The single most informative clue is that the hormone level is consistent with the feedback rule, which points the diagnosis away from the gland.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: with normally responsive glands, a high calcium should suppress PTH, so the low PTH is appropriate and the calcium excess must come from a non-parathyroid source.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: parathyroid failure gives low PTH and therefore low, not high, calcium — this reverses the physiological effect of PTH on blood calcium.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: PTH promotes renal calcium reabsorption, so a low PTH would reduce reabsorption; this reverses the direction of PTH's action on the kidney.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: an autonomous PTH-secreting tumour would show a high (inappropriate) PTH, not a low one; this ignores the feedback-inconsistent value and reflexively blames the parathyroids.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: low PTH with high calcium is precisely what functioning feedback predicts; the misconception is that a hormone and its controlled variable must always move in the same direction.

subtopic: Glucose homeostasis: amino-acid-stimulated insulin and the counter-regulatory role of glucagon after a protein-only meal
learningObjective: Integrate the dual secretion of insulin and glucagon in response to amino acids and predict the outcome of selectively removing one arm of an opposing (push–pull) hormonal control system.
stem: After a meal of pure protein that contains no carbohydrate, the absorbed amino acids stimulate the pancreatic beta cells to release insulin. In a healthy person the same amino acids also stimulate the pancreatic alpha cells to release glucagon. Suppose a drug completely blocked this glucagon release while leaving the insulin response fully intact. What would be the most likely consequence of eating such a protein-only meal, and why?
choices: Insulin secretion would cease altogether, because glucagon is required for the beta cells to release insulin.
Blood glucose would rise sharply, because without glucagon the liver stores less glucose and releases more of it into the blood.
Blood glucose would rise, because the blocked glucagon can no longer oppose the direct glucose-raising effect of the amino acids.
Blood glucose would fall to abnormally low levels, because the amino-acid-driven insulin would lower blood glucose with no glucagon released to mobilise hepatic glucose in compensation.
Blood glucose would remain exactly constant, because a protein meal contains no glucose and therefore cannot change the blood glucose level.
explanation: Amino acids stimulate insulin secretion, and insulin lowers blood glucose by promoting cellular uptake and suppressing hepatic glucose output. After a carbohydrate-free meal there is no dietary glucose entering the blood to offset this insulin action, so on its own the insulin would tend to drive blood glucose downward. The physiological safeguard is that the same amino acids also stimulate glucagon, which makes the liver release glucose (glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis) and thereby cancels the hypoglycaemic tendency of the insulin. The two hormones normally balance so that blood glucose stays roughly constant after a protein meal. Removing glucagon leaves insulin unopposed, so blood glucose falls to abnormally low levels — this is the key reason both hormones are released together.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: the insulin response is stated to be intact, and beta-cell insulin release does not require glucagon; this misconstrues the two hormones as co-dependent for secretion.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: this reverses glucagon's action. Glucagon raises blood glucose by mobilising hepatic glucose, so blocking it cannot cause the liver to release more glucose.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong on two counts: amino acids do not directly raise blood glucose in this scenario, and glucagon raises rather than lowers glucose, so removing glucagon would not produce a rise.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: amino-acid-stimulated insulin lowers glucose, and with no glucagon released to mobilise hepatic glucose, the unopposed insulin drives blood glucose into hypoglycaemia.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: it assumes only dietary glucose can change blood glucose, ignoring that insulin secreted in response to the amino acids continues to act on the glucose already circulating.

subtopic: Hypothalamic–pituitary axis: pituitary-stalk section raises prolactin (loss of tonic dopamine inhibition) while other anterior-pituitary hormones fall
learningObjective: Distinguish stimulatory from inhibitory hypothalamic control of the anterior pituitary and predict the divergent effect of cutting the portal supply on hormones under opposite modes of control.
stem: The anterior pituitary is controlled by hypothalamic hormones delivered through the hypophyseal portal blood vessels. Most anterior-pituitary hormones are held under stimulatory hypothalamic control, but the secretion of prolactin is restrained by a continuous (tonic) inhibitory signal from the hypothalamus — the neurotransmitter dopamine. A patient suffers an injury that cleanly severs the pituitary stalk, interrupting all flow through the portal vessels while leaving the anterior-pituitary cells themselves alive and healthy. Compared with the situation before the injury, what happens to the blood concentrations of the anterior-pituitary hormones?
choices: All anterior-pituitary hormones remain unchanged, because the surviving pituitary cells continue to secrete autonomously.
Prolactin secretion increases, while the secretion of the other anterior-pituitary hormones decreases.
All anterior-pituitary hormones increase, because the pituitary has been released from hypothalamic control.
Prolactin secretion decreases, while the secretion of the other anterior-pituitary hormones increases.
All anterior-pituitary hormones, including prolactin, decrease, because every one of them depends on a hypothalamic releasing hormone.
explanation: Cutting the stalk stops all hypothalamic signals from reaching the anterior pituitary through the portal vessels. For the hormones under stimulatory control (ACTH, TSH, LH, FSH and growth hormone), losing their releasing hormones causes their secretion to fall. Prolactin is the exception: its dominant hypothalamic signal is inhibitory (dopamine), so losing that signal removes the brake and prolactin secretion rises. The divergent behaviour of prolactin is the direct consequence of it being under tonic inhibition while the others are under stimulation, and it is why stalk injury characteristically produces a rise in prolactin alongside a fall in the other anterior-pituitary hormones.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: the anterior pituitary is not autonomous; unlike the posterior pituitary its secretion depends on hypothalamic hormones arriving through the portal vessels, so cutting the supply must change output.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: removing the portal supply withdraws the stimulatory releasing hormones (so the other hormones fall) and simultaneously withdraws inhibitory dopamine (so prolactin, freed from its brake, rises).
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: it assumes all hypothalamic control is inhibitory, so that cutting it releases every hormone; in reality most hormones are stimulated and would decrease.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: this is the exact inversion of the correct pattern — it mislabels prolactin as the stimulated hormone and the rest as inhibited.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: this treats every anterior-pituitary hormone as stimulated by the hypothalamus and overlooks that prolactin is under inhibitory control, so it would rise, not fall.

subtopic: Pancreatic zymogen activation cascade and its site: enteropeptidase (enterokinase) deficiency and selective protein malabsorption
learningObjective: Explain why pancreatic proteases are secreted as inactive zymogens and are activated in the duodenum by an initiating brush-border enzyme, and deduce the nutrient-specific consequence of failing to initiate that activation cascade.
stem: Pancreatic proteases are secreted into the duodenum as inactive zymogens. There, the brush-border enzyme enteropeptidase (enterokinase) converts trypsinogen to trypsin; trypsin then activates further trypsinogen and also chymotrypsinogen and procarboxypeptidase. A newborn is found to have a congenital total deficiency of enteropeptidase. Salivary and pancreatic amylase, pancreatic lipase, gastric acid and pepsin are all secreted and function normally. Which statement best predicts this child's digestion?
choices: Protein digestion remains normal because trypsinogen autoactivates spontaneously at duodenal pH without any enteropeptidase.
Only fat digestion is impaired, because enteropeptidase is normally required to activate pancreatic lipase in the duodenum.
Carbohydrate digestion is impaired because trypsin is required to activate pancreatic amylase before it can hydrolyse starch.
Digestion of all three macronutrients is normal, because pepsin and salivary amylase fully compensate for the missing pancreatic activation step.
Protein digestion is markedly impaired because the pancreatic proteases cannot be activated, whereas starch digestion is essentially unaffected.
explanation: Enteropeptidase is the single physiological trigger that starts the pancreatic protease cascade: it makes the first trypsin, and trypsin then activates all the other proteolytic zymogens (and more trypsinogen). Remove that initiating step and the whole cascade stays inactive, so protein digestion in the small intestine collapses even though the pancreas secretes normal amounts of enzyme. Carbohydrate digestion is unaffected because amylase is secreted in its active form (it is not a zymogen and does not depend on trypsin), so starch continues to be hydrolysed to maltose/dextrins and then to glucose by brush-border enzymes. This is the mechanism of the real disorder (congenital enteropeptidase deficiency), which presents with failure to thrive and hypoproteinaemia but preserved carbohydrate handling.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: it overstates trypsinogen autoactivation. Spontaneous autoactivation is negligible in vivo, which is precisely why a dedicated activator (enteropeptidase) is required; protein digestion therefore does not proceed normally.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: it treats pancreatic lipase as a zymogen activated by enteropeptidase. Lipase is secreted in an active form and is not part of the trypsin activation cascade, so this misidentifies which enzyme depends on enteropeptidase.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: it assumes amylase must be activated by trypsin. Amylase is not a zymogen and requires no proteolytic activation, so carbohydrate digestion does not depend on the protease cascade.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: it assumes upstream enzymes fully substitute for the pancreatic proteases. Pepsin performs only limited gastric protein breakdown and cannot replace the trypsin-headed cascade, so protein digestion is not normal (compensation misconception).
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: with no enteropeptidase the initiating trypsin is never formed, so the entire pancreatic protease cascade remains inactive and protein digestion is severely impaired; amylase is secreted active, so starch digestion continues essentially normally.

subtopic: Bile function — emulsification increases the lipid–water interfacial area for pancreatic lipase (physical, not chemical, digestion)
learningObjective: Distinguish the physical action of bile salts (emulsification, which increases the surface area at which lipase acts) from the chemical hydrolysis carried out by lipase, and interpret an in-vitro experiment separating the two.
stem:
A student sets up four test tubes, each containing the same mass of triglyceride and buffered to duodenal pH at 37 °C, and measures the rate of free fatty-acid release from each:

• Tube 1: triglyceride + water only
• Tube 2: triglyceride + bile salts
• Tube 3: triglyceride + pancreatic lipase (with colipase)
• Tube 4: triglyceride + bile salts + pancreatic lipase (with colipase)

Which interpretation of the results is correct?
choices: Tube 3 releases fatty acids just as fast as Tube 4, because emulsification does not influence the rate at which lipase works.
Tube 2 releases fatty acids rapidly, because bile salts chemically hydrolyse the ester bonds of triglycerides.
No tube releases fatty acids, because pancreatic lipase must first be activated by gastric acid that is absent here.
Tube 4 releases fatty acids fastest, because emulsification by bile salts greatly increases the lipid–water surface area available to lipase, whereas bile salts alone release none.
Tube 4 gives the same rate as Tube 2, because bile salts are the principal fat-digesting agent in the duodenum.
explanation: Bile salts are amphipathic; they coat and break up large fat globules into many tiny droplets (emulsification). This is a purely physical change: it does not break any chemical bonds, so bile salts alone (Tube 2) release essentially no free fatty acids. Pancreatic lipase carries out the chemical hydrolysis, but it can only act at the water–lipid interface. On a single large fat mass (Tube 3) the interfacial area is small, so hydrolysis is slow; once bile salts have hugely increased the total surface area (Tube 4), the same amount of lipase has far more interface to work on and the rate is greatest. The experiment therefore separates the physical role of bile from the chemical role of the enzyme, and shows the two act synergistically.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: it denies that surface area affects enzyme rate. Lipase acts only at the lipid–water interface, so increasing the interfacial area by emulsification markedly speeds hydrolysis; Tube 4 is faster than Tube 3.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: it treats bile salts as digestive enzymes. Bile salts emulsify fat physically and hydrolyse no ester bonds, so Tube 2 releases essentially no fatty acids (bile-as-chemical-digester misconception).
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: it assumes pancreatic lipase needs acid activation like a zymogen. Pancreatic lipase is secreted active and works at duodenal (near-neutral) pH, so hydrolysis does occur.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: bile salts increase the interfacial surface area (physical emulsification) but release no fatty acids themselves, while lipase supplies the hydrolysis; the two together (Tube 4) give the fastest fatty-acid release.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: it again casts bile salts as the main digester. Bile salts alone produce no hydrolysis, so Tube 4 (enzyme + emulsification) cannot equal Tube 2 (emulsification only).

subtopic: Absorptive surface amplification: multiplicative contribution of circular folds, villi and microvilli, and the effect of villous/microvillous loss
learningObjective: Combine the multiplicative surface-area contributions of circular folds, villi and microvilli, and calculate the factor by which absorptive area falls when the villi and microvilli are lost but the folds remain.
stem: A smooth cylindrical tube modelling the small intestine has internal surface area A. In the real intestine three features amplify this area, each acting on the surface produced by the previous one: circular folds multiply the smooth area by 3, villi then multiply the folded area by a further 10, and microvilli then multiply the villous area by a further 20. In an untreated coeliac patient the villi are flattened and the microvilli are destroyed, so that only the circular folds remain. By what factor is the absorptive surface area of the diseased intestine reduced compared with the fully healthy intestine?
explanation: The three features act in series, so their contributions multiply. The healthy amplification relative to the smooth tube is 3 × 10 × 20 = 600, giving an area of 600A. In disease the villi and microvilli are gone but the circular folds persist, leaving 3 × A = 3A. The reduction factor is the ratio of the two: 600A / 3A = 200. In other words the patient loses exactly the villous and microvillous layers, whose combined contribution is 10 × 20 = 200, which is why absorptive capacity is so severely reduced in coeliac disease.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: the villi (×10) and microvilli (×20) are both lost while the folds remain, so the area falls by 10 × 20 = 200, i.e. 600A → 3A.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 33 comes from adding the three factors (3 + 10 + 20) instead of multiplying them, mishandling how the layers combine.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 20 counts only the loss of the microvilli (the ×20 layer) and forgets that the villi (×10) are also flattened, so it underestimates the reduction.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 30 comes from multiplying only two of the factors (3 × 10) and misidentifies which layers are retained versus lost.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 600 is the full healthy amplification and assumes the entire structure is lost; it ignores that the circular folds (×3) are retained, so it overstates the reduction.

topic: Human physiology — the liver and nitrogen metabolism
subtopic: Amino-acid deamination to ammonia and its conversion to urea; hyperammonaemia from portosystemic shunting and hepatocyte failure
learningObjective: Integrate amino-acid deamination, the liver's conversion of toxic ammonia to urea, and the hepatic portal route to explain the blood ammonia/urea pattern when liver function fails and blood is shunted past the liver.
stem: Amino acids taken in beyond metabolic need are deaminated, and the nitrogen is released as ammonia, which is highly toxic; the liver normally converts this ammonia to urea for excretion. A patient with advanced liver cirrhosis develops episodes of confusion. Blood from the intestines is partly diverted around the diseased liver through abnormal (portosystemic) vessels, and the remaining hepatocytes function poorly. The episodes are worsened by a high-protein meal; blood ammonia is elevated and blood urea is low. Which statement best explains this picture?
choices: Blood urea is low only because the kidneys excrete urea much faster than normal during liver disease.
The confusion is caused by urea itself, which is neurotoxic and accumulates because the diseased liver over-produces it.
The ammonia is made in skeletal muscle by transamination, and the liver normally clears it by excreting it unchanged in the bile.
Blood ammonia rises because the failing liver runs the urea reaction in reverse, converting urea back into ammonia to conserve nitrogen.

Deamination of amino acids releases ammonia that the liver normally converts to urea; with hepatocyte failure and portosystemic shunting the ammonia bypasses detoxification, so blood ammonia rises and urea synthesis falls.
explanation: Dietary amino acids in excess are deaminated, chiefly in the liver, releasing ammonia. Normally, blood leaving the gut travels in the hepatic portal vein straight to the liver, where hepatocytes trap the ammonia and convert it to urea (via the urea cycle) for safe renal excretion. In cirrhosis two things go wrong at once: many hepatocytes are lost, and portosystemic shunts let portal blood skip the liver. Ammonia therefore escapes conversion and accumulates in the systemic blood (neurotoxic → encephalopathy), while urea production falls because the failing/bypassed liver makes less of it. A high-protein meal supplies more amino acids (and more substrate for gut bacteria), generating still more ammonia and worsening symptoms. The correct answer links deamination, the detoxifying role of the liver and the portal route.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: it blames low urea on faster renal excretion. The urea is low because a failing/bypassed liver synthesises less of it, not because the kidneys clear it more quickly (source-vs-clearance confusion).
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: it identifies urea as the toxin. Urea is relatively non-toxic and is in fact low here; the neurotoxic agent is ammonia (toxin-misidentification, also inconsistent with the low urea).
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: transamination transfers an amino group without releasing free ammonia, and the liver excretes ammonia as urea (via blood and kidney), not unchanged in bile (mislocates ammonia production and its route of disposal).
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: it imagines the urea reaction running backwards. Urea synthesis is effectively unidirectional in the body, so the liver does not regenerate ammonia from urea; the rise reflects failure to detoxify, not reversal (reverse-reaction misconception).
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: deamination produces ammonia that the liver normally converts to urea; hepatocyte failure plus portosystemic shunting lets ammonia bypass this detoxification, raising blood ammonia and lowering urea synthesis.

topic: Human physiology — the liver and bile
subtopic: Bilirubin conjugation, solubility and gut/urobilinogen handling; post-hepatic (obstructive) jaundice pattern
learningObjective: Trace bilirubin from red-cell breakdown through hepatic conjugation, biliary excretion and gut conversion to stercobilin/urobilinogen, and predict the blood, urine and stool pattern when the bile duct is completely obstructed.
stem: When aged red blood cells are broken down, haem is converted to unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin, which is lipid-soluble and travels in the blood bound to albumin. The liver conjugates it with glucuronic acid to form conjugated (direct) bilirubin, which is water-soluble and secreted in the bile; in the gut, bacteria convert it to stercobilin (which colours the faeces) and urobilinogen (partly reabsorbed and excreted in the urine). A patient's common bile duct becomes completely blocked by a gallstone. Which pattern of findings is expected?
choices: Urinary urobilinogen is greatly increased, because the blockage forces bilirubin out of the bile, into the blood and then into the urine.
Blood unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin is raised while conjugated bilirubin stays normal, because the blockage prevents the liver from conjugating bilirubin.
Blood conjugated (direct) bilirubin is raised, the urine is dark because bilirubin appears in it, the stools are pale, and urinary urobilinogen is reduced.
The stools are darker than normal, because more bilirubin than usual now reaches the intestine.
Unconjugated bilirubin appears in the urine, because it is water-soluble and is readily filtered by the kidney.
explanation: With the bile duct completely blocked, the liver still conjugates bilirubin normally, but the water-soluble conjugated bilirubin cannot leave via the bile and backs up into the blood. Because it is water-soluble, it is filtered by the kidney and appears in the urine, making the urine dark (bilirubinuria). At the same time, no bilirubin reaches the gut, so bacteria cannot form stercobilin — hence pale, clay-coloured stools — and little or no urobilinogen is made, so reabsorbed urinary urobilinogen falls. This is the classic obstructive (post-hepatic) picture, and it depends on knowing which form of bilirubin is water-soluble and how gut bacteria generate the pigments of stool and urine.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: urobilinogen is made by gut bacteria from bilirubin that reaches the intestine; obstruction cuts off that supply, so urinary urobilinogen falls rather than rises (confuses bilirubin with its bacterial product).
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: it assumes obstruction blocks conjugation. Conjugation occurs normally in the hepatocytes; it is excretion that is blocked, so conjugated (direct) bilirubin — not unconjugated — rises (site-of-block misconception).
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: obstruction backs up water-soluble conjugated bilirubin into the blood and urine (dark urine), while no pigment reaches the gut, giving pale stools and reduced urinary urobilinogen.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: it predicts darker stools. Obstruction stops bilirubin reaching the gut, so less stercobilin is formed and the stools become pale, not dark (reversed logic on pigment flow).
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble and albumin-bound, so it is not filtered into the urine; only water-soluble conjugated bilirubin appears in urine (solubility confusion).

subtopic: Weak-acid titration / buffer region
learningObjective: Recognise the half-equivalence point of a weak-acid titration where pH = pKa.
stem: 25.0 mL of 0.100 mol/L ethanoic (acetic) acid (Ka = 1.8 × 10^-5) is titrated with 0.100 mol/L sodium hydroxide. What is the pH of the solution after exactly 12.5 mL of the sodium hydroxide has been added? (log 1.8 ≈ 0.26)
explanation: The acid initially contains 25.0 mL × 0.100 mol/L = 2.50 mmol. Adding 12.5 mL × 0.100 mol/L = 1.25 mmol of NaOH neutralises exactly half of the acid, leaving equal amounts of acetic acid and acetate. At this half-equivalence point the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation gives pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]) = pKa + log 1 = pKa. pKa = -log(1.8 × 10^-5) = 5 - 0.26 = 4.74.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct. Half-equivalence ⇒ [HA] = [A⁻] ⇒ pH = pKa = 4.74.
optionAnalysis.B: Incorrect. pH 7 would apply to a strong acid–strong base equivalence point, not a weak-acid buffer.
optionAnalysis.C: Incorrect. pH 1 corresponds to a strong acid at ~0.1 mol/L, not a weak acid part-way through titration.
optionAnalysis.D: Incorrect. 2.87 is roughly the pH of the original 0.100 mol/L acetic acid before any base is added.
optionAnalysis.E: Incorrect. 8.72 is the (basic) pH at the full equivalence point, where only acetate remains.

subtopic: Gas-phase dissociation and total pressure
learningObjective: Relate the degree of dissociation of a gas to the change in total pressure at constant volume and temperature.
stem: Pure dinitrogen tetroxide is placed in a rigid, sealed container and allowed to reach equilibrium at constant temperature according to: N2O4(g) ⇌ 2 NO2(g). At equilibrium the total pressure in the container is 1.5 times the pressure the N2O4 exerted before any dissociation occurred. What fraction of the original N2O4 has dissociated?
explanation: Let the initial pressure of pure N2O4 be P0 and let a fraction α dissociate. At equilibrium the partial pressures are: N2O4 = P0(1 − α) and NO2 = 2·P0·α (two moles of NO2 per mole of N2O4). Total pressure = P0(1 − α) + 2P0α = P0(1 + α). Setting this equal to 1.5 P0 gives 1 + α = 1.5, so α = 0.50. Half of the N2O4 has dissociated.

optionAnalysis.A: Incorrect. 0.25 results from wrongly writing total pressure as P0(1 + 2α) and solving.
optionAnalysis.B: Incorrect. 0.75 would require a total pressure of 1.75 P0, not 1.5 P0.
optionAnalysis.C: Incorrect. 0.67 inverts the relationship or mis-assigns the NO2 stoichiometry.
optionAnalysis.D: Incorrect. 0.33 comes from treating the 1.5-fold increase as if moles rather than the (1+α) factor scaled directly.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct. Total pressure factor (1 + α) = 1.5 ⇒ α = 0.50.

subtopic: Le Chatelier's principle
learningObjective: Predict the net direction of an equilibrium shift when two simultaneous stresses (temperature and volume) act on an endothermic gas-phase reaction with unequal mole numbers.
stem: Consider the gas-phase equilibrium N_2O_4(g) ⇌ 2 NO_2(g), for which the forward reaction is endothermic. A sample at equilibrium is simultaneously heated and, using a piston, compressed to half its original volume at the new (higher) temperature. Compared with the original state, what is the combined effect on the position of equilibrium?
choices: Compression favours NO_2 because it increases the total pressure, while heating has no effect on an endothermic reaction.
Heating favours NO_2 while compression favours N_2O_4, so the two effects oppose each other and the net shift depends on their relative magnitudes.
Neither change affects the position of equilibrium, because the value of K depends only on the amount of catalyst present.
Both heating and compression favour N_2O_4, so the equilibrium shifts strongly towards reactants.
Both heating and compression favour NO_2, so the equilibrium shifts strongly towards products.
explanation: Two independent stresses act in opposite senses. Heating an endothermic reaction (heat is effectively a reactant) shifts equilibrium towards the products, favouring NO_2. Halving the volume raises the pressure, so Le Chatelier's principle favours the side with fewer gas moles; here the reactant side has 1 mol vs 2 mol of product, so compression favours N_2O_4. The two effects therefore oppose one another, and the net direction cannot be stated without quantitative information on their relative sizes. Recognising that temperature and pressure changes can conflict is the key idea.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: it inverts the pressure effect and denies the (real) temperature effect on an endothermic reaction; heating certainly shifts an endothermic equilibrium.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: heating drives an endothermic reaction forward (towards NO_2) while compression favours the fewer-moles side (N_2O_4), so the effects oppose and the net shift is indeterminate without magnitudes.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: a catalyst changes neither K nor the equilibrium position, and both temperature and volume changes genuinely perturb this equilibrium.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: it correctly reads the pressure effect but inverts the temperature effect, treating the endothermic reaction as if heating favoured reactants.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: it correctly identifies heating's effect but mistakenly thinks higher pressure also favours the products; compression favours the side with fewer gas moles, which is N_2O_4.

subtopic: Kc and degree of dissociation
learningObjective: Compute an equilibrium constant Kc from the initial amount, vessel volume, and degree of dissociation of a dissociating gas.
stem: Exactly 1.00 mol of N_2O_4 is introduced into an empty, rigid 2.00 L vessel and allowed to reach equilibrium according to N_2O_4(g) ⇌ 2 NO_2(g). At equilibrium, 20.0% of the N_2O_4 has dissociated. What is the value of Kc for this reaction at the temperature of the experiment?
explanation: With α = 0.20, at equilibrium n(N_2O_4) = 1.00(1−0.20) = 0.80 mol and n(NO_2) = 2×1.00×0.20 = 0.40 mol. Dividing by V = 2.00 L gives [N_2O_4] = 0.40 M and [NO_2] = 0.20 M. Then Kc = [NO_2]^2/[N_2O_4] = (0.20)^2/0.40 = 0.040/0.40 = 0.10 M. The trap is remembering the stoichiometric factor of 2 for NO_2 formed and squaring the NO_2 concentration.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: obtained by omitting the square on [NO_2] (0.20/0.40 = 0.50 mis-stated, or by using [NO_2]=0.40 M raw moles) — it drops the correct exponent handling.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: uses concentrations of NO_2 and N_2O_4 without dividing consistently by volume (e.g. treating moles as molarities), inflating Kc.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: results from forgetting the stoichiometric factor of 2, taking n(NO_2)=0.20 mol so [NO_2]=0.10 M and Kc=(0.10)^2/0.40=0.025 mis-scaled — reflects the missing-factor-of-2 slip.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: combines the missing factor of 2 with a squaring giving (0.10)^2/0.40=0.025 M; encodes two compounded stoichiometric errors.

topic: physical chemistry: acids, bases and buffers
subtopic: buffer pH after addition of strong base
learningObjective: Apply the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation to a buffer after neutralising part of the weak acid with added strong base.
stem: A buffer is prepared by dissolving 0.20 mol of acetic acid (CH_3COOH, pKa = 4.74) and 0.20 mol of sodium acetate in water to give 1.00 L of solution. To this buffer, 0.050 mol of solid NaOH is added, with no appreciable change in volume. What is the pH of the resulting solution? (log 5/3 ≈ 0.22)
explanation: The added strong base converts an equal amount of the weak acid into its conjugate base: n(CH_3COOH) = 0.20 − 0.05 = 0.15 mol and n(CH_3COO^-) = 0.20 + 0.05 = 0.25 mol. Because both species share the same volume, the mole ratio can be used directly: pH = pKa + log([base]/[acid]) = 4.74 + log(0.25/0.15) = 4.74 + log(5/3) = 4.74 + 0.22 = 4.96. The pH rises modestly, as expected when a small amount of base is added to a buffer.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: treats the system as if all acid were neutralised to give a solution of pure acetate, computing a hydrolysis pH and ignoring the large excess of remaining buffer.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: base 0.25 mol, acid 0.15 mol, pH = 4.74 + log(5/3) = 4.74 + 0.22 = 4.96.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: adds twice the shift or double-counts the 0.05 mol (e.g. acid 0.10, base 0.30), overestimating the log term.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: applies the ratio in the reverse sense, pH = 4.74 + log(0.15/0.25) = 4.74 − 0.22, treating the base as if it were consuming the conjugate base.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: assumes the added NaOH leaves the acid/base ratio unchanged (still 1:1), ignoring that NaOH consumes acid and creates conjugate base.

subtopic: Hess's law from combustion enthalpies
learningObjective: Use Hess's law with standard enthalpies of combustion to obtain the enthalpy change of a hydrogenation reaction.
stem: For the hydrogenation of ethene, C_2H_4(g) + H_2(g) → C_2H_6(g), determine the standard enthalpy change using the following standard enthalpies of combustion: ΔH°c[C_2H_4(g)] = −1411 kJ mol^-1, ΔH°c[H_2(g)] = −286 kJ mol^-1, ΔH°c[C_2H_6(g)] = −1560 kJ mol^-1.
choices: −137 kJ mol^-1
+137 kJ mol^-1
explanation: By Hess's law, for a reaction ΔH°rxn = Σ ΔH°c(reactants) − Σ ΔH°c(products). Here ΔH°rxn = [ΔH°c(C_2H_4) + ΔH°c(H_2)] − ΔH°c(C_2H_6) = [(−1411) + (−286)] − (−1560) = (−1697) − (−1560) = −137 kJ mol^-1. The reaction is exothermic, consistent with a favourable hydrogenation. The common trap is the sign convention: with combustion enthalpies it is reactants minus products, the opposite of the formation-enthalpy expression.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: subtracts reactant sum from product with a further sign slip, e.g. −1560 − (−1411 − 286) with a wrong sign, giving a large positive value.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: computes ΔH°c(C_2H_6) − [ΔH°c(C_2H_4)+ΔH°c(H_2)] as if products minus reactants but then mis-signs one term, yielding a large negative value.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: sums all three combustion enthalpies (−1411 − 286 − 1560) instead of subtracting the product term.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: correct magnitude but reversed sign, from using products-minus-reactants (the formation-enthalpy convention) with combustion data.

subtopic: Kc with degree of dissociation from moles at equilibrium
learningObjective: Combine a measured equilibrium amount of a product with an ICE analysis to evaluate Kc for a dissociation that increases the number of gas moles.
stem: 1.00 mol of PCl_5 is placed in an evacuated, rigid 10.0 L vessel and heated to a fixed temperature, where it partially dissociates: PCl_5(g) ⇌ PCl_3(g) + Cl_2(g). At equilibrium the vessel is found to contain 0.500 mol of Cl_2. What is the value of Kc at this temperature?
explanation: Each mole of Cl_2 formed corresponds to one mole of PCl_5 consumed and one mole of PCl_3 formed. So at equilibrium n(Cl_2) = n(PCl_3) = 0.500 mol and n(PCl_5) = 1.00 − 0.500 = 0.500 mol. Dividing by V = 10.0 L: [Cl_2] = [PCl_3] = [PCl_5] = 0.0500 M. Then Kc = [PCl_3][Cl_2]/[PCl_5] = (0.0500 × 0.0500)/0.0500 = 0.0500 M. The trap is dividing every amount by the volume before forming the ratio and not confusing moles with molarity.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: forgets to divide one concentration by the volume consistently, halving the result, or mis-cancels the PCl_5 term.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: uses raw moles for the numerator product but molarity for the denominator (mixing units), doubling the true value.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: all three species are 0.0500 M, so Kc = (0.0500×0.0500)/0.0500 = 0.0500 M.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: treats n(PCl_5) as 1.00 mol (forgetting the 0.500 consumed), giving (0.05×0.05)/0.10 = 0.0125 M.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: computes the ratio in moles without dividing by volume at all, inflating Kc tenfold.

subtopic: rate-law order determination and prediction
learningObjective: Determine the individual reaction orders and rate constant from initial-rate data, then predict the rate at new concentrations.
stem: For the reaction 2 A + B → products, the following initial-rate data were obtained at constant temperature. Experiment 1: [A] = 0.10 M, [B] = 0.10 M, initial rate = 2.0×10^-3 M s^-1. Experiment 2: [A] = 0.20 M, [B] = 0.10 M, initial rate = 8.0×10^-3 M s^-1. Experiment 3: [A] = 0.10 M, [B] = 0.20 M, initial rate = 4.0×10^-3 M s^-1. What is the predicted initial rate when [A] = 0.30 M and [B] = 0.30 M?
explanation: Comparing Exp 1→2: [A] doubles at constant [B] and the rate quadruples (×4), so the order in A is 2. Comparing Exp 1→3: [B] doubles at constant [A] and the rate doubles (×2), so the order in B is 1. Hence rate = k[A]^2[B], overall third order. Using Exp 1: k = 2.0×10^-3 / [(0.10)^2(0.10)] = 2.0×10^-3 / 1.0×10^-3 = 2.0 M^-2 s^-1. For [A]=0.30, [B]=0.30: rate = 2.0 × (0.30)^2 × (0.30) = 2.0 × 0.09 × 0.30 = 5.4×10^-2 M s^-1. Note the stoichiometric coefficient of A (2) does not set the order — orders come only from the data.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: assumes the order in A equals its stoichiometric coefficient plus over-counts B, using an inflated overall order.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: orders are 2 in A and 1 in B, k = 2.0 M^-2 s^-1, so rate = 2.0×(0.30)^2×0.30 = 5.4×10^-2 M s^-1.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: takes the order in A as 1 (assuming rate ∝ [A]) rather than 2, giving 2.0×0.30×0.30 = 1.8×10^-2 M s^-1.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: simply triples the Exp-1 rate (treating both concentration increases as linear and additive) rather than applying the actual rate law.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: correct concentration factors but a power-of-ten slip in k (using 0.20 instead of 2.0), off by a factor of 10.

subtopic: Limiting reagent and percentage yield
learningObjective: Identify the limiting reagent from given masses and combine it with a percentage yield to predict the actual mass of product.
stem: The thermite reaction proceeds as 2 Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2 Fe. A mixture containing 5.4 g of aluminium and 24.0 g of iron(III) oxide is ignited and reacts to 80.0% yield. What mass of iron metal is obtained? (Molar masses in g mol⁻¹: Al = 27.0, Fe₂O₃ = 160.0, Fe = 55.85.)
explanation: Moles: Al = 5.4/27.0 = 0.200 mol; Fe₂O₃ = 24.0/160.0 = 0.150 mol. The equation needs Al:Fe₂O₃ = 2:1, so 0.200 mol Al requires only 0.100 mol Fe₂O₃. Fe₂O₃ is in excess and Al is limiting. From 2 Al → 2 Fe, moles of Fe = moles of Al = 0.200 mol, giving a theoretical mass of 0.200 × 55.85 = 11.17 g. Applying the 80.0% yield: 0.800 × 11.17 = 8.9 g.

optionAnalysis.A: Obtained by wrongly treating Fe₂O₃ as limiting (0.150 mol) to get 0.300 mol Fe = 16.8 g, then a further arithmetic slip — it uses the wrong limiting reagent.
optionAnalysis.B: This is the theoretical (100%) yield of Fe; it ignores the 80% yield factor.
optionAnalysis.C: Uses Fe₂O₃ as limiting (0.150 mol Fe₂O₃ → 0.300 mol Fe = 16.8 g) at 100% yield — wrong limiting reagent and no yield correction.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: Al is limiting (0.200 mol Fe theoretical = 11.17 g), and 80% of 11.17 g = 8.9 g.
optionAnalysis.E: Halves the correct answer, as if only 1 mol Fe formed per 2 mol Al (misreading the 2:2 stoichiometry as 2:1).

subtopic: Gas laws combined with stoichiometry
learningObjective: Combine reaction stoichiometry with the ideal gas equation to compute the volume of gas released under stated conditions, accounting for incomplete conversion.
stem: A 12.5 g sample of calcium carbonate is heated and 90.0% of it decomposes according to CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g). The carbon dioxide released is collected at 27 °C and 1.00 atm. What volume does it occupy? (M(CaCO₃) = 100.0 g mol⁻¹; R = 0.0821 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.)
explanation: Moles of CaCO₃ = 12.5/100.0 = 0.125 mol. Only 90.0% decomposes, so moles of CO₂ = 0.900 × 0.125 = 0.1125 mol. The absolute temperature is 27 + 273 = 300 K. Using PV = nRT: V = nRT/P = (0.1125 × 0.0821 × 300)/1.00 = 2.77 L.

optionAnalysis.A: Uses T = 27 K (forgets to convert °C to kelvin) with the correct 0.1125 mol — but the wrong T; the value shown reflects using 273 K instead of 300 K.
optionAnalysis.B: Doubles the moles of CO₂, as if 2 mol CO₂ formed per mol CaCO₃, then applies the gas law.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: 0.1125 mol CO₂ at 300 K and 1.00 atm gives V = 2.77 L.
optionAnalysis.D: Ignores the 90% conversion and uses the full 0.125 mol, giving 3.08 L.
optionAnalysis.E: Uses T = 27 K (treating the Celsius value as an absolute temperature) with 0.1125 mol, giving only 0.281 L.

subtopic: Oxidation numbers and electron balance
learningObjective: Assign oxidation-state changes in a redox reaction, balance electron transfer, and use the electron stoichiometry to relate moles of oxidant and reductant.
stem: In acidic solution, dichromate oxidises iron(II): Cr₂O₇²⁻ + Fe²⁺ + H⁺ → Cr³⁺ + Fe³⁺ + H₂O (unbalanced). If 0.0200 mol of Cr₂O₇²⁻ is completely reduced, how many moles of Fe²⁺ are oxidised?
explanation: Each Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻ is +6 and becomes +3 in Cr³⁺, a gain of 3 electrons per Cr. With two Cr atoms per dichromate ion, one Cr₂O₇²⁻ accepts 6 electrons. Each Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ loses 1 electron. To balance electrons, 6 mol Fe²⁺ are needed per mol Cr₂O₇²⁻. Therefore 0.0200 × 6 = 0.120 mol Fe²⁺.

optionAnalysis.A: Uses a 3:1 ratio, counting 3 electrons per dichromate (one Cr only) rather than 6 for the pair.
optionAnalysis.B: Assumes a 1:1 mole ratio, ignoring that the electron counts differ (6 vs 1).
optionAnalysis.C: Uses a 12:1 ratio, double-counting by taking +6 charge change per Cr and doubling again over the two atoms.
optionAnalysis.D: Uses a 2:1 ratio, counting only the two Cr atoms but forgetting each Cr transfers 3 electrons.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: 6 electrons accepted per Cr₂O₇²⁻ (2 Cr × 3 e), so 6 × 0.0200 = 0.120 mol Fe²⁺.

subtopic: First ionization energy irregularities
learningObjective: Predict relative first ionization energies across a period, including the dips caused by electron-pair repulsion in np⁴ and the stability of ns² and half-filled np³ configurations.
stem: Consider the second-period elements boron (Z = 5), carbon (Z = 6), nitrogen (Z = 7) and oxygen (Z = 8). Which one of the following statements about their first ionization energies is correct?
choices: Boron has a higher first ionization energy than carbon, because carbon must lose an electron from a doubly occupied 2p orbital.
Carbon and nitrogen have equal first ionization energies because both have singly occupied 2p orbitals only.
Oxygen has the highest first ionization energy of the four because it has the greatest nuclear charge.
Nitrogen has a higher first ionization energy than oxygen, because removing an electron from N breaks a stable half-filled 2p³ configuration whereas O loses a paired 2p electron.
First ionization energy increases strictly in the order B < C < N < O, following the increase in nuclear charge across the period.
explanation: First ionization energy generally rises across a period, but there is a well-known dip at group 16 (oxygen): O has configuration 2p⁴, so ionization removes one of a spin-paired pair, and the relief of electron–electron repulsion makes removal easier than expected. Nitrogen (2p³) has a stable half-filled subshell with all p electrons unpaired, so its ionization energy is higher than oxygen's. Hence IE₁(N) > IE₁(O), even though O has the larger nuclear charge. The correct trend is B < C < O < N.

optionAnalysis.A: Reverses the B/C order; carbon actually has the higher IE₁ (there is no B<... anomaly here — the anomaly is the small Be/B dip, not C/B this way).
optionAnalysis.B: Wrongly claims equality; C (2p²) and N (2p³) differ, with N higher due to greater nuclear charge and half-filled stability.
optionAnalysis.C: Equates highest nuclear charge with highest IE, ignoring the half-filled/paired-electron effect that puts N above O.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: the 2p³ half-filled stability of N and the pairing repulsion in O's 2p⁴ make IE₁(N) > IE₁(O).
optionAnalysis.E: Assumes a strictly monotonic increase, missing the O dip; the real order is B < C < O < N.

subtopic: Molecular geometry and polarity
learningObjective: Apply VSEPR theory to species with lone pairs, determine molecular geometry, and judge net polarity from the vector sum of bond dipoles.
stem: Four of the following molecules possess a net dipole moment. Which molecule is NON-polar despite containing polar bonds? (All are stable, known molecules.)
choices: SF₄
XeF₄
ClF₃
NF₃
OF₂
explanation: XeF₄ has 6 electron domains around Xe (4 bonding pairs + 2 lone pairs). The two lone pairs occupy opposite axial positions of the octahedral arrangement, leaving the four Xe–F bonds in a square-planar geometry. The four equal Xe–F bond dipoles point to the corners of a square and cancel exactly, so the molecule is non-polar. SF₄ is see-saw (one lone pair) – polar; NF₃ is trigonal pyramidal – polar; ClF₃ is T-shaped – polar; OF₂ is bent – polar. Only XeF₄ has a symmetry that cancels the bond dipoles.

optionAnalysis.A: SF₄ is see-saw shaped due to one equatorial lone pair; the dipoles do not cancel, so it is polar.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: square-planar XeF₄ (2 lone pairs axial) cancels all four bond dipoles, giving zero net moment.
optionAnalysis.C: ClF₃ is T-shaped (two lone pairs); the asymmetric arrangement leaves a net dipole — polar.
optionAnalysis.D: NF₃ is trigonal pyramidal; the three N–F dipoles and the lone pair give a net moment — polar.
optionAnalysis.E: OF₂ is bent (two lone pairs on O); the two O–F dipoles add to a net moment — polar.

subtopic: Functional-group and structural isomerism
learningObjective: Enumerate all constitutional (structural) isomers of a given molecular formula, correctly including both carbon-skeleton and functional-group isomers while excluding stereoisomers and duplicates.
