optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: This is valid (modus tollens / contrapositive): denying the consequent validly yields denial of the antecedent. Misconception: assuming any conditional syllogism containing a negation shares the stem's flaw.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: This argument is actually valid, because its first premise is the converse ('everything that scratches glass is a sapphire'); given that premise the conclusion follows by modus ponens. Misconception: judging arguments parallel because they reach the same conclusion ('it is a sapphire') rather than by shared logical form.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: This is a valid argument (modus ponens): it affirms the antecedent 'is a sapphire' and validly concludes 'scratches glass'. Matching a flawed argument to a valid one fails. Misconception: matching surface vocabulary rather than logical form.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: This is a fallacy, but a different one — denying the antecedent ('not a sapphire, therefore does not scratch glass'). Misconception: treating any invalid conditional argument as 'the same flaw' regardless of its specific form.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: It has the stem's structure — 'all S are G; this is G; therefore this is S' — affirming the consequent and invalidly inferring the antecedent, exactly parallel to the dehydration argument.

subtopic: Principle identification: selecting the principle that best justifies a differential judgement
learningObjective: Identify the general principle that, if adopted, would most strongly justify a specific differential judgement between two cases.
stem: An anti-doping panel considers two swimmers, X and Y. Both test positive for the same banned stimulant at identical concentrations. The panel establishes that X took the substance knowingly in order to gain an advantage, whereas Y ingested it unknowingly in a contaminated dietary supplement. The panel bans X but clears Y. Which of the following principles, if accepted, would most strongly justify the panel's decision to treat the two cases differently?
choices: An athlete should be sanctioned whenever a banned substance is detected above the permitted threshold, irrespective of how it entered the body.
An athlete should be sanctioned only if he or she bears personal responsibility for the banned substance entering the body.
An athlete should be sanctioned only if the banned substance measurably improved his or her performance.
An athlete should be sanctioned only if he or she has previously been found guilty of a doping offence.
The severity of a sanction should be proportional to the measured concentration of the banned substance.
explanation: To justify treating the two swimmers differently, the chosen principle must turn on the one feature that actually differs between them — X acted knowingly, Y did not — while everything else (substance, concentration) is identical. A responsibility-based principle bans the athlete who is responsible (X) and clears the one who is not (Y), exactly reproducing the panel's decision. The other principles either treat both cases alike or hinge on a factor the scenario does not distinguish.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: This strict-liability principle would require banning BOTH swimmers, since both exceeded the threshold, so it cannot justify differential treatment. Misconception: assuming any anti-doping principle supports any anti-doping decision.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: Making personal responsibility the criterion tracks precisely the knowing/unknowing difference between X and Y, justifying banning the responsible swimmer while clearing the blameless one.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: The scenario never states that performance effects differed between the swimmers, so this principle does not track the knowing/unknowing distinction. Misconception: importing a plausible-sounding but irrelevant criterion.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: The cases are distinguished by intent, not by prior record; nothing indicates that either swimmer has a previous offence. Misconception: choosing a fair-sounding principle that is orthogonal to the stated difference between the cases.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: The concentration is identical for the two swimmers, so a concentration-based principle predicts identical, not different, treatment. Misconception: seizing on the salient 'same concentration' detail as if it were the operative reason.

subtopic: Multi-premise quantifier deduction (must-be-true) from a short passage
learningObjective: Draw a valid must-be-true inference by combining several quantified statements in a short passage, while rejecting invalid conversions and over-generalisations.
stem: Read the following passage: "At Northgate Hospital, everyone who serves on the finance committee also serves on the audit board. Some members of the audit board are external consultants brought in from other organisations. Under the hospital's rules, no external consultant may vote on the annual budget, whereas every member of the finance committee is entitled to vote on it." If all of the statements in the passage are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Every member of the audit board may vote on the annual budget.
Some members of the finance committee are external consultants.
No member of the finance committee is an external consultant.
No member of the audit board may vote on the annual budget.
Every external consultant serves on the audit board.
explanation: Combine the two voting statements: every finance-committee member is entitled to vote, but no external consultant may vote. Anyone who may vote therefore cannot be an external consultant, so no finance-committee member can be an external consultant — a valid must-be-true conclusion. The other options either reverse a 'some' statement, or over-extend a rule that applies only to consultants or only to finance-committee members.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: Some audit-board members are external consultants, who may not vote, so not every audit-board member may vote. Misconception: over-generalising the finance committee's voting right to the whole audit board.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: This is in fact impossible — finance members may all vote and consultants may not, so no finance member can be a consultant. Misconception: assuming that groups sharing the audit board must overlap everywhere.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: Every finance member may vote and no external consultant may vote; therefore no finance-committee member can be an external consultant, a valid deduction combining the two voting rules.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: Finance-committee members serve on the audit board and are entitled to vote, so some audit-board members certainly can vote. Misconception: extending 'no consultant may vote' to the entire audit board.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: The passage states only that SOME audit-board members are consultants; it does not follow that every consultant is on the audit board. Misconception: illicitly converting 'some A are C' into 'all C are A'.

subtopic: Ordering five items from relative-position clues and identifying a forced conclusion
learningObjective: Combine several relative-order constraints (adjacency, 'ahead of', 'not first', 'after') to pin down a unique ordering and identify which statement is necessarily true.
stem: Five runners — P, Q, R, S and T — finish a race in positions first to fifth, with no dead heats (no ties). The following facts are known: (1) R finishes immediately ahead of P, with no runner between them. (2) Q finishes somewhere ahead of R, but Q is not first. (3) S finishes at some point after P. On the basis of these facts alone, which one of the following must be true?
choices: Q finishes fourth.
R finishes fifth.
S finishes ahead of Q.
P finishes ahead of R.
T finishes first.
explanation: From the clues, among P, Q, R and S the order is forced: Q is ahead of R (clue 2), R is immediately ahead of P (clue 1), and S is after P (clue 3), giving the relative sequence Q, R, P, S. The only remaining runner, T, must be slotted in. If T were anywhere except first, then Q — the earliest of the other four — would be first, contradicting clue 2 (Q is not first). Therefore T must finish first, and the unique full order is T (1st), Q (2nd), R (3rd), P (4th), S (5th). Hence 'T finishes first' must be true.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: in the forced order Q finishes second, not fourth.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: R finishes third; S is the runner in fifth (last) place.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: S finishes fifth (last) and Q second, so S is behind Q, not ahead.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: clue 1 puts R immediately AHEAD of P, so P is behind R (P is 4th, R is 3rd), never ahead of it.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: placing T anywhere but first would make Q first (Q leads the other four), which clue 2 forbids; so T must be first, giving the unique order T, Q, R, P, S.

subtopic: Identifying a suppressed (bridging) assumption linking a per-unit cost saving to a total-cost conclusion
learningObjective: Identify the necessary unstated assumption that must hold for a conclusion about total cost to follow from evidence about cost per unit.
stem: A bakery wants to reduce the total cost of the ingredients it buys. It has decided to replace the butter in its cakes with a margarine that costs less per kilogram than butter. The owner reasons: 'Because margarine is cheaper per kilogram than butter, making this substitution will lower our ingredient costs.' Which of the following is an assumption on which the owner's argument depends?
choices: The price of butter is expected to rise faster than the price of margarine over the coming year.
Margarine is nutritionally healthier for consumers than butter is.
Customers will be unable to taste any difference between cakes made with butter and cakes made with margarine.
No other bakery in the area has already switched from butter to margarine.
Producing the same range of cakes will not require the bakery to use a substantially greater mass of margarine than the mass of butter it replaces.
explanation: The conclusion is about total ingredient cost, but the evidence is only about price per kilogram. A lower price per kilogram guarantees a lower total cost only if the quantity used does not rise enough to cancel the saving. The argument therefore silently assumes the bakery will not need substantially more margarine (by mass) than the butter it replaces. Applying the negation test: if far more margarine were required, total cost could rise, and the argument would collapse, confirming this is a necessary assumption. Taste, health, future price trends and competitors' choices are all irrelevant to whether this substitution lowers cost.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: the argument concerns the present substitution, and a per-kilogram saving already exists now; future price trends are not needed for the conclusion. (Misconception: supplying an extra strengthening fact rather than a necessary assumption.)
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: nutritional health is irrelevant to a comparison of ingredient costs. (Misconception: importing an unrelated 'better product' consideration.)
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: whether customers can taste the difference bears on sales and revenue, not on whether ingredient costs fall; the conclusion is only about cost. (Misconception: treating an assumption about product acceptance as required by a cost argument.)
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: what rival bakeries have done has no bearing on this bakery's own costs. (Misconception: appeal to what others do.)
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: a lower price per kilogram lowers total cost only if the mass used stays comparable; if far more margarine were required, the total cost could rise. Negating this assumption defeats the argument, so the argument depends on it.

subtopic: Principal flaw: generalising from a self-selected, unrepresentative sample (representativeness, not sample size)
learningObjective: Diagnose an argument that generalises to a population from a self-selected sample, distinguishing representativeness bias from mere small sample size and from unrelated fallacies.
stem: A magazine aimed at keen runners emailed a survey to its 40,000 subscribers, asking whether they take vigorous exercise regularly. Of the 6,000 subscribers who chose to reply, 95% said they exercise at least five times a week. The magazine concluded that most adults in the country exercise at least five times a week. The reasoning is most vulnerable to which one of the following criticisms?
choices: It confuses a factor that is necessary for good health with one that is sufficient for it.
It concludes that a property of a group as a whole must be shared by each individual member of that group.
It assumes that because two variables are correlated, one of them must cause the other.
It draws a conclusion about adults in general from a group of people who are unlikely to be representative of adults in general.
It generalises to the whole population from a sample that is too small to be statistically reliable.
explanation: The sample consists of people who subscribe to a runners' magazine and who then chose to reply, a doubly self-selected group of exercise enthusiasts. Generalising from them to 'most adults in the country' is unsound because the sample is unrepresentative of adults in general. Crucially, the defect is not sample size: 6,000 respondents is a large sample, yet a large biased sample is still misleading. The other options name fallacies (necessary/sufficient confusion, correlation-causation, fallacy of division) that the argument does not actually commit.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: no necessary-versus-sufficient condition is confused in this argument; that is a different flaw that is not present. (Misconception: mislabelling with an unrelated fallacy.)
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: this describes the fallacy of division (whole-to-part), which the argument does not commit; it reasons from a part (the sample) to a whole, if anything. (Misconception: mislabelling with a different structural fallacy.)
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: the argument makes no causal claim linking two correlated variables; it makes a generalisation from a sample. (Misconception: reaching reflexively for 'correlation is not causation'.)
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: the respondents are self-selected readers of a runners' magazine, so they are unlikely to represent adults in general, making the leap to 'most adults' unwarranted. This names the actual flaw: generalisation from an unrepresentative, self-selected sample.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: the sample was large (6,000 replies), so 'too small' is not the defect; a large but biased sample is still misleading. (Misconception: blaming sample size when the real problem is representativeness.)

subtopic: Combined work/rate with a two-phase schedule (one pipe opened then closed)
learningObjective: Model a filling task with two phases (both agents then one alone) using additive rates and solve for an unknown duration.
stem: A cistern can be filled by pipe A alone in 20 minutes and by pipe B alone in 30 minutes. Both pipes are opened together on an empty cistern. After a while, pipe A is closed, and pipe B alone fills the rest of the cistern. The cistern becomes completely full exactly 18 minutes after the two pipes were first opened. For how many minutes was pipe A open?
choices: 12 minutes
8 minutes
3 minutes
9 minutes
6 minutes
explanation: Let pipe A be open for t minutes. During those t minutes both pipes run at a combined rate of 1/20 + 1/30 = 1/12 of the cistern per minute; then pipe B runs alone at 1/30 per minute for the remaining (18 - t) minutes. Setting the filled fraction equal to 1: t(1/12) + (18 - t)(1/30) = 1. Multiplying through by 60 gives 5t + 2(18 - t) = 60, so 5t + 36 - 2t = 60, giving 3t = 24 and t = 8. Pipe A was open for 8 minutes.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: this ignores the second phase and reports how long the two pipes together would take to fill the cistern (1 ÷ 1/12 = 12 minutes). (Misconception: dropping the single-pipe finishing phase.)
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: with both pipes on for t minutes then B alone for (18 - t) minutes, t(1/12) + (18 - t)(1/30) = 1 gives 5t + 2(18 - t) = 60, so t = 8.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: this results from swapping the roles of the pipes (assuming pipe B is closed early and pipe A finishes), which solves a different scenario. (Misconception: misreading which pipe stops.)
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 9 is half of 18, obtained by assuming pipe A was open for exactly half of the total time. (Misconception: unjustified symmetry assumption.)
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: this comes from adding the rates incorrectly as 1/20 + 1/30 = 1/10 instead of 1/12, which yields t = 6. (Misconception: faulty addition of fractional rates.)

subtopic: Two-set overlap: greatest and least possible intersection via inclusion–exclusion bounds
learningObjective: Determine the greatest and least possible size of the intersection of two subsets of a finite universe when some elements may belong to neither set, and combine the two extremes.
stem: At a conference of 150 delegates, 96 can speak French and 72 can speak German. Some delegates may speak neither language. Let b be the number of delegates who can speak both French and German. What is the difference between the greatest possible value of b and the least possible value of b?
explanation: The greatest overlap occurs when the German speakers are contained as far as possible within the French speakers, so b can be at most min(96, 72) = 72 (feasible, since the remaining 150 - 96 = 54 delegates speak neither). The least overlap occurs when the two groups are spread as far apart as possible; because 96 + 72 = 168 exceeds 150, they must overlap by at least 168 - 150 = 18, so the least value of b is 18 (achieved when no delegate speaks neither language). The required difference is 72 - 18 = 54.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 24 is the difference of the two group sizes (96 - 72), mistaken for the overlap answer. (Misconception: subtracting the group totals directly.)
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 18 is only the least possible value of b, not the difference between the greatest and least. (Misconception: answering a different sub-question.)
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: greatest b = min(96, 72) = 72; least b = 96 + 72 - 150 = 18; the difference is 72 - 18 = 54.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 90 comes from adding the greatest and least values (72 + 18) instead of subtracting them. (Misconception: sum-versus-difference slip.)
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 72 is only the greatest possible value of b, not the difference. (Misconception: reporting one extreme instead of the difference.)

subtopic: Resolving an apparent discrepancy: distinguishing an absolute count from a per-capita rate (exposure/volume effect)
learningObjective: Select the statement that best resolves an apparent paradox by recognising that a fall in per-person risk is consistent with a rise in an absolute count when exposure increases.
stem: In a certain country, a new law requiring all cyclists to wear helmets was introduced. In the year after the law took effect, the total number of cyclists admitted to hospital with head injuries was higher than in the year before, even though helmets are known to reduce a cyclist's risk of head injury. Which of the following, if true, best explains this apparent discrepancy?
choices: After the law was introduced, the number of people who regularly cycled increased substantially.
Helmets are more effective at preventing head injuries in low-speed collisions than in high-speed collisions.
In neighbouring countries that did not introduce a helmet law, the number of cycling head injuries stayed about the same over the same period.
Many cyclists ignored the new law and continued to ride without wearing a helmet.
Helmets protect the head but give no protection against injuries to other parts of the body.
explanation: The claim that helmets reduce head-injury risk is a statement about the risk per cyclist (a rate), whereas the reported rise is in the absolute number of cyclists admitted (a count). If far more people cycle after the law, total exposure increases, so the absolute number of head injuries can rise even while each individual cyclist is safer. Only option D supplies the increase in exposure that reconciles the two facts. The other options attack helmet effectiveness, shift outside the scope of head injuries, or fail to explain any rise above the previous level.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: helmets lower each cyclist's head-injury risk (a rate), but if many more people cycle after the law, total exposure rises, so the absolute number of head injuries can increase even though each cyclist is safer, reconciling the two facts.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: variation in helmet effectiveness with collision speed does not explain why the total number of head injuries rose after helmets were introduced. (Misconception: attacking helmet efficacy without explaining an increase.)
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: a stable trend elsewhere does not explain the domestic rise; if anything it deepens the puzzle. (Misconception: offering a comparison that fails to account for the change.)
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: if many rode without helmets, their injury rate would resemble the pre-law situation, which explains no rise above the previous level. (Misconception: explaining reduced benefit rather than an actual increase.)
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: that helmets do not protect other body parts is irrelevant, since the discrepancy concerns head injuries specifically. (Misconception: shifting to injuries outside the scope of the puzzle.)

subtopic: Weakening a causal claim by a pre-existing trend (the outcome was already declining before the intervention)
learningObjective: Weaken a before-after causal claim by identifying that the outcome was already following a pre-existing trend independent of the intervention.
stem: Two years ago a town council replaced the street lighting on Maple Road with much brighter LED lamps. In the two years since, the number of night-time road accidents on Maple Road has fallen by 30%. The council concludes that the brighter lighting caused this reduction and now plans to fit the same lamps on every road in the town. Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the council's argument?
choices: Night-time accidents on Maple Road had already been falling by roughly 30% every two years throughout the decade before the new lighting was fitted.
The brighter LED lighting cost considerably more to install and maintain than the council had originally budgeted for the project.
Since the new lighting was installed, the number of daytime accidents on Maple Road has remained essentially unchanged.
Surveys show that most drivers say they feel noticeably safer and more confident when driving along well-lit roads at night.
Since the new lighting was installed, thefts from cars parked overnight on Maple Road have also fallen noticeably.
explanation: The argument infers causation purely from a before-after change. It is weakened most by evidence that the fall would have happened even without the new lamps. Option C shows the 30%-per-two-years decline is simply the continuation of a long-standing pre-existing trend, so the lighting need not have contributed anything, and the case for rolling it out town-wide collapses.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: If night-time accidents were already dropping by about 30% every two years before the lamps were fitted, the observed fall is just the continuation of a pre-existing trend and need not be due to the lighting at all, destroying the causal inference.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: The cost of the scheme is irrelevant to whether the lighting caused the fall in accidents. Misconception: attacking a proposal on grounds (expense) unrelated to the causal claim actually being made.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: Unchanged daytime accidents act as a control that, if anything, strengthens the case, since a general cause would have lowered daytime accidents too. Misconception: assuming any 'no change' comparison must weaken a causal claim, when here it supports it.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: Drivers' subjective feelings of safety, if anything, lend mild support to the council and give no reason to doubt the causal claim. Misconception: treating supportive or merely subjective evidence as though it undermines the argument.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: A fall in overnight car thefts concerns a completely different outcome and does not bear on whether the lighting reduced accidents. Misconception: treating an unrelated additional effect as evidence for or against the accident claim.

subtopic: Necessary and sufficient conditions: valid deduction via the contrapositive of a sufficient condition
learningObjective: Combine a necessary condition ('only if') and a sufficient condition ('if...then') and use the contrapositive to draw the one valid conclusion.
stem: At a certain university all of the following are true: (i) a student is awarded the Dean's Scholarship only if she has a first-class average; (ii) every student who has a first-class average and has also completed a research project is awarded the Dean's Scholarship; (iii) Anna has completed a research project but was not awarded the Dean's Scholarship. Which one of the following can be validly concluded?
choices: Had Anna not completed a research project, she would have been awarded the scholarship.
Anna does not have a first-class average.
Anna has a first-class average but chose to turn the Dean's Scholarship down.
No student who completes a research project is ever awarded the Dean's Scholarship.
At least some students who have a first-class average are not awarded the scholarship.
explanation: Statement (ii) says that having a first-class average AND a completed research project is sufficient for the scholarship. Its contrapositive: anyone not awarded the scholarship must lack a first-class average or lack a research project (or both). Anna was not awarded it, so the antecedent of (ii) fails; yet she did complete a research project, so the missing ingredient can only be the first-class average. Statement (i), a necessary condition, is not even required for this step. Hence Anna does not have a first-class average.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: This denies the antecedent of the sufficient condition (ii); completing the project was never established as her only obstacle, and without it she might still fail to qualify. Misconception: treating a sufficient condition as though it were necessary (denying the antecedent).
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: By the contrapositive of (ii), not being awarded the scholarship while having completed a research project forces the absence of a first-class average.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: Nothing in the premises mentions declining the award; turning it down is invented information. Misconception: supplying an unstated explanation instead of drawing only what the premises force.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: One student's failure cannot support a universal claim about all research-project students; indeed (ii) says such students are awarded the scholarship whenever they also have a first-class average. Misconception: over-generalising from a single case.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: The premises only let us conclude that Anna lacks a first-class average, so she is not an example of a first-class student who was denied the award; no first-class student is shown to have been refused. Misconception: confusing 'a first-class average is necessary for the award' with 'some first-class students are denied the award'.

subtopic: Change in a rate under differential percentage growth of numerator and denominator; percentage points vs relative change
learningObjective: Compute the change in a rate when numerator and denominator grow by different percentages, and distinguish percentage points from relative percentage change.
stem: In 2023 a diagnostic laboratory tested a batch of samples, and 60% of them gave a positive result. In 2024 the laboratory tested 50% more samples than in 2023, and the number of positive results was 20% higher than in 2023. By how much did the laboratory's positivity rate (the percentage of tested samples that are positive) change from 2023 to 2024?
choices: It rose by 12 percentage points, from 60% to 72%.
It rose by 15 percentage points, from 60% to 75%.
It fell by 12 percentage points, from 60% to 48%.
It stayed the same, at 60%.
It fell by 20 percentage points, from 60% to 40%.
explanation: Take 100 samples in 2023, of which 60 are positive. In 2024 there are 150 samples (50% more) and 60 x 1.20 = 72 positives, so the positivity rate is 72/150 = 48%. The rate therefore falls by 60 - 48 = 12 percentage points. Because the denominator (samples) grew faster (50%) than the numerator (positives, 20%), the rate had to drop.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 72 is the 2024 positive count, not the rate; treating the 20% rise in positives as a rise in the rate ignores the larger rise in the denominator. Misconception: confusing a change in the numerator's count with a change in the rate.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 75% comes from dividing by the smaller growth factor (60 x 1.5 / 1.2), i.e. swapping which quantity grew by which percentage. Misconception: inverting the numerator (positives) and denominator (total samples) growth factors.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: 72 positives out of 150 samples is 48%, a fall of 12 percentage points from 60%.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: The rate is unchanged only if numerator and denominator grow by the same factor; here they grow by 20% and 50%, so the rate must change. Misconception: assuming a rate is unaffected whenever both of its parts increase.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 48% is 20% below 60% in relative terms (48 = 0.8 x 60), but that is a 20% relative decrease, not 20 percentage points. Misconception: reporting a relative percentage change as though it were a change in percentage points.

subtopic: Scheduling five items across weekday slots from a fixed slot, ordering, gap and exclusion constraints
learningObjective: Combine fixed-slot, ordering, gap and exclusion constraints to deduce a unique schedule and identify the forced conclusion.
stem: Five students - G, H, J, K and L - each give exactly one presentation. The presentations take place on five consecutive weekdays, Monday to Friday, with exactly one presentation per day. The schedule satisfies all of the following: G presents on Wednesday; J presents on an earlier day than K; H presents on an earlier day than L; exactly two presentations are scheduled on the days between H's presentation and L's presentation; K does not present on Friday. Which one of the following must be true?
choices: K presents on Friday.
J presents on a later day than H.
K presents on Thursday.
L presents on Thursday.
H presents on Monday.
explanation: G is fixed on Wednesday (day 3). 'Exactly two presentations between H and L' means H and L sit three days apart, and with H before L the only options are (Monday, Thursday) or (Tuesday, Friday). If H = Monday and L = Thursday, the free days Tuesday and Friday must take J and K; since K cannot be on Friday, K = Tuesday and J = Friday, but that makes J later than K, violating 'J before K'. So H = Tuesday and L = Friday. The free days Monday and Thursday take J and K, and 'J before K' forces J = Monday, K = Thursday. The unique schedule is Mon = J, Tue = H, Wed = G, Thu = K, Fri = L, so K presents on Thursday.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: The constraints explicitly forbid K on Friday, and in the valid schedule Friday is taken by L. Misconception: ignoring the 'K not on Friday' exclusion.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: In the valid schedule J presents on Monday and H on Tuesday, so J is earlier, not later, than H. Misconception: assuming the two separate order chains (J before K, H before L) force H into the earliest slot.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: The constraints yield the unique schedule Mon = J, Tue = H, Wed = G, Thu = K, Fri = L, in which K presents on Thursday.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: L = Thursday also comes from the rejected (Monday, Thursday) arrangement. Misconception: overlooking that keeping K off Friday makes that arrangement violate 'J presents before K'.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: H = Monday belongs to the rejected (Monday, Thursday) arrangement, which fails because, once K is kept off Friday, it cannot satisfy 'J before K'. Misconception: adopting that placement for H and L without checking the ordering and Friday constraints.

subtopic: Resolving an apparent paradox via an overlooked queueing stage (faster processing yet longer total time under higher load)
learningObjective: Resolve an apparent paradox by identifying an overlooked stage (queue waiting time) whose growth outweighs a faster processing step.
stem: A factory replaced its single processing machine with a new one that handles items twice as fast as the old machine. Surprisingly, after the change the average time an item spent in the factory, from arrival to dispatch, actually increased. Which one of the following, if true, best resolves this apparent paradox?
choices: The old machine had been in continuous service at the factory for more than twenty years.
The new machine only reaches its full speed after a short warm-up period at the start of each working day.
Customers are now willing to pay a higher price in return for faster delivery of their orders.
After the new machine was installed the factory accepted about three times as many orders, so items now wait much longer in a queue before they reach the machine.
The new machine occasionally breaks down and is then out of action while it is repaired within a day.
explanation: The time an item spends in the factory is its waiting (queueing) time plus its processing time. The new machine halved the processing time, so for the total to rise, waiting time must have grown by more. Option A supplies exactly this: tripling the order volume created long queues, so items now wait far longer before processing even though each item is handled faster once it starts.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: The old machine's age is background information that says nothing about why times rose after the change. Misconception: mistaking an irrelevant historical fact for an explanation.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: A brief daily warm-up still leaves the machine at least as fast as the old one for most of the day, so it cannot push the overall average above the old baseline. Misconception: treating a small, partial slowdown as if it could outweigh a full doubling of speed.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: Customers' willingness to pay concerns pricing and demand, not the mechanism by which processing-to-dispatch time increased. Misconception: mistaking a statement of motivation or demand for a causal explanation of the delay.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: Total dwell time = waiting time + processing time. Tripling the order volume lengthens the queue so much that the extra waiting time outweighs the halved processing time, so the average time in the factory rises despite the faster machine.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: Occasional breakdowns repaired within a day cannot systematically outweigh a doubling of processing speed and would not reliably raise the long-run average. Misconception: seizing on any negative detail without checking it is large and consistent enough to reverse the effect.

subtopic: Absolute-value equations
learningObjective: Solve an absolute-value equation by splitting into cases and count the distinct real solutions.
stem: How many distinct real values of x satisfy the equation |x² − 4| = 3 ?
explanation: The equation splits into two cases. Case 1: x² − 4 = 3 ⇒ x² = 7 ⇒ x = ±√7 (two real solutions). Case 2: x² − 4 = −3 ⇒ x² = 1 ⇒ x = ±1 (two more real solutions). Because √7 ≈ 2.65 and 1 are all distinct, there are four distinct real solutions in total.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct. ±√7 and ±1 give four distinct real roots.
optionAnalysis.B: Incorrect. 3 would require one repeated root, but none of the four values coincide.
optionAnalysis.C: Incorrect. Solutions clearly exist, so 0 is wrong.
optionAnalysis.D: Incorrect. 2 results from solving only the case x² − 4 = 3 (or only x² = 1).
optionAnalysis.E: Incorrect. 1 ignores that each x² value yields two opposite roots.

subtopic: Combinatorial probability with 'at least'
learningObjective: Compute an 'at least' probability using combinations and the complement rule.
stem: A committee of 4 people is chosen at random from a group of 5 men and 4 women. What is the probability that the committee contains at least 2 women?
explanation: The total number of committees is C(9,4) = 126. Use the complement of 'fewer than 2 women': committees with 0 women = C(5,4) = 5; committees with exactly 1 woman = C(4,1)·C(5,3) = 4·10 = 40. So committees with at least 2 women = 126 − 5 − 40 = 81. The probability is 81/126 = 9/14.

optionAnalysis.A: Incorrect. 3/7 = 54/126 does not match any correct combination of the cases.
optionAnalysis.B: Incorrect. 20/63 = 40/126 is the probability of exactly one woman only.
optionAnalysis.D: Incorrect. 5/14 = 45/126 is the probability of the complement (0 or 1 woman) after simplification error.
optionAnalysis.E: Incorrect. 2/3 = 84/126 slightly over-counts and is not obtained from the correct case analysis.

subtopic: Change-of-base substitution in a logarithmic equation
learningObjective: Solve a logarithmic equation by reducing it to a quadratic through a substitution and combine the roots.
stem: Consider the equation log₂(x) + logₓ(2) = 5/2, defined for x > 0 with x ≠ 1. What is the product of all real solutions of this equation?
explanation: Let t = log₂(x). By change of base logₓ(2) = 1/log₂(x) = 1/t, so the equation becomes t + 1/t = 5/2, i.e. 2t² − 5t + 2 = 0, giving t = 2 or t = 1/2. Hence x = 2² = 4 or x = 2^(1/2) = √2, both valid (positive, ≠ 1). Their product is 4·√2 = 4√2. Equivalently, the product equals 2^(t₁+t₂) = 2^(5/2) = 4√2.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: x = 4 and x = √2 give a product of 4√2 = 2^(5/2).
optionAnalysis.B: Keeps only t = 2 and squares it, or multiplies the exponents (2 · 1/2 mishandled) to reach 2³ = 8.
optionAnalysis.C: Keeps only the root t = 1/2, reporting the single solution √2.
optionAnalysis.D: Uses the product of the t-values (2 · 1/2 = 1) as an exponent: 2¹ = 2, misapplying the exponent law.
optionAnalysis.E: Adds the two solutions (4 + √2) instead of multiplying them.

subtopic: Hypergeometric probability without replacement
learningObjective: Compute a probability for sampling without replacement using combinations rather than independent trials.
stem: A box contains 12 electronic components, of which exactly 4 are defective. Three components are drawn at random simultaneously (that is, without replacement). What is the probability that exactly one of the three drawn components is defective?
explanation: Because the draws are simultaneous, use combinations. Favourable outcomes = choosing 1 of the 4 defective and 2 of the 8 good: C(4,1)·C(8,2) = 4·28 = 112. Total outcomes = C(12,3) = 220. Probability = 112/220 = 28/55. Independent-trial (with-replacement) reasoning is invalid here because the composition changes with each draw.

optionAnalysis.A: Uses C(4,1)/C(12,3) = 4/220 = 1/55-type slip, omitting the C(8,2) factor (here rounded to 4/55).
optionAnalysis.B: Halves the favourable count (uses C(8,2)/2 or forgets the factor 2 in a pair count), giving 56/220 = 14/55.
optionAnalysis.D: Treats draws as independent with p = 1/3 defective: 3·(1/3)(2/3)² = 27/64-style with-replacement error.
optionAnalysis.E: Simply reports the defective fraction 4/12 = 1/3, ignoring the 'exactly one of three' condition.

subtopic: Counting real solutions of an absolute-value quadratic equation
learningObjective: Solve an equation containing an absolute value of a quadratic by case analysis and discard extraneous roots.
stem: How many distinct real solutions does the equation |x² − 4| = x + 2 have?
explanation: First, the right side must be non-negative, so x ≥ −2. Case 1 (|x| ≥ 2, where x² − 4 ≥ 0): x² − 4 = x + 2 ⇒ x² − x − 6 = 0 ⇒ x = 3 or x = −2; both satisfy x ≥ −2 and x² − 4 ≥ 0, so both are valid. Case 2 (|x| < 2, where x² − 4 < 0): −(x² − 4) = x + 2 ⇒ x² + x − 2 = 0 ⇒ x = 1 or x = −2; only x = 1 lies in |x| < 2 (x = −2 is a boundary already counted). The distinct valid solutions are x = −2, 1, 3 — three in total.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: valid roots are x = −2, 1, 3, giving three distinct solutions.
optionAnalysis.B: Counts all four algebraic roots (3, −2, 1, −2) without noticing x = −2 repeats and without the x ≥ −2 check.
optionAnalysis.C: Discards x = −2 for wrongly requiring x > −2 (strict), keeping only x = 3 or only x = 1.
optionAnalysis.D: Concludes no solution by assuming |x² − 4| can never equal a linear expression, skipping case analysis.
optionAnalysis.E: Solves only the case x² − 4 = x + 2 (roots 3 and −2), missing the sign-flipped case that yields x = 1.

subtopic: Law of cosines with the circumradius (law of sines)
learningObjective: Integrate the law of cosines and the law of sines to find the circumscribed-circle radius of a triangle.
stem: In triangle ABC the angle at vertex A measures 60°, the side AB = 8 and the side AC = 5. What is the radius of the circle circumscribed about the triangle?
explanation: The side opposite A is BC = a. By the law of cosines, a² = AB² + AC² − 2·AB·AC·cos 60° = 64 + 25 − 2·8·5·(1/2) = 89 − 40 = 49, so a = 7. By the law of sines, 2R = a/sin A = 7/sin 60° = 7/(√3/2) = 14/√3, hence R = 7/√3 = 7√3/3.

optionAnalysis.A: Uses R = a·(√3/2)/... i.e. multiplies by sin A instead of dividing, giving 7√3/2.
optionAnalysis.B: Uses 2R = a/sin A but reports 2R = 14/√3 = 14√3/3 as R, forgetting to halve.
optionAnalysis.C: Divides by an extra factor of 2, using R = a/(4 sin A) and getting 7√3/6.
optionAnalysis.D: Sets R = a/2 = 7/2, forgetting the sin A denominator (treating a as a diameter).
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: a = 7 and R = a/(2 sin A) = 7/√3 = 7√3/3.

subtopic: Exponential equation reducible to a quadratic
learningObjective: Solve an exponential equation by substitution and sum its real solutions.
stem: What is the sum of all real solutions x of the equation 2^(2x) − 5·2^x + 4 = 0 ?
explanation: Let u = 2^x (so u > 0). The equation becomes u² − 5u + 4 = 0, which factors as (u − 1)(u − 4) = 0, giving u = 1 or u = 4. Then 2^x = 1 ⇒ x = 0, and 2^x = 4 ⇒ x = 2. Both are valid (u > 0). The sum of the solutions is 0 + 2 = 2.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 5 is the sum of the roots in u (1 + 4), not the sum of the x-values.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 3 does not correspond to the solution set.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 6 mis-solves 2^x = 4 as x = 4 or similar.
optionAnalysis.D: CORRECT: the solutions are x = 0 and x = 2, summing to 2.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 0 is only one of the two solutions (x = 0), not their sum.

subtopic: Probability of an even product (complement)
learningObjective: Compute the probability of an even product using the complement (all-odd) and combinations.
stem: Two distinct integers are chosen at random from the set {1, 2, 3, …, 10}. What is the probability that their product is even?
explanation: The product is even unless BOTH chosen numbers are odd. There are 5 odd numbers {1,3,5,7,9}, so the number of all-odd pairs is C(5,2) = 10, out of C(10,2) = 45 total pairs. P(product odd) = 10/45 = 2/9, so P(product even) = 1 − 2/9 = 7/9.

optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 5/9 does not follow from the correct count of pairs.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 2/9 is the probability the product is ODD (both numbers odd), i.e. the complement.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 4/9 mis-counts the favourable or total pairs.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 1/2 assumes even/odd are equally likely, ignoring that only an all-odd pair gives an odd product.

subtopic: Sum of an infinite geometric series (repeated-dose steady state)
learningObjective: Model a repeated-dose accumulation process as an infinite geometric series and evaluate its steady-state sum.
stem: A patient is treated with a drug taken as a single 60 mg dose at the same time every day. Over each 24-hour interval the body eliminates 75% of the drug present, so that just before the next dose only 25% of the previous amount remains in the body. Assuming this pattern continues indefinitely, what amount of drug is present in the body immediately after a dose is taken in the long-term (steady) state?
choices: 60 mg
20 mg
80 mg
240 mg
75 mg
explanation: Let L be the amount present immediately after a dose in the steady state. Each day the previous amount decays to 25% of itself, then a fresh 60 mg is added, so at equilibrium L = 60 + 0.25 L. Hence 0.75 L = 60 and L = 80 mg. Equivalently, the doses form an infinite geometric series 60 + 60(0.25) + 60(0.25)^2 + ... with first term 60 and ratio r = 0.25, summing to 60/(1 − 0.25) = 80 mg.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: takes the steady-state level to equal a single dose (60 mg), ignoring the drug carried over from previous doses — i.e. omitting the accumulation entirely.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: reports the trough level just before the next dose (0.25 × 80 = 20 mg), misreading 'immediately after' as 'immediately before'.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: at equilibrium L = 60 + 0.25L gives L = 60/(1 − 0.25) = 80 mg, the sum of the infinite geometric series with a = 60, r = 0.25.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: uses the eliminated fraction r = 0.75 instead of the retained fraction 0.25 in the sum, giving 60/(1 − 0.75) = 240 mg.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: adds only the first two doses (60 + 0.25×60 = 75 mg), truncating the geometric series after two terms instead of summing it to its limit.

subtopic: Vieta's formulas: sum of squares of the roots of a cubic
learningObjective: Apply Vieta's formulas to evaluate a symmetric function (the sum of the squares) of the roots of a cubic without solving it.
stem: Let p, q and r be the three roots (real or complex) of the cubic equation 2x^3 − 3x^2 + 4x − 5 = 0. What is the value of p^2 + q^2 + r^2?
explanation: For 2x^3 − 3x^2 + 4x − 5 = 0, Vieta's formulas give p + q + r = 3/2, pq + pr + qr = 4/2 = 2, and pqr = 5/2. Using the identity p^2 + q^2 + r^2 = (p + q + r)^2 − 2(pq + pr + qr) = (3/2)^2 − 2(2) = 9/4 − 4 = −7/4. (The value is negative because two of the roots are complex conjugates; the symmetric function is nonetheless real.)

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: computes only (p + q + r)^2 = (3/2)^2 = 9/4, forgetting to subtract the 2(pq + pr + qr) term.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: divides only the sum of roots by the leading coefficient but forgets to divide the pairwise sum, giving (3/2)^2 − 2(4) = −23/4.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: p^2 + q^2 + r^2 = (3/2)^2 − 2(2) = 9/4 − 4 = −7/4, applying Vieta's formulas with the leading coefficient 2.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: reads the coefficients directly as the symmetric sums (sum = 3, pairwise sum = 4), ignoring the leading coefficient 2, giving 3^2 − 2×4 = 1.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: uses the wrong sign, (p + q + r)^2 + 2(pq + pr + qr) = 9/4 + 4 = 25/4, adding rather than subtracting the pairwise term.

subtopic: Rational inequality solved by sign analysis
learningObjective: Solve a rational inequality by collecting terms on one side and analysing the sign of the resulting quotient, respecting domain restrictions.
stem: Determine the complete solution set of the inequality (2x − 1)/(x + 3) ≥ 1.
explanation: Move everything to one side: (2x − 1)/(x + 3) − 1 ≥ 0, i.e. (2x − 1 − (x + 3))/(x + 3) ≥ 0, which simplifies to (x − 4)/(x + 3) ≥ 0. The critical values are x = 4 (numerator zero, included) and x = −3 (denominator zero, excluded). A sign chart shows the quotient is positive for x < −3 and for x > 4, and equals 0 at x = 4. Hence the solution set is (−∞, −3) ∪ [4, +∞).

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: multiplies both sides by (x + 3) as if it were always positive, obtaining 2x − 1 ≥ x + 3 → x ≥ 4, and loses the branch where the denominator is negative.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: includes x = −3, but there the denominator is zero and the expression is undefined, so −3 must be excluded.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: rearranging gives (x − 4)/(x + 3) ≥ 0; the quotient is non-negative for x < −3 or x ≥ 4, so the solution is (−∞, −3) ∪ [4, +∞).
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: excludes x = 4, but the inequality is non-strict (≥) and the numerator (x − 4) is zero there, so x = 4 must be included.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: selects the interval between the critical values, where the quotient is actually negative — the sign of the quotient has been reversed.

subtopic: System of exponential equations via common-base exponents
learningObjective: Solve a system of exponential equations by rewriting each term to a common base and equating exponents to form and solve a linear system.
stem: Real numbers x and y satisfy the system: 2^x · 8^y = 2^11 and 9^x / 3^y = 3. What is the value of x + y?
explanation: Rewrite with common bases. First equation: 2^x · 2^(3y) = 2^(x + 3y) = 2^11, so x + 3y = 11. Second equation: 3^(2x) / 3^y = 3^(2x − y) = 3^1, so 2x − y = 1. From the second, y = 2x − 1; substituting: x + 3(2x − 1) = 11 → 7x − 3 = 11 → x = 2, and then y = 3. Therefore x + y = 5.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: treats 8^y as 2^y (dropping the exponent 3 in 8 = 2^3), so the first equation reads x + y = 11 directly.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: rewriting to bases 2 and 3 gives x + 3y = 11 and 2x − y = 1, whose solution is x = 2, y = 3, so x + y = 5.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: solves the system correctly to x = 2, y = 3 but reports x alone instead of the requested sum x + y.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: simply adds the two right-hand exponents (11 from 2^11 and 1 from 3^1) to get 12, without solving the system.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: treats 9^x as 3^x (dropping the exponent 2 in 9 = 3^2), giving the second equation as x − y = 1 and hence x + y = 6.

subtopic: Interplay of arithmetic and geometric progressions
learningObjective: Combine the defining conditions of arithmetic and geometric progressions to determine an unknown common ratio.
stem: In an arithmetic progression with non-zero common difference, the first term is 3, and the first, second and fifth terms are (in that order) three consecutive terms of a geometric progression. What is the common ratio of that geometric progression?
explanation: Let the arithmetic progression have first term a = 3 and common difference d. The first, second and fifth terms are a, a + d and a + 4d. For these to be consecutive terms of a geometric progression, (a + d)^2 = a(a + 4d). Expanding: a^2 + 2ad + d^2 = a^2 + 4ad, so d^2 − 2ad = 0, i.e. d(d − 2a) = 0. Since d ≠ 0, d = 2a = 6. The three geometric terms are 3, 9, 27, so the common ratio is 27/9 = 9/3 = 3.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: computes d/a = 6/3 = 2, confusing the relationship between the common difference and the first term with the geometric common ratio.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: the geometric condition gives d = 6, producing terms 3, 9, 27 with common ratio 9/3 = 3.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: inverts the ratio, dividing an earlier term by a later one (3/9) instead of a later term by an earlier one.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: reports the second geometric term (a + d = 9) itself rather than the ratio between successive terms.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: reports the common difference d = 6 of the arithmetic progression instead of the common ratio of the geometric progression.

subtopic: Infinite geometric series: sum and sum of squares
learningObjective: Set up and solve simultaneous equations from the sum and the sum of squares of an infinite geometric series.
stem: An infinite geometric series has first term a and common ratio r with |r| < 1. The sum of the series is 9, and the sum of the squares of its terms is 40.5. What is the value of the common ratio r?
explanation: The sum of the series is a/(1 − r) = 9. The squares of the terms form a geometric series with first term a² and ratio r², so their sum is a²/(1 − r²) = 40.5. Substituting a = 9(1 − r) into the second equation: [9(1 − r)]²/(1 − r²) = 81(1 − r)²/[(1 − r)(1 + r)] = 81(1 − r)/(1 + r) = 40.5. Hence (1 − r)/(1 + r) = 0.5, giving 1 − r = 0.5 + 0.5r, so 1.5r = 0.5 and r = 1/3. (Check: a = 6, sum = 6/(2/3) = 9; sum of squares = 36/(8/9) = 40.5.)

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 1/9 confuses r with r² or misreads the ratio of the two sums.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: r = 1/4 comes from mishandling the 1 − r² factorisation (e.g. treating it as (1 − r)²).
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: r = 2/3 makes the terms fall off too slowly; the sum of squares would exceed 40.5.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: r = 1/2 gives (1 − r)/(1 + r) = (1/2)/(3/2) = 1/3, not 0.5, so the sum of squares would not be 40.5.

subtopic: Power of a point: tangent–secant relationship from an external point
learningObjective: Apply the power-of-a-point (tangent–secant) theorem to relate a tangent length to a secant line and extract the interior chord.
stem: From a point P outside a circular pond, a straight walkway PT of length 8 m runs to the point T where it just touches (is tangent to) the edge of the pond. A second straight walkway from P crosses the pond, meeting the edge first at A and then at B, with PA = 4 m. What is the length AB, the distance across the pond along this walkway?
choices: 8 m
explanation: For a tangent PT and a secant through A and B drawn from the same external point P, the power of the point gives PT² = PA·PB. Thus 8² = 4·PB, so PB = 64/4 = 16 m. AB is the chord between the two intersection points: AB = PB − PA = 16 − 4 = 12 m.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: gives PB, the full distance from P to the far edge (or applies PT² = PA·AB), forgetting that AB is measured from A, so the external segment PA must be subtracted.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: PT² = PA·PB gives PB = 16 m, hence the chord AB = PB − PA = 12 m.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: adds PA + PB = 4 + 16, treating the answer as the total secant path from P through B.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: takes the arithmetic mean of PA and PB, (4 + 16)/2 = 10, with no geometric justification.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: reports the tangent length PT (8 m) itself as the chord, ignoring the power-of-a-point relation entirely.

subtopic: Length of a chord cut on a circle by a line via the perpendicular distance from the centre
learningObjective: Determine the length of a chord cut on a circle by a line using the perpendicular distance from the centre and the Pythagorean relationship.
stem: A circle has equation x² + y² − 2x − 4y − 20 = 0. Find the length of the chord that the line 3x + 4y = 26 cuts on this circle.
explanation: Completing the square gives (x − 1)² + (y − 2)² = 25, so the centre is (1, 2) and the radius r = 5. The perpendicular distance from the centre to the line 3x + 4y − 26 = 0 is |3(1) + 4(2) − 26|/√(3² + 4²) = |−15|/5 = 3. The half-chord is √(r² − d²) = √(25 − 9) = 4, so the full chord length is 2 × 4 = 8.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: returns the half-chord √(r² − d²) = 4, forgetting to double it to obtain the full chord.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: assumes the line passes through the centre and returns the diameter, 2r = 10.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: computes 2√(r² + d²), adding d² instead of subtracting it in the Pythagorean step.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: uses 2d = 6, mistaking twice the centre-to-line distance for the chord length.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: chord = 2√(r² − d²) = 2√(25 − 9) = 8.

subtopic: Trigonometric equation via the double-angle identity
learningObjective: Solve a trigonometric equation by reducing a double-angle term to a quadratic in cosine and count all solutions on a given interval.
stem: Determine the number of values of x in the interval [0, 2π) that satisfy cos 2x + cos x = 0.
explanation: Using cos 2x = 2cos²x − 1, the equation becomes 2cos²x + cos x − 1 = 0, which factors as (2cos x − 1)(cos x + 1) = 0. So cos x = 1/2 or cos x = −1. On [0, 2π), cos x = 1/2 gives x = π/3 and x = 5π/3, while cos x = −1 gives x = π. That is three solutions in total.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: the roots are x = π/3, x = π, and x = 5π/3 — three solutions.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: mis-expands cos 2x (mixing 1 − 2sin²x with cos terms) and picks up an extra spurious root.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: keeps only one factor (e.g. cos x = 1/2), overlooking the cos x = −1 branch.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: counts cos x = −1 as producing two solutions in the interval, whereas it yields only x = π.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: counts every root of the quadratic in cos over a doubled range such as 0 ≤ x < 4π.

subtopic: Combining the area formula with the cosine rule; selecting the obtuse-angle case
learningObjective: Integrate the triangle area formula with the cosine rule, selecting the correct obtuse-angle solution to determine a side.
stem: In triangle ABC, AB = 8, AC = 5, and the area of the triangle is 10. Given that angle A is obtuse, find BC².
explanation: Area = ½·AB·AC·sin A = ½·8·5·sin A = 20 sin A = 10, so sin A = 1/2. Since A is obtuse, A = 150° and cos A = −√3/2. By the cosine rule, BC² = AB² + AC² − 2·AB·AC·cos A = 64 + 25 − 2·8·5·(−√3/2) = 89 + 40√3.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: uses the acute solution A = 30° (cos A = +√3/2), giving 89 − 40√3, and so ignores the stated condition that A is obtuse.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: sets cos A = −1/2, confusing the value of sin A with cos A; this gives 89 + 2·40·(1/2) = 129.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: with cos A = −√3/2, BC² = 89 + 40√3.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: omits the −2·AB·AC·cos A term (equivalently treats A as 90°), leaving just 64 + 25 = 89.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: drops the factor of 2, using AB·AC·cos A instead of 2·AB·AC·cos A, giving 89 + 20√3.

subtopic: Radius of a sphere inscribed in a right circular cone via the inradius of the axial cross-section
learningObjective: Find the radius of a sphere inscribed in a cone by identifying it with the inradius of the axial cross-sectional triangle.
stem: A right circular cone has base radius 5 cm and vertical height 12 cm. A sphere is inscribed in the cone so that it touches the base and the entire lateral surface. What is the radius of the sphere?
choices: 5/2 cm
5/3 cm
explanation: The slant height is √(5² + 12²) = 13 cm. Cutting the cone through its axis gives an isosceles triangle with base 2R = 10, two equal sides of 13, and height 12. The inscribed sphere's radius equals the inradius of this triangle: r = Area / semiperimeter = (½·10·12) / ((10 + 13 + 13)/2) = 60/18 = 10/3 cm.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: takes half the base radius, R/2 = 5/2, wrongly assuming the sphere spans half the base width.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: divides the cross-section area by the full perimeter instead of the semiperimeter, 60/36 = 5/3.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: uses Rh/(R + h) = 60/17, substituting the vertical height for the slant length in the tangency relation.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: uses Rh/L = 60/13, an incorrect similar-triangle ratio.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: the sphere's radius is the inradius of the axial section, 60/18 = 10/3 cm.

subtopic: Circles tangent to both coordinate axes through a fixed point; two-solution locus
learningObjective: Model a circle tangent to both coordinate axes with centre (r, r), solve the resulting quadratic, and compute the distance between the two solution centres.
stem: In the coordinate plane, a circle lies in the first quadrant, is tangent to both the x-axis and the y-axis, and passes through the point (2, 1). Two such circles exist. What is the distance between their centres?
explanation: A circle in the first quadrant tangent to both axes has centre (r, r) and radius r. Passing through (2, 1): (2 − r)² + (1 − r)² = r². Expanding gives r² − 6r + 5 = 0, so r = 1 or r = 5. The centres are (1, 1) and (5, 5), and the distance between them is √((5 − 1)² + (5 − 1)²) = √32 = 4√2.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: mis-solves the quadratic as r = 1, 3, placing centres at (1, 1) and (3, 3) and giving 2√2.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: places the centres at (0, 0) and (6, 6) (radii mis-added into the coordinates), giving 6√2.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: distance = √(4² + 4²) = 4√2.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: takes only one coordinate difference, 5 − 1 = 4, ignoring the second dimension of the distance.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: adds the two radii, 1 + 5 = 6, instead of finding the distance between the centres.

subtopic: Expected value of a discrete random variable: fair price of a prize-draw ticket
learningObjective: Compute the expected value of a discrete random variable and use it to determine the mathematically fair price of a lottery or prize-draw ticket.
stem: A charity organises a prize draw with 200 numbered tickets, each equally likely to be drawn. The prizes are: one prize worth €300, four prizes worth €50 each, and ten prizes worth €10 each; every remaining ticket wins nothing, and no single ticket can win more than one prize. The organisers wish to set the ticket price equal to the expected winnings of a single ticket (a mathematically 'fair' price). What price should they charge per ticket?
explanation: The expected winnings of one ticket is the sum of each prize value multiplied by the probability that this ticket wins it. Each ticket has probability 1/200 of being the one drawn for any particular prize, so E = 300·(1/200) + 50·(4/200) + 10·(10/200) = 1.50 + 1.00 + 0.50 = €3.00. Equivalently, the total prize money (300 + 4·50 + 10·10 = €600) shared over the 200 tickets gives 600/200 = €3.00. The fair price is €3.00.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: divides the €600 total prize money by the number of prizes (15) instead of the number of tickets (200), confusing the average prize won by a winner with the expected value of an arbitrary ticket.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: counts only the €300 grand prize (300/200 = 1.50) and ignores the €50 and €10 prizes — the expected value must sum the contribution of every prize, not just the largest.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: includes the grand prize and the four €50 prizes ((300 + 200)/200 = 2.50) but forgets the ten €10 prizes; all prize tiers contribute to the expected value.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: E = 300·(1/200) + 50·(4/200) + 10·(10/200) = 1.50 + 1.00 + 0.50 = €3.00, equal to the €600 total prize money divided by 200 tickets.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: divides the €600 total prize money by 100 rather than by the 200 tickets — a misreading of the number of tickets in the draw.

subtopic: Permutations of a multiset with a non-adjacency restriction (gap method with identical letters)
learningObjective: Count arrangements of a multiset subject to a non-adjacency restriction using the gap (slot) method, applying a combination rather than a permutation for identical objects.
stem: The seven letters A, A, A, B, C, D, E are arranged in a row to form strings (the three A's are identical to one another, so two strings are the same if they read identically). In how many of these arrangements are no two A's adjacent to one another?
explanation: First arrange the four distinct non-A letters B, C, D, E in a row: 4! = 24 ways. These four letters create five gaps (one before, three between, one after) into which A's may be placed. To keep the A's apart, place at most one A in each gap, so choose 3 of the 5 gaps; because the A's are identical this is a combination, C(5,3) = 10. Total = 24 × 10 = 240.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 5! = 120 treats the three A's as a single block 'AAA', giving five items to arrange — this counts arrangements where the A's are all together, the exact opposite of the requirement.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 840 = 7!/3! is the total number of distinguishable arrangements with no restriction at all, ignoring the non-adjacency condition.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: 4! ways to arrange B, C, D, E (=24) times C(5,3) ways to place the three identical A's in the five gaps (=10) gives 24 × 10 = 240.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 1440 = 24 × P(5,3) treats the three identical A's as distinguishable, using the permutation P(5,3) = 60 instead of the combination C(5,3) = 10.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 600 is the complementary count (arrangements in which at least two A's are adjacent), obtained as 840 − 240; the question asks for the non-adjacent arrangements themselves.

subtopic: Bayes' theorem: posterior probability of the source given a defective item
learningObjective: Apply the law of total probability and Bayes' theorem to compute the posterior probability of a source given observed evidence.
stem: A workshop assembles a component using two machines. Machine X assembles 60% of the components and 2% of its output is defective; Machine Y assembles the remaining 40% and 5% of its output is defective. A finished component is selected at random from the combined output and found to be defective. What is the probability that it was assembled by Machine Y?
explanation: By the law of total probability, P(defective) = 0.60·0.02 + 0.40·0.05 = 0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032. By Bayes' theorem, P(Y | defective) = P(Y and defective)/P(defective) = 0.020/0.032 = 0.625.

optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 0.400 is the prior P(Y); it ignores the defective evidence entirely instead of updating on it.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 0.050 is P(defective | Y), the defect rate of Machine Y; this inverts the conditional, confusing P(Y | defective) with P(defective | Y).
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 0.375 = 0.012/0.032 is P(X | defective), the posterior for the other machine; the question asks for Machine Y.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 0.020 is the joint probability P(Y and defective); it omits the final step of dividing by P(defective) to normalise.

subtopic: Binomial distribution: cumulative 'at least k' probability under random guessing
learningObjective: Model repeated independent trials with the binomial distribution and compute a cumulative 'at least k' probability by summing the relevant terms.
stem: A multiple-choice quiz has 5 questions, each with 4 answer options exactly one of which is correct. A student who has not studied answers every question by guessing independently at random. The quiz is passed only by answering at least 4 of the 5 questions correctly. What is the probability that this student passes?

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 1/256 = (1/4)^4 drops the binomial coefficient C(5,4) and the fifth question's factor, treating 'four correct' as a single fixed outcome.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 1/1024 = (1/4)^5 counts only the all-five-correct outcome and omits the exactly-four-correct case, which also passes.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 15/1024 counts only P(X=4) and omits P(X=5); passing requires 'at least 4', so both cases must be added.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 3/16 comes from using p = 1/2 (as if each question had two options): P(X≥4) with p=1/2 = (5+1)/32 = 6/32 = 3/16; here each question has four options, so p = 1/4.

subtopic: Derangements: probability of exactly one fixed point in a random permutation
learningObjective: Combine a combination with a derangement count to find the probability of exactly one fixed point in a uniformly random permutation.
stem: In a class, five students each hand in a homework sheet labelled with their own name. The teacher shuffles the five sheets thoroughly and returns them at random, one to each student, with every ordering equally likely. What is the probability that exactly one student receives their own sheet?
explanation: There are 5! = 120 equally likely orderings. For exactly one fixed point, first choose which student gets their own sheet: C(5,1) = 5 ways. The remaining four sheets must all go to the wrong students, i.e. be a derangement of 4 objects, and the number of such derangements is D₄ = 9. So the count is 5 × 9 = 45, giving probability 45/120 = 3/8.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 1/5 treats 'exactly one of five' as a plain 1-in-5 chance, ignoring the requirement that the remaining four sheets must all be misplaced.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 1/3 = 40/120 uses an incorrect derangement count D₄ = 8 instead of the correct 9, so (5 × 8)/120 = 1/3.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 3/40 = 9/120 = D₄/5! omits the factor C(5,1) for choosing which of the five students is the one fixed point.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: choose the single fixed student (C(5,1) = 5) and derange the other four (D₄ = 9): (5 × 9)/120 = 45/120 = 3/8.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 11/30 = 44/120 = D₅/5! is the probability that NO student receives their own sheet (a full derangement), which is a different event.

subtopic: Hypergeometric probability: exactly k successes without replacement
learningObjective: Compute the probability of exactly k successes in draws without replacement using combinations.
stem: A bag contains 4 red marbles and 6 blue marbles, identical apart from colour. Three marbles are drawn at random, all at once (without replacement). What is the probability that exactly two of the three drawn marbles are red?
explanation: Choosing 3 marbles from 10 can be done in C(10,3) = 120 equally likely ways. 'Exactly two red' means choosing 2 of the 4 red marbles and 1 of the 6 blue marbles: C(4,2) × C(6,1) = 6 × 6 = 36. The probability is 36/120 = 3/10.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 1/5 = 24/120 miscounts the favourable outcomes (e.g. C(4,2)×C(6,1) done incorrectly).
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 1/6 treats the draws as if order mattered or uses the wrong denominator.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 2/5 = 48/120 over-counts the favourable selections.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 3/5 is far too large and corresponds to no correct combination count.

subtopic: Exponential growth: fitting y = y0·e^(kt) to two data points and back-extrapolating the initial value
learningObjective: Fit an exponential model to two measured data points and use it to recover an unknown initial value by back-extrapolation.
stem: A microbiologist models the mass m (in grams) of a bacterial culture by m(t) = m0·e^(kt), where t is the time in hours after the start of the experiment and m0 and k are positive constants. The mass is measured as 3 g when t = 2 h and as 24 g when t = 5 h. What was the mass m0 of the culture at the start of the experiment (t = 0)?
choices: 6 g
explanation: Dividing the two readings eliminates m0: m(5)/m(2) = 24/3 = 8 = e^(k(5-2)) = e^(3k), so e^(3k) = 8 and therefore e^k = 2 (the culture doubles each hour). To go back from t = 2 to t = 0 requires dividing by two factors of e^k: m0 = m(2)/e^(2k) = 3/(e^k)^2 = 3/2^2 = 3/4 = 0.75 g. (Check: m0·e^(5k) = 0.75·32 = 24 g.)

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 3/2 = 1.5. Having found e^k = 2, the candidate divided the t = 2 reading by only a single factor of e^k, back-extrapolating one hour instead of the required two hours.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 3 × 2 = 6. The candidate reversed the direction for one step, multiplying by the growth factor when going backwards in time instead of dividing.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 3/8 = 0.375. The candidate stepped back from t = 2 to t = 0 using the 3-hour growth factor e^(3k) = 8 instead of the correct 2-hour factor e^(2k) = 4 — mismatching the interval length with its growth factor.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: e^(3k) = 8 gives e^k = 2, and stepping back two hours divides by e^(2k) = 4, so m0 = 3/4 = 0.75 g.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 3 × 4 = 12. The candidate multiplied by e^(2k) = 4 instead of dividing by it, applying the growth factor in the wrong direction over the whole interval.

subtopic: Factor and remainder theorems: determining coefficients from two conditions and locating the remaining root
learningObjective: Use the remainder and factor theorems to set up and solve for unknown coefficients, then factorise a cubic to identify its remaining root.
stem: The cubic polynomial p(x) = 2x^3 + ax^2 + bx - 3 has real coefficients a and b. When p(x) is divided by (x - 1) the remainder is -4, and (x + 1) is a factor of p(x). Given these two conditions, find the root of the equation p(x) = 0 that is different from x = -1.
explanation: Remainder theorem: p(1) = 2 + a + b - 3 = -4, so a + b = -3. Factor theorem: p(-1) = -2 + a - b - 3 = 0, so a - b = 5. Solving gives a = 1, b = -4, hence p(x) = 2x^3 + x^2 - 4x - 3. Dividing by the known factor (x + 1): p(x) = (x + 1)(2x^2 - x - 3) = (x + 1)(x + 1)(2x - 3) = (x + 1)^2(2x - 3). The roots are x = -1 (repeated) and 2x - 3 = 0, i.e. x = 3/2.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 1. The candidate misused the remainder theorem, treating the division point x = 1 as though the remainder -4 still identified it as a root of p(x).
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: -3/2. The candidate read the remaining linear factor as (2x + 3) rather than (2x - 3), a sign slip on the constant term of the quotient.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: solving the two conditions gives a = 1, b = -4 and p(x) = (x + 1)^2(2x - 3), whose non-(-1) root is x = 3/2.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 1/2. The candidate mis-derived the quotient's linear factor as (2x - 1) — typically from an arithmetic error in b — and solved 2x - 1 = 0.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 3. The candidate obtained the factor 2x - 3 correctly but solved it as x = 3, failing to divide by the leading coefficient 2.

subtopic: Vieta's relations: constructing a quadratic whose roots are the squares of the original roots
learningObjective: Apply the sum and product of the roots of a quadratic to construct a new quadratic whose roots are a symmetric transformation of the original roots.
stem: The equation x^2 - 6x + 7 = 0 has roots alpha and beta. Without solving for alpha and beta individually, find the monic quadratic equation whose roots are alpha^2 and beta^2.
explanation: By Vieta's formulas, alpha + beta = 6 and alpha·beta = 7. The new roots are alpha^2 and beta^2. Their sum is alpha^2 + beta^2 = (alpha + beta)^2 - 2·alpha·beta = 36 - 14 = 22, and their product is (alpha·beta)^2 = 49. A monic quadratic with roots summing to S and multiplying to P is x^2 - Sx + P = 0, giving x^2 - 22x + 49 = 0.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: the candidate forgot that the linear coefficient is minus the sum of the roots, writing +22x instead of -22x.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: the candidate used (alpha + beta)^2 = 36 directly as alpha^2 + beta^2, omitting the -2·alpha·beta correction term.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: the correct coefficients but a sign error on the product term; the product of the squared roots is (alpha·beta)^2 = +49, not -49.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: sum of new roots = 36 - 14 = 22 and product = 7^2 = 49, so the quadratic is x^2 - 22x + 49 = 0.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: the candidate computed alpha^2 + beta^2 = (alpha + beta)^2 + 2·alpha·beta = 36 + 14 = 50, taking the sign of the 2·alpha·beta term as positive.

subtopic: Recovering an unknown outer function from a given composition, then evaluating its inverse
learningObjective: Recover an unknown function from a stated composition and then evaluate that function's inverse at a given value.
stem: The functions f and g are defined for all real numbers. It is given that f(x) = 3x - 2 and that the composite function (g o f)(x) = g(f(x)) = 6x + 1 for all x. Determine the value of g^(-1)(4).
explanation: First recover g. Since g(f(x)) = g(3x - 2) = 6x + 1, substitute u = 3x - 2, so x = (u + 2)/3. Then g(u) = 6·(u + 2)/3 + 1 = 2(u + 2) + 1 = 2u + 5, i.e. g(x) = 2x + 5. To find g^(-1)(4), solve g(x) = 4: 2x + 5 = 4, so 2x = -1 and x = -1/2. Hence g^(-1)(4) = -1/2.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 2. The candidate inverted the wrong function, computing f^(-1)(4) = (4 + 2)/3 = 2 instead of g^(-1)(4).
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 13. The candidate evaluated the function g(4) = 2·4 + 5 = 13 instead of its inverse.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: g is recovered as g(x) = 2x + 5, and solving 2x + 5 = 4 gives g^(-1)(4) = -1/2.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 9/2. The candidate found g(x) = 2x + 5 correctly but made a sign error solving 2x + 5 = 4, writing 2x = 4 + 5 = 9.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 1/2. The candidate ignored the inner function f and treated the composition itself as g, taking g(x) = 6x + 1 and computing (4 - 1)/6 = 1/2.

subtopic: Vieta's formulas: symmetric function of the roots of a cubic
learningObjective: Use Vieta's relations to evaluate a symmetric function (sum of reciprocals) of the roots of a cubic without finding the roots.
stem: The cubic equation x³ − 7x² + 14x − 8 = 0 has three real roots a, b and c. What is the value of 1/a + 1/b + 1/c?
explanation: By Vieta's formulas for x³ − 7x² + 14x − 8 = 0: a+b+c = 7, ab+bc+ca = 14, and abc = 8. The sum of the reciprocals is 1/a + 1/b + 1/c = (bc + ca + ab)/(abc) = 14/8 = 7/4. (Indeed the roots are 1, 2 and 4, whose reciprocals sum to 1 + 0.5 + 0.25 = 1.75 = 14/8.)

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: (ab+bc+ca)/(abc) = 14/8 = 7/4.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 7/14 uses (a+b+c)/(ab+bc+ca), which is not the sum of reciprocals.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 7/8 uses (a+b+c)/(abc) instead of (ab+bc+ca)/(abc); the numerator for the sum of reciprocals is the sum of pairwise products.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 1/8 is 1/(abc), the reciprocal of the product of the roots, not the sum of their reciprocals.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 8/7 inverts the correct ratio (abc over the pairwise-product sum).

subtopic: Inverse of a rational (Möbius) function
learningObjective: Find the inverse of a rational function by solving y = f(x) for x.
stem: The function f is defined by f(x) = (2x + 1)/(x − 3) for all real x ≠ 3. Which of the following is its inverse function f⁻¹(x)?
explanation: Set y = (2x + 1)/(x − 3) and solve for x. Then y(x − 3) = 2x + 1 ⇒ yx − 3y = 2x + 1 ⇒ yx − 2x = 3y + 1 ⇒ x(y − 2) = 3y + 1 ⇒ x = (3y + 1)/(y − 2). Renaming the variable, f⁻¹(x) = (3x + 1)/(x − 2). (Check: substituting back into f returns x.)

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: (x+3)/(2x−1) does not result from correctly isolating x.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: solving y = (2x+1)/(x−3) for x gives x = (3y+1)/(y−2), so f⁻¹(x) = (3x+1)/(x−2).
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: (2x+1)/(x+3) merely changes a sign in the denominator; it is not obtained by solving y = f(x) for x.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: (3x−1)/(x+2) has sign errors from mishandling the rearrangement.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: (x−3)/(2x+1) is the reciprocal of f(x), not its inverse function.

subtopic: Half-life: expressing a threshold as a power of one half to count half-lives and find an elapsed time
learningObjective: Convert a remaining-amount threshold into a power of 1/2, count the number of half-lives, and translate this into elapsed time.
stem: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 8 hours. A freshly prepared sample contains 240 mg of the isotope. A measurement using the sample is regarded as valid only while at least 7.5 mg of the isotope remains. What is the greatest whole number of hours after preparation at which a measurement is still valid?
choices: 24 hours
32 hours
48 hours
80 hours
40 hours
explanation: The remaining fraction at the threshold is 7.5/240 = 1/32 = (1/2)^5, so exactly 5 half-lives must elapse to reach 7.5 mg. Each half-life is 8 hours, so this occurs at 5 x 8 = 40 hours. At t = 40 h the mass is exactly 7.5 mg, which still satisfies 'at least 7.5 mg', so the measurement remains valid; only after 40 h does it fall below the threshold. The greatest whole number of hours at which it is still valid is therefore 40.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: mis-simplifies the ratio 7.5/240 to 1/8 = (1/2)^3, obtaining 3 half-lives and 3 x 8 = 24 hours.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: off-by-one interval count. Listing the reduced masses 120, 60, 30, 15, 7.5 gives five numbers but the student counts only 4 halving steps (4 x 8 = 32); 32 is also seductive because it equals the denominator of the fraction 1/32.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: the student counts one half-life too many (6 half-lives, halving on to 3.75 mg) and computes 6 x 8 = 48 hours, overshooting the threshold.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: uses the wrong duration per half-life (treats it as 16 hours) or reads 240/7.5 as a time, giving 80; confuses the half-life value with a doubling/quantity relationship.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: 7.5/240 = 1/32 = (1/2)^5 gives 5 half-lives, and 5 x 8 = 40 hours, at which the mass is exactly at (not below) the threshold.
